name: Minnesota Reformer
title: What Angie Craig’s most controversial vote says about her
description: U.S. Rep. Angie Craig regrets that she didn’t see it coming: thousands of masked federal agents flooding American streets, arresting law-abiding immigrants without warrants and packing them in disease-ridden detention centers. If she had, she said she would not have voted for the Laken Riley Act, the first piece of legislation President Donald Trump signed [[...]
text:
Rep. Angie Craig talks to Haven Watch volunteers as a black SUV drives by after she conducted an inspection in the Henry Whipple Federal Building in Minneapolis to conduct an inspection Thursday, April 9, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)U.S. Rep. Angie Craig regrets that she didn’t see it coming: thousands of masked federal agents flooding American streets, arresting law-abiding immigrants without warrants and packing them in disease-ridden detention centers.
If she had, she said she would not have voted for the Laken Riley Act, the first piece of legislation President Donald Trump signed in his second term, mandating the detention of undocumented immigrants accused of theft, assault of law enforcement and certain other crimes.
That vote has become perhaps her greatest liability in her tough Democratic primary for U.S. Senate against Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan — another thing Craig didn’t see coming — as she seeks the support of voters disgusted by Trump’s violent immigration crackdown in Minnesota that left two Americans dead.
Craig is now campaigning on her record fighting Trump and standing up to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement by helping introduce articles of impeachment against former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, conducting oversight of ICE facilities and trying to free detained constituents.
“My regret to give them a f***ing inch does drive my commitment to making sure that the Trump administration pays for what they’ve done,” Craig said in an interview with the Reformer. “I will spend the rest of my career ensuring that my immigrant neighbors are able to be part of the fabric of America.”
But Flanagan and a wave of high-profile progressive surrogates — including Sens. Bernie Sanders and Tina Smith — say the Laken Riley vote isn’t an anomaly. It’s part of a pattern of Craig voting for self-preservation over principles, for the corporate and special interest donors pumping millions into her campaign over the working people she promises to fight for.
“AIPAC, crypto, health insurance companies, billionaires, and special interests … these powerful interests are coming together behind Angie Craig,” Flanagan said at a recent rally headlined by Sanders. “It begs the question: Who is she fighting for?”
Swing votes from a swing district
Craig, whose face betrays an almost constant intensity, can point to a biography and political career of fighting, scrapping — and winning. She grew up with a single mother in a rural Arkansas trailer park, put herself through college and rose to become an executive at a major medical device company.
She fought for custody of her first son in the late 1990s in Tennessee when gay parents couldn’t both be recognized as the adoptive parents. She won, helping pave the way for other gay parents in the state. She raised four sons and in 2018 became the first openly lesbian mother elected to Congress — beating an incumbent Republican who had just several years earlier openly opposed same-sex marriage and mused that gay parents could be harmful to children.
Rep. Angie Craig meets with veterans for a roundtable discussion at the Uptown VFW Friday, July 17, 2026 in Minneapolis. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)
Craig has been ranked among the 20% most bipartisan lawmakers by the nonpartisan Lugar Center, based on how often she has co-sponsored legislation with Republicans, a fact she’s touted to hold her seat in the competitive 2nd Congressional District.
Craig has also voted with Democrats the vast majority of the time — 96% this term, according to UCLA’s Voteview — although Flanagan frames it as voting with Trump more than any other Minnesota Democrat given the high party fidelity in Congress.
Despite the campaign’s acrimony, Craig and Flanagan agree on almost everything — if not in degree, then at least in direction: banning corporate campaign contributions, expanding the Supreme Court, allowing Medicare to negotiate drug prices, making it easier for workers to unionize, providing undocumented immigrants a path to legal status, eliminating taxes on Social Security.
But the rarer votes in which she broke with Democrats are now coming back to haunt her — an unusual position for someone seeking statewide office, which often requires candidates to move to the middle to appeal to more voters.
“As a swing-district Democrat, I tried really hard to represent the people in my district, and as a U.S. senator, I would have a broader audience to consider,” Craig said.
Formidable fundraiser or corporate captive?
She’s been able to market herself to Democrats statewide with one of the most impressive fundraising performances in state history, and the help of outside groups spending on her behalf — a double-edged sword given the widespread mistrust of corporate influence among Minnesota Democrats.
The primary could be the most expensive in state history. Craig has raised $12 million for her campaign compared with Flanagan’s $6 million. The main super PAC backing Craig, North Star Dawn, has spent more than $18 million in support of her campaign with spending by other groups likely to bring the total over $20 million. The main PAC backing Flanagan, the Democratic Lieutenant Governors Association, has spent about $2 million to support Flanagan with ads attacking Craig.
Flanagan’s criticism over campaign contributions aims to turn one of Craig’s assets — a formidable war chest to beat a Republican in the general election like the well-known and well-funded Michele Tafoya — into another liability in the primary.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Flanagan points to Craig’s vote for the GENIUS Act, widely seen as a victory for the volatile cryptocurrency industry, after a crypto-aligned super PAC spent about $1 million backing her 2024 congressional campaign.
Craig says that as ranking member of the House Agriculture Committee, which oversees the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, she had no choice but “to be involved in this space.” She said she supports stricter guardrails, but that doing nothing was “not an answer.”
Flanagan also points to Craig’s votes to send weapons to Israel and the hundreds of thousands of dollars in support her congressional campaigns have received from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee — now a scarlet letter among many Democrats. While Craig said she hasn’t taken money from the group in her Senate race, AIPAC did hold about a dozen campaign events for her since she announced her bid last year, according to MinnPost.
Most recently she voted against a proposal to cut $3.3 billion in aid to Israel. She was the only Minnesota Democrat to vote against it, with Reps. Betty McCollum and Kelly Morrison voting present. Craig said it was an overly broad amendment that would have also cut humanitarian aid to Palestinians, and on principle, she doesn’t vote present.
“I’ve never voted ‘present’ one time in Congress … you look at the bill and you make the tough decision,” Craig said.
U.S. Rep. Angie Craig announces she will forgo seeking the Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party endorsement in her race for U.S. Senate on May 27, 2026. (Photo by Max Nesterak/Minnesota Reformer)
Craig, who has also been a vocal critic of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, said the United States must “reexamine” its relationship with the state of Israel. She criticized the lack of aid to Gaza and Israeli settler violence in the West Bank.
‘Times changed real fast’
Given the fresh memories of Operation Metro Surge, voters’ belief in the sincerity of Craig’s mea culpa over her immigration vote may be what determines the election. Craig’s vote for the Laken Riley Act wasn’t surprising in January 2025, given her swing district status and the 2024 election results. She was among 46 Democrats in the House and 12 in the Senate to do so — though the only from Minnesota.
At the time, Democrats were once again agonizing over a loss that put Trump and Republicans in control of government, a defeat attributed in part to the migrant crisis in major cities like New York and the perception that the Biden administration had allowed the immigration system to spin out of control.
The attempted rape and brutal murder of 22-year-old Laken Riley by an undocumented immigrant while she was out for a morning run in Georgia crystallized for many people the sense of chaos.
The man had been apprehended at the border but released into the country. According to ICE, he was then arrested in New York on a charge of endangering a child and released — an assertion disputed by New York police — before traveling to Georgia where he was cited on a shoplifting charge.
“There was very much a feeling that Democrats had gone too far in allowing open borders,” Craig said.
And then came the masked agents, the military-like occupation of Chicago and the Twin Cities, the widespread arrest of immigrants without warrants and the explosion of detention centers run by for-profit contractors with a population now surpassing 65,000, up from about 39,000 when Trump took office.
“Times changed real fast with the Trump administration … they said they would go after the worst of the worst. They didn’t go after the worst of the worst,” Craig said.
Rep. Angie Craig speaks at a press conference calling for Andrea Pedro-FranciscoÕs release from ICE custody Monday, April 13, 2026 on an intersection in Burnsville, Minnesota close to where Pedro-Francisco was detained by agents. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)
Craig noted the bill didn’t say anything about deportation, and argues the president’s deportation machine has been lawless and didn’t require the Laken Riley Act. To justify detaining immigrants who entered the country illegally — whether or not they have criminal records, and no matter how long they’ve lived here — the Trump administration asserted a new interpretation of a 1996 law that has sharply divided the federal courts.
While the vote has made her a pariah among some Democrats even after her apology, there are plenty who feel she has been judged too harshly.
St. Paul Mayor Kaohly Her, who came to the United States as a Hmong refugee when she was 3 years old, has endorsed Craig for Senate. At a news conference where Craig announced she would not seek the party endorsement, Her urged voters to look at Craig’s entire career.
Craig co-sponsored legislation to provide a pathway to citizenship for people brought to the U.S. illegally as children, known as Dreamers, and to limit the president’s authority to block noncitizens from entering the country in response to Trump’s travel bans.
“It’s easy to point out some of the votes that people take that we can criticize, but we don’t lift up the things that they do that are right,” Her said.
Public sentiment has swung quickly against the Trump administration’s immigration policies. The share of Americans who disapprove of the way Trump is handling immigration increased from about 42% in January 2025 to 54% in July 2026, according to polling averages by Silver Bulletin. Two-thirds of Minnesotans said tactics by ICE and Border Patrol agents went too far, according to an NBC News/KARE 11/Star Tribune poll.
Notably, polling data show the public’s support for strong border security has held up. Craig, long a border hawk, has not shied away from that position.
“I refuse to believe that we can’t be a nation of strong borders and a nation of immigrants,” Craig said.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: KY scientists learned what causes sleep loss in Alzheimer’s patients — and how to stop it
description: University of Kentucky scientists have discovered the cause of sleep loss in patients with Alzheimer’s disease and how to help restore hours of rest.  They originally set out to see how sleep loss worsened over the course of the disease, believing Alzheimer’s patients lost sleep because their neurons were dying or because of amyloid plaques, […]
text:
Alzheimer's disease. Illustration of amyloid plaques amongst neurons and neurofibrillary tangles inside neurons. Amyloid plaques are characteristic features of Alzheimer's disease. They lead to degeneration of the affected neurons, which are destroyed through the activity of microglia cells. (Getty Images)University of Kentucky scientists have discovered the cause of sleep loss in patients with Alzheimer’s disease and how to help restore hours of rest. 
They originally set out to see how sleep loss worsened over the course of the disease, believing Alzheimer’s patients lost sleep because their neurons were dying or because of amyloid plaques, which are proteins that form in the brain and are believed to be a significant driver of Alzheimer’s. 
Instead, they discovered that microglia, which are brain immune cells, are so busy trying to address amyloid plaques that they are keeping the brain active and causing sleep loss. 
Shannon Macauley, an associate professor of physiology in the UK College of Medicine, said these findings, which were published last month in Alzheimer’s & Dementia, which is the Alzheimer’s Association’s journal, means sleep could be also used as an early  diagnostic tool for the disease. 
“The idea that we can find sleep as this early biomarker of when we start to see these pathological changes, and that maybe it’s just more binary than having to know exactly what the threshold is, is actually really exciting to consider if you think about sleep as a biomarker,” she told the Lantern. “That was just really exciting to us and completely opposite of what we all had hypothesized. We thought that aging in and of itself would really just make your sleep really poor, and that’s not what we found. Certainly, it does impact sleep in some regards, but not to the extent that we would have hypothesized, meaning that there is something pathological about sleep problems.”  
Natalie Sutton, the executive director for the Alzheimer’s Association’s Kentucky Chapter, said early detection and early diagnoses can help people make lifestyle changes that can help slow the disease and may open doors to research trials and expanded treatment options. 
Natalie Sutton, the executive director for the Alzheimer’s Association Kentucky Chapter. (Photo provided)
 
“With sleep, similar to any other symptoms, it’s important for people to be aware of what is normal for them and what they might see as a change for them, and then when they experience that change, to make sure that they’re talking with a healthcare provider about that change,” Sutton said. 
Quality of life 
Alzheimer’s disease, which falls under the umbrella of dementia, is characterized by memory loss and is incurable. Treatments exist, though, including Lecanemab (brand name Leqembi), which underwent clinical trials at the University of Kentucky. This is an antibody that targets — and in some cases, removes — amyloid plaques from the brain, and has shown some success in slowing cognitive decline. 
Report shows effects of Alzheimer’s in KY, the disease ‘you can’t see’ 

Nicholas Constantino, a recent PhD neuroscience graduate who works in Macauley’s lab and is the first author of the new research, said it’s unclear if sleep restoration could increase a patient’s lifespan, but it can certainly improve quality of life. 
“If you’ve ever pulled an all-nighter, you notice the effects pretty quickly the next day of how it’s hard to concentrate, it’s hard to focus, you don’t feel good, your whole body doesn’t feel good, and that there’s a rebound period to that,” he said.
With the right medication — the UK lab is now studying a way to use drugs already approved by the Food and Drug Administration to calm microglia cells — Alzheimer’s patients could gain back hours of sleep a night. 
“Quality of life is so important. As we think broadly about people who are living in their later years of life, having not only time but quality time is really what most people want, right?” Sutton said. “It’s what they’re looking for, and so I wouldn’t underestimate what it means to those living with the disease and their families to improve that quality.” 
Research that helps more people get screened, diagnosed early and treated will help a huge number of people in Kentucky, from patients to their families and loved ones to the health care system. 

The Alzheimer’s Association has a 24/7 helpline to support people who live with Alzheimer’s as well as their loved ones, caregivers and others. The number is 800-272-3900. 

There were around 80,000 Kentuckians aged 65 and older living with an Alzheimer’s diagnosis last year, according to a report that the Lantern reported on at the time. There are also nearly 200,000 Kentucky residents providing unpaid care for a loved one with Alzheimer’s — care Sutton said, that is worth nearly $7 billion.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Kendall Qualls’ running mate, picked for business acumen, owes workers money
description: Brian Nicholson told his workers earlier this month at an Albertville manufacturer that he was doing everything in his power — and even seeking divine intervention — to strike one of five “Hail Mary” deals so he could pay them what they’re owed. “I’m praying on my knees every night before I go to bed […]
text:
Brian Nicholson, left, and Kendall Qualls spoke at a Capitol press conference on March 3, 2026. (Photo by Michelle Griffith/Minnesota Reformer)Brian Nicholson told his workers earlier this month at an Albertville manufacturer that he was doing everything in his power — and even seeking divine intervention — to strike one of five “Hail Mary” deals so he could pay them what they’re owed.
“I’m praying on my knees every night before I go to bed that that’s what happens,” Nicholson told workers at Advanced Volumetric Alliance on July 8, according to a recording of the meeting obtained by the Reformer. “I’m working night and day to try to get this fixed … I’m sorry.”
Nicholson, who is the lieutenant governor running mate of Kendall Qualls, told the workers they would be furloughed, and that he’d find the money to pay them — for the first time since June 19 — as soon as possible.
Workers at Advanced Volumetric Alliance — some of whom have filed wage theft claims with the Minnesota Department of Labor and Industry — were left disappointed.
“We all live paycheck-to-paycheck,” Shannon Morey, who worked on Advanced Volumetric Alliance’s assembly line doing final touch ups and paint jobs, said in an interview. 
The company, which employs around 100 people and manufactures modular buildings, has ceased operations. Workers have not received pay for their work between June 19 and July 8, the date they were furloughed.
Qualls, who won the GOP endorsement at the spring convention, is running against MyPillow CEO Mike Lindell and House Speaker Lisa Demuth for the Republican nomination for governor in the Aug. 11 primary election.
Qualls and Nicholson have touted their business acumen as important preparation to be governor and lieutenant governor, arguing the government needs to run more like a business.
“Bringing some business leadership to government is sorely missing,” Nicholson said on a local podcast in March.
In a statement, Nicholson confirmed he furloughed his employees and said that a deal Advanced Volumetric Alliance was working on for the past year “fell apart at the last minute.”
“At times, I personally covered payroll out of my own pocket because I refused to let my employees down. This is a terrible situation but furloughing our employees was the best move for them while we work toward a solution,” Nicholson said. “Under Minnesota Democrats, too many businesses are facing similar situations and I’m running with Kendall Qualls to ensure our businesses can thrive.”
The Reformer recently asked Qualls whether he was aware employees at one of Nicholson’s companies have not received the wages they were owed. Qualls said this situation was “normative behavior in the business economic cycle.”
“A lot of businesses, even the ones I was involved in … go through peaks and valleys. We need leaders that can take companies through those peaks and valleys. And if he’s going through a valley right now, he’s the kind of guy that would bring it back to a peak,” Qualls said.
A previous furlough
The July furlough isn’t the first example of financial problems at Advanced Volumetric Alliance, however. The company furloughed some of its workers back in April, and many workers received their paychecks a week late, according to an email from Nicholson obtained by the Reformer.
Nicholson in an April 10 email said the tardy pay was “a timing issue of inbound cash.”
When Nicholson informed his workers that they would finally receive their paycheck a week late, he assured them that the company’s future was bright.
“This week, I was traveling and presenting AVA and its capabilities to the Dept of War to help solve the problem of barracks quality for our armed forces,” Nicholson said in an email sent out to employees on April 17. 
“Both President Trump and Secretary (Pete) Hegseth have described the soldier housing problem as one of national security … The prototype projects are the tip of the iceberg — when we’re successful with those, then we have the ability to become part of the bigger solution worldwide.”
The government contract hasn’t come to fruition.
Nicholson has said he’s been involved in starting dozens of companies throughout this career. Vendors have occasionally sued him for lack of payment.
Minnetonka-based KLC Financial sued Advanced Volumetric Alliance this month for $637,000, according to Minnesota court records. KLC Financial financed equipment for the company, and the bank said Nicholson’s company has failed to make monthly payments on the loan.
Nicholson has also been accused of financial misconduct by a former chief financial officer, who alleged that Nicholson and his business partner used company funds for personal expenses. Brian McCaw, the former CFO, also alleges that Nicholson’s company “was over-leveraged, failing to pay vendors on a timely basis, and was not providing timely or sufficient communications to the company’s investors.”
In May, a court ruled that two companies closely associated with Nicholson owed $77,000 to an insulation contractor that never got paid.
Advanced Volumetric Alliance is housed in a new 180,000 square-foot facility in Albertville, a black warehouse visible off of I-94.
Morey, the line worker, said in an interview she was excited to start working at Advanced Volumetric Alliance because it offered training, holiday pay, a good hourly wage and a four-day workweek.
The furlough earlier this month and the company’s inability to pay them their final paycheck has hurt many working-class employees who have rent and mortgages to pay, Morey said.
She’s been frustrated by the lack of communication from Advanced Volumetric Alliance executives, and she probably would not return if the company did finally have enough cash to pay them and end their furlough.
“There are a lot of people in AVA that are negative in their accounts and are not okay,” Morey said. “I just want them to be held accountable.”

title: Prescriptions for nutrition: Nevada program connects food banks to health care
description: For families across northern Nevada, fresh groceries can mean the difference between costly health outcomes and fewer trips to the emergency room.  Poor nutrition remains one of the leading risk factors for cardiovascular disease and other health disparities in the U.S., according to health experts. text:
Mobile harvest delivery. (Photo coutresy of Food Bank of Northern Nevada)For families across northern Nevada, fresh groceries can mean the difference between costly health outcomes and fewer trips to the emergency room. 
Poor nutrition remains one of the leading risk factors for cardiovascular disease and other health disparities in the U.S., according to health experts. Early research also indicates that “food as medicine” initiatives including medically tailored groceries and meals are a cost-effective way to improve community health outcomes.
The Food Bank of Northern Nevada’s Prescription Pantry Program is one of the solutions nutrition advocates in the state have launched to pair local health clinics with fresh food and nutrition support for neighbors facing hunger.
Thousands of groceries have been delivered to medically vulnerable Nevadan’s through the program, which is supported by 14 health care partners and 14 partner food pantries across northern Nevada.
“Nutritious food plays an important role in health and well-being, but many people in our region do not have consistent access to the foods that support their health, preferences, and families,” said Frankie Ortiz, health equity manager at the Food Bank of Northern Nevada. 
The model is also supported by the Feeding America’s Food as Medicine program, a national initiative funded by Anthem Blue Cross and Blue Shield Foundation and evaluated by the Center for Nutrition & Health Impact, a nonprofit research center. 
A report published by Feeding America in July found that pairing food assistance with health care support led to real health gains for participants in Nevada, including a 13% drop in emergency room visits. 
Program participants who picked up food more frequently were also less likely to report having to miss or delay medical care due to cost, compared with those who picked up food less often, according to the report. 
Between April 2023 and December 2025, nearly 41,000 patients received food through the Nevada program, and nearly 100 were referred to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP).
The report is based on a total of 103 participants who responded to the baseline survey and follow-up surveys. The majority of participants were women (80%) and around two-thirds of participants identified as either Hispanic or Latino.
“There’s a lot of moving parts to this program. It’s really exciting because it finally proves that nutritious food is not only important, but can influence health outcomes. That’s important,” said Jocelyn Lantrip, the director of marketing  and communications for the Food Bank of Northern Nevada.
Under the program, patients facing a cardiovascular condition or diabetes are screened for food insecurity and connected with food banks that offer the Prescription Pantry Program. Eligible Nevadan’s receive “a food prescription” that provides them access to a wide variety of nutritious foods, including lower-sodium options, dairy, and lean proteins.
“We know that heart disease and diabetes are significant health issues in our community. They’re very typical diagnoses that can be helped by nutrition,” Lantrip said. “Groceries in those pantries will have even more fresh produce and lean protein and whole grains and foods that are good for those diagnoses.”
The Food Bank of Northern Nevada launched the program in 2017, and expanded to rural areas in 2021 after receiving additional funding from Anthem Blue Cross and Blue Shield Foundation. 
Nationally, the report found a 14% decrease in hospitalizations and an 11% drop in emergency room visit rates for patients participating in the program compared to the baseline. Food security among participants also rose nearly 7% under the program.

name: VTDigger
title: A Department of Corrections policy is quietly reshaping how long people are incarcerated in Vermont
description:
The department said the policy is about protecting public safety. Advocates have raised concerns.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  A Department of Corrections policy is quietly reshaping how long people are incarcerated in Vermont.
text:
Burlington Police Chief Jon Murad speaks at a press conference in Burlington in August 2024. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
When the man signed a plea deal from a Vermont prison in May 2025, he thought he knew what he was agreeing to. 
He was already incarcerated when he pleaded guilty to fentanyl trafficking, burglary and carrying a weapon during the commission of a felony, agreeing to serve a minimum of three years and a maximum of 10 years incarcerated. While his full name appears in court documents, VTDigger is identifying him only as “G.” because he is not a public figure and could not be reached while he’s incarcerated to discuss the story. 
Because G. could get credit for some of the time he’d already spent in prison, his minimum release date was in early October 2025, less than six months after he signed his plea. 
What G. didn’t know was that there was a new Department of Corrections policy, one that would change what he thought he’d agreed to. 
After his sentencing, G. learned that the department was reviewing him under a new policy known as risk containment. Under the policy, the department can use a risk containment classification to incarcerate a person past their minimum release date because of concerns that the person poses a risk to others if they are released. 
If he was risk contained, G. would be ineligible for furlough — the mechanism through which many incarcerated Vermonters leave prison — until the department chose to lift the classification. Parole would remain technically available, but the department likely would not recommend him for it.
“I took my plea agreement on the grounds of being released on my minimum release date,” G. wrote to the court in August 2025. He asked the judge to change his sentence to five and a half years of incarceration, a plea deal that had previously been on the table and that would give him more certainty about when he would be released. 
“If I had known (about risk containment) prior to sentencing I would have never taken anything other than the 5 year to 5 year 6 months,” he later wrote in a letter to the court. 
If he is risk contained, G. might end up staying incarcerated until the end of his maximum sentence — in 2032, more than six years away. 
G. is one of dozens of people incarcerated in Vermont’s prison system who have been impacted by the new policy. As of July 8, G. had been waiting for over a year for the department to decide whether to risk contain him. Like other people who are awaiting review under the policy, he has not been allowed to participate in required risk intervention services while he waits for the department to decide whether to risk contain him. And if he ends up risk contained, he will face the uncertainty of not knowing when he might be released or how to get the classification lifted. 
The internal Department of Corrections policy, quietly introduced in July 2024, has expanded the criteria it uses to keep people imprisoned past their minimum sentence — and prosecutors and defense attorneys say it is reshaping sentencing across the state. Some incarcerated Vermonters, including G., are challenging the policy in court on the grounds that it changes the meaning of their sentence. 
Vermont uses an indeterminate sentencing structure, meaning people are sentenced to a minimum and a maximum sentence. The department has long had the power to incarcerate people past the minimum, but the norm largely was to release most people at or near their minimum onto community supervision once they completed required programs, prosecutors and defense attorneys said. Those programs include educational, job-skills and emotional regulation training; some people are required to complete such programs to be eligible for furlough.
Other common reasons that the department incarcerates people past their minimum sentence include not having DOC-approved housing or being reincarcerated after a violation of furlough, according to DOC data.

Under the new risk containment policy introduced under former DOC Commissioner Nicholas Deml, more people are being held past their minimum, prompting concerns from advocates about due process and from prosecutors about new uncertainty in sentencing.
Impetus from the Governor
The policy grew out of direction from Gov. Phil Scott, according to court testimony from Jordan Pasha, a DOC employee who helped write it. Pasha testified in Vermont Superior Court as part of a case in which an incarcerated person asked the court to reconsider their sentence because of the risk containment policy. 
“We had received direction from the Governor’s office to look at mechanisms that the department had to slow down releases in the interest of public and victim safety,” Pasha testified in December 2025, according to a hearing transcript obtained by VTDigger. 
The governor’s office referred questions about the origins of the policy to the DOC. The department did not make Pasha available for an interview.
Jon Murad, who became commissioner after Deml stepped down in August 2025, said he was not familiar with the origins of the policy but that the change may reflect rising community concern about crime.
“It’s my responsibility to ensure that people leaving our custody are both safe for the community and are as best positioned as possible to be successful in the community,” Murad said in an interview, adding that the policy only applies to people with certain convictions whom the department determines would pose a threat if released. 
People with convictions for sex offenses, listed offenses (a category that includes some of the most serious crimes, such as murder and manslaughter), or felonies can be considered for risk containment. In Vermont, a felony is any crime for which the maximum punishment is more than two years of incarceration.
Falko Schilling, who directs advocacy at the ACLU of Vermont, said in an interview that keeping people locked up for longer wasn’t likely to reduce their risk of committing new crimes when released. 
“Generally, the research shows that longer incarcerative sentences don’t reduce the risk of recidivism,” Schilling said in an interview.
In a period when the department has struggled with overcrowding, Schilling also raised concerns that the policy adds to pressure on an already strained system. 
Expanding criteria
What’s changed is not the department’s power to hold people past their minimum, but who it chooses to hold.
Under the previous policy, in effect for over 20 years, people convicted of a listed offense whose crime was deemed “egregious” and who posed a moderate-to-high reoffending risk were typically incarcerated past their minimum. These individuals, classified as “Level C,” had to show long-term stability and completion of treatment goals before release. In June 2023, there were eight people incarcerated past their minimum sentence under the Level C policy, according to DOC data. 
Other people –– even those convicted of listed offenses –– were released at their minimum onto community supervision, provided they finished required programming and had somewhere to live outside of prison that met DOC standards. Risk containment changed that. 
Now anyone convicted of a sex offense, listed offense or felony can be reviewed for risk containment. To be designated risk contained the department must find the person poses “a threat to the life, safety, or physical or mental well-being of others.” A committee of DOC employees makes that call, weighing past charges, behavior inside, supervision history and other factors, Pasha testified.
Someone who is risk contained gets no furlough and no positive parole recommendation from the DOC, Pasha testified. The expected release date vanishes. The only guarantee left is the maximum, sometimes years away.
The parole board can still choose to grant parole for someone who is risk contained, and it is not bound by the department’s recommendation. But parole board director Mary Jane Ainsworth said the board does not track how often it approves release in cases where DOC has not recommended it, and couldn’t say whether anyone classified as risk contained has been paroled. 
Whatever the theoretical path to release, it does not appear to be functioning. Sixty-three of the roughly 75 people classified as risk contained are currently incarcerated past their minimum sentence, according to the department. 

Tim Burgess, an advocate for incarcerated Vermonters who spent several years incarcerated in the early 2000s, said in an interview that the uncertainty takes a toll. 
“It’s your every focus,” Burgess said of a release date. “When you’re an inmate in an incarcerative setting, you’re working, hopefully, to do everything you can to make that date.”
 “Your mindset changes,” Burgess said of the uncertain release date. “You’re now all of a sudden in a posture of trying to say, ‘Well, what am I going to do now? Because I’ve made other plans based on what I’ve been told.’“
Just waiting for a risk containment decision can itself keep people incarcerated past their minimum –– even those the committee ultimately doesn’t classify. G. remains incarcerated more than nine months after his minimum sentence passed in October 2025. As of early July, the department had still not made a final decision about whether to risk contain him, one of his lawyers said in court.
It is not uncommon for the DOC committee to take more than 6 months to make a final decision on whether to risk contain someone, Pasha testified.
Fifty-three people were awaiting a risk containment decision as of early July. 
‘It’s very unclear’
While the policy lays out a process through which a person can challenge a risk containment classification, advocates questioned whether that process is adequate. 
“The lack of transparency around the decisions or substantive opportunities to challenge those decisions is one of the most concerning aspects of how we’re hearing about this policy being implemented,” said Schilling, the ACLU advocate. 
Murad pushed back on concerns about transparency in how the department decides who meets the threshold.
“It’s a fair process,” he said. “It is a thorough-going process. It is not a process that has a foregone conclusion in either direction.” 
A risk-contained person can challenge the decision through the prison’s grievance system. Burgess, the formerly incarcerated advocate, said that process can be grindingly slow, and the court challenges that often follow can take years. A state auditor’s report in 2022 found significant issues with the DOC’s grievance process; the department undertook some changes in response to the report. 

A risk-contained person can petition once a year for a change if they show “substantive evidence that they have addressed one or more of the factors that contributed to their risk,” according to the policy. But the prisons have added no new programming for risk-contained people, Pasha testified, leaving advocates and at least one judge to wonder how anyone demonstrates change.
Vermont Superior Court Judge John Pacht pressed the point during the hearing in which Pasha testified. 
“It’s very unclear that you folks have, and I don’t say this judgmentally, it’s just a brand new program, have developed a really clear set of just how much it will take to get off the risk containment policy once you’re on it,” Pacht said. “You could just, by virtue of history, no matter how well you do, just remain risk contained.”
Pasha replied that “the department is hesitant to very clearly say you need to do this and this and this and risk containment will be removed.” 
“We’re looking for meaningful change,” he added. 
An impossible uncertainty for defense attorneys
For longtime defense attorney David Sleigh, the policy undercuts the intent of sentences imposed before it existed. He argued that judges and prosecutors already take risk factors into account when they impose or agree to a sentence.
“It’s like, wait a second, you know, the judge knew about all this stuff, that’s what he or she sentenced me to. Who are you, head of programming at DOC, to make this decision on your own?” Sleigh said in an interview.
Pacht, for his part, wrote in one case that the policy “had the likely effect of significantly increasing the length of the in-prison incarcerative portion of a to-serve sentence that a person with [the defendant’s] criminal history would serve.” That case has yet to be resolved.
Murad disputed that risk containment decisions rest solely on information that’s available when a person is sentenced, saying the decisions take into account a person’s behavior while incarcerated. 
“The idea that this is entirely predicated on things that happen prior to sentencing is erroneous,” he said.
Four top prosecutors from different counties said sentencing has shifted over the past year, driven by uncertainty about who the policy will impact.
“Policies that don’t have clear guidelines are impossible for defense attorneys to give adequate legal advice on,” Sarah George, the top prosecutor for Chittenden County, said in an interview.
Prosecutors said that prior to risk containment, they often used sentences with low minimums and high maximums, assuming that the person would serve the minimum inside and the rest on supervision. 
“The idea behind those types of sentences is to get a little bit of time on the front end, and then allow corrections to furlough, parole somebody out near or close to their minimum,” Steven Brown, the lead prosecutor for Windham County, said in an interview.
Furlough and parole are forms of community supervision more intensive than probation, with reincarceration a possible consequence of violations.
“The reason why we’d want to have that type of sentence structure is to provide supervision of an individual for a set amount of time,” Brown added. “Usually we would do that in cases where probation no longer provided the level of supervision that we wanted to have.”
Now, because no one knows at sentencing whether a defendant will be risk contained, fewer will accept a low-minimum, high-maximum deal for fear of serving the whole thing.
“You had a whole class of people, dozens, who made these sort of low minimum, high maximum deals with the understanding if they did the programming that they’d be eligible for parole,” said Sleigh, the defense attorney. 
“I won’t agree to that kind of sentence structure as a general rule these days,” he said. 
The result, prosecutors said, is more “split” sentences — a fixed term inside, then probation. That worries George, who says some of those defendants are too high-risk for probation.
“I think it’s actually doing the exact opposite of what it’s claiming to do,” George said of the policy’s public-safety impact.
“We’re experiencing maybe some … unintended effects, in that it’s making it harder for us to negotiate cases with a furlough sentence involved,” Bram Kranichfeld, the lead prosecutor for Franklin County, said in an interview.
George and Kranichfeld are both running to be top prosecutor in Chittenden County, a role George has held since 2017. 
Jared Bianchi, a prosecutor in Bennington County, disagreed that the policy has impacted sentencing. 
“From my perspective, I think that there’s a lot of hand-wringing over what I don’t perceive to be a substantial change,” Bianchi said in an interview, noting DOC always had the power to hold people past their minimum.
Broad authority 
Sleigh said the department’s broad authority to incarcerate people past their minimum may limit legal challenges to the policy, though a defendant might argue they lacked full information at their plea, or that the policy substantively changed the length of confinement. 
Several cases that attempt to challenge the policy are currently moving through the courts, including G.’s case. 
Meanwhile, George and Kranichfeld said they are exploring whether DOC could screen people for risk containment before sentencing, so everyone knows the odds up front.
While Murad said he is willing to engage with prosecutors about their concerns, he said pre-sentencing screening isn’t possible because behavior in prison is part of the calculus. 
“When we become soothsayers, and when we become fortune tellers, perhaps that would make sense,” Murad said.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  A Department of Corrections policy is quietly reshaping how long people are incarcerated in Vermont.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Connecticut Primary Election 2026 Voter Guide
description: Connecticut's primary election will take place on Aug. 11. Here's what to know about how to register, vote and know who's running.
text:
Connecticut Primary Election 2026Voter Guide
How to register, vote, and know who’s running.

IN THIS GUIDE:    KEY DATES    CANDIDATES    FAQ    GENERAL ASSEMBLY    COVERAGE
Connecticut residents will head to the polls on Aug. 11 to cast ballots in party primaries for governor, U.S. Congress and state legislative and constitutional races. Many will have questions about where to vote, how to vote and for whom to vote when Primary Election Day rolls around. The Connecticut Mirror, a nonprofit and nonpartisan news organization, is here to help with this primary voter guide — a comprehensive look at the key dates to know ahead of Aug. 11, a one-stop-shop for election-related information. 

KEY DATES FOR THE 2026 PRIMARY ELECTIONS


July 21
First day absentee ballots are issued


August 3
First day of early voting


August 6
Last day to register to vote by mail


August 9
Last day of early voting


August 10
Last day to request an absentee ballot and register to vote in person


August 11: Primary Election Day! Polls open 6 a.m. to 8 p.m.

FAQ
Any questions we haven’t answered here? Send us an email and we’ll try to answer them for you.
Am I eligible to vote? What if I’m unaffiliated with a party?
Connecticut residents are eligible to vote if they are a U.S. citizen and turn 18 on or before Nov. 3, 2026. If a person has been convicted of a felony, they must also have completed confinement.
You must be registered with a party to vote in that party’s primary elections. If you are unaffiliated with a party, you can register with one until 12 p.m. on Aug. 10. The deadline to change your affiliation from one party to another has passed.

How do I register to vote?
Those eligible to vote can visit the state’s online voter registration portal to sign up, apply in person to your town clerk or registrar, or download a paper form in English or Spanish and mail it in to your town’s registrar of voters office. 
The deadline to register in person is 12 p.m. on Aug. 10. For voters affiliated with a party, the deadline to register by mail is Aug. 6, and your application must be postmarked or received by this date. The deadline for new voters and unaffiliated voters to register by mail was July 24. 

What if I miss the deadline? Can I vote on primary election day or during early voting?
You can register every day at an early voting location from Aug. 3 through Aug. 9. Same-day registration is not available for primary elections.

Tell me about early voting. Who can vote? When does it begin? Where do I go?
Anyone eligible to vote in the primary election can vote during the early voting period. Early voting begins on Aug. 3 and runs through Aug. 9. Early voting locations will be posted on a rolling basis on the state’s Early Voting Locations page.
If you are unaffiliated with a party and wish to vote during early voting, you must register with a party by 12 p.m. on July 31.

Are polling locations the same on primary election day as they are during early voting?
No. Early voting locations can and will be different from regular polling locations. To find out where to cast a ballot on primary election day, registered voters can visit the secretary of the state’s voter registration lookup and polling place locator here.

What time are the polls open on primary election day?
Polls will be open from 6 a.m. to 8 p.m. If you are in line at 8 p.m., you will still be able to vote.

Do I need to bring an ID to vote? 
No, but you can. Before you receive a ballot at the polls, you will be asked to provide a government-issued ID, a different ID with your name and photo, or a document such as a utility bill or checkbook that has your name and address. You may use your current driver’s license at the polls even if it is marked “not for federal identification.”
If you can not provide any of these, you will be asked to sign an affidavit instead.

Can I vote by using an absentee or mail-in ballot? 
For the first time this year, anyone eligible to vote in the primary election can request an absentee ballot. Voters can submit requests through the Online Absentee Ballot Request Portal, or mail or hand-deliver a printed ballot to their town clerk. Voters no longer need to specify reasons for requesting an absentee ballot. The deadline to request an absentee ballot is Aug. 10.
Absentee ballots will be issued and mailed to voters starting July 21. The ballot must be returned to the voter’s town clerk by using the United States Postal Service, in person at the town clerk’s office or in a drop box in their town. Voters must return their absentee ballot in the same envelope that housed the ballot and ensure that they print and sign their name on the envelope. 
All ballots must be received by 8 p.m. on Aug. 11 to be counted. Voters can check if their ballot has been received on the state’s Voter Registration Lookup and should contact their town clerk if their ballot has not been received.
For additional questions about absentee voting, contact the state Legislation and Election Administration at LEAD@ct.gov or (860) 509-6100.

I’m a college student. How do I vote? 
Students eligible to vote in the primary can do so in one of two ways: vote by absentee ballot in your home town or register to vote in your college town.

GUBERNATORIAL CANDIDATES
The Democratic primary for governor is the only statewide primary this year and the first challenge to a governor for their party’s nomination since 1978, when Lt. Gov. Robert Killian failed to wrest the top spot from Gov. Ella T. Grasso.
Gov. Ned Lamont, a fiscal centrist and social progressive who is seeking a rare third term, is being challenged from the left by state Rep. Josh Elliott of Hamden.
Lamont, 72, of Greenwich is waging his fifth statewide campaign and his fourth for governor. Making national news as anti-war candidate in 2006, he won a Democratic primary against U.S. Sen. Joseph I. Lieberman in 2006, but Lieberman won his fourth and final term as an independent candidate. Lamont lost a gubernatorial primary to former Gov. Dannel P. Malloy in 2010.
Elliott, 41, was elected to the state House of Representatives in 2016, running with the backing of the Working Families Party for the seat then held by House Speaker J. Brendan Sharkey. Ultimately, Sharkey did not seek another term. Elliott helped resurrect the progressive caucus in the House. This year, Elliott is hedging his bets, running for reelection to the House while challenging the governor.

CT CONGRESSIONAL DISTRICT CANDIDATES


All five of Connecticut’s U.S. House seats are on the general election ballot in November. But there are only three primaries in August: a Democratic primary in the 1st District and Republican primaries in the 4th District and the 5th District.
Democrats hold all five seats and have advantages again this year. The 1st District is the most heavily Democratic in the state, with a Republican last winning in 1956. Republicans haven’t won the 4th District since 2006 or the 5th since 2004. The 5th District is considered the most competitive in Connecticut.
Here’s who’s running in the congressional primaries:




Democratic primary in Connecticut’s 1st Congressional District
The district is centered around Hartford, wrapping around up to the northwest toward Torrington and down and over to Bristol. It is currently represented by Democrat John B. Larson.
Luke Bronin is the former mayor of Hartford, serving between 2016 and 2024. He served as an intelligence officer in the U.S. Navy Reserve and was deployed to Afghanistan in 2010. Before becoming mayor, he worked in the Obama administration and served as general counsel to former Gov. Dannel P. Malloy. He won the party’s endorsement at the nominating convention.
Ruth Fortune is an estate lawyer and first-time candidate for elected office. She’s an appointed member of the Hartford Board of Education. Fortune failed to win enough support from local delegates at the nominating convention, but she secured the signatures needed via petition to get a spot on the August primary ballot.
Jillian Gilchrest is a state representative from West Hartford who has been in office since 2019 after unseating a longtime incumbent. Before her tenure in the General Assembly, Gilchrest served in leadership positions for the Connecticut Coalition Against Domestic Violence, NARAL Pro-Choice Connecticut and the Connecticut Alliance to End Sexual Violence.
Larson has represented the district since 1999. He serves as the ranking member of the Ways and Means’ Social Security Subcommittee. Prior to Congress, he served in the Connecticut Senate and worked as a history teacher before his time in politics. This is the first time he’s faced a primary in his 28-year congressional tenure.
Republican primary in Connecticut’s 4th Congressional District
The district covers the southwestern corner, including Stamford and Bridgeport. It is currently represented by Democrat Jim Himes.
Michael Goldstein is a physician and attorney who has run to represent the district multiple times. He lost the Republican primary in 2022 but became the GOP nominee in 2024, eventually losing to Himes. In this year’s primary, Goldstein is the party-endorsed candidate.
Daniel Miressi is a former professional hockey player who coaches youth hockey and has worked in the hospitality industry. He’s run for elected office before, including in an unsuccessful race to unseat state Senate Majority Leader Bob Duff, D-Norwalk, in 2022.
Republican primary in Connecticut’s 5th Congressional District
The district spans the western part of the state, including sections of Fairfield, Litchfield, New Haven and Hartford counties. It is currently represented by Democrat Jahana Hayes.
Republican challenger Chris Shea is a North Haven firefighter and retired Navy SEAL. He founded the nonprofit Hero to Hero, which encourages military veterans to consider a second career as first responders. Shea is the party-endorsed candidate.
Republican challenger Jonathan De Barros has worked as a mentor for at-risk youth. He shot and killed a man in 1996 and was convicted of murder, but it was overturned on appeal. He was granted an “absolute pardon” in 2022. He filed a defamation lawsuit against Republicans who have called him a murderer.

CT GENERAL ASSEMBLY CANDIDATES
The only Democratic primaries for state legislative nominations are in two Senate and seven House districts currently represented by Democrats. In all nine districts, whoever wins the primary is favored to prevail in November.
Two races to watch involve challenges to incumbents: Sen. Doug McCrory of Hartford in the 2nd Senate District and Rep. Patricia Dillon of New Haven in the 92nd House District.
McCrory’s role in delivering earmarks is the subject of a continuing FBI investigation. Dillon is the longest-serving member of the House seeking reelection and faces a generational challenge.
A third Democratic primary is a bit of an oddity. Rep. Jill Barry of Glastonbury lost the Democratic endorsement in a caucus to Moise “Moses” Carelus. He now faces a primary, but not from Barry. She is running as an independent.
On the Republican side, the only primary getting attention turns on the Republican Party working to defeat convention-endorsed candidate Jadon MacCormack of Brooklyn over his homophobic statements.
Rep. William Pizzuto of Middlebury is the only Republican incumbent facing a primary.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Company at center of NJ voter registration scandal has multiple state contracts
description: Gov. Mikie Sherrill has blamed state contractor Idemia for allowing non-citizens to register to vote. The company has three multimillion-dollar contracts with New Jersey.
text:
Gov. Mikie Sherrill has blamed state contractor Idemia for allowing non-citizens to register to vote. The company has three multimillion-dollar contracts with New Jersey. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)
The French company under fire after Gov. Mikie Sherrill blamed it for allowing non-citizens to register to vote holds three multimillion-dollar contracts with the state of New Jersey.


Besides the contract with the state Motor Vehicle Commission that is at the center of the voter registration debacle, the company, Idemia, also holds contracts to handle fingerprinting for the New Jersey State Police and a third one to provide fingerprinting, background searches, and other services for various state agencies, state records show.


State taxpayers have paid the company about $61.1 million so far total, the records show.


A spokesman for Gov. Mikie Sherrill, who said last week that her administration is moving to terminate Idemia’s contract with the motor vehicle agency, declined to say whether the other two contracts are in jeopardy. Idemia, which has denied responsibility for registering non-citizens, did not respond to a request for comment.


Assemblywoman Dawn Fantasia (R-Sussex), who is among the Republicans who has called for a bipartisan legislative committee to investigate the voter registration matter, said it doesn’t make sense for the Sherrill administration to target only Idemia’s contract with the Motor Vehicle Commission.


“If Idemia really was the problem here and lost the state’s confidence, why would we be concerned with that and not actual background checks?” she said.


Sherrill last week announced that about 6,600 non-citizens had been added to the state voter rolls for a year starting in June 2023 because of what she called a software glitch on Idemia’s part. She said non-citizens who were prompted at the agency to say whether they were citizens would respond no, but the software identified them as citizens anyway. About 400 of them cast ballots, she said.


Sherrill said Thursday that the motor vehicle commissioner had moved to end Idemia’s work with the agency because the company “was at the heart” of the agency’s failures.


“The commissioner was already in the process of removing them for their incompetence,” Sherrill said.


Idemia’s contract to assist with enhanced driver’s licenses was issued in January 2010 and ends in January 2027. It has been paid $35.7 million so far, records show.


It also holds a contract with the State Police related to an electronic fingerprinting system, a contract that started in January 2019, runs through January 2027, and has cost the state roughly $3.8 million so far, the records show.


Another contract that began in May 2019 and expires in May 2027 allows Idemia to provide electronic fingerprinting for background checks and other “noncriminal justice purposes” for agencies across state government. New Jersey has spent about $21.6 million on that contract to date, the records show.


Fantasia thinks moving to sever Idemia’s contract now would be a mistake. She said she does not believe Sherrill’s story that the 6,600 non-citizens were registered because of a software error.


“Without an investigation, I think we’re setting ourselves up for a serious lawsuit,” Fantasia said. “If the flag we’re carrying is we’re getting rid of them because of this software glitch, that has yet to be proven. That’s an assertion by the governor. The vendor denies it. So to me, that’s hardly irrefutable evidence.”


The company is also a contractor with the federal government. Rep. Josh Gottheimer, a Democrat, last week requested a government-wide audit of every federal contract involving Idemia, suggesting there could be a deeper problem as the company “sits at the center of the federal government’s identity, screening, and border infrastructure.” He pointed to contracts for TSA PreCheck, U.S. Customs and Border Protection’s biometric entry-exit system, and identity operations at the U.S. Department of Defense, including contracts with driver’s license systems in 36 states.


“A ‘small’ software issue like what happened in New Jersey could, right now, be allowing improperly vetted individuals to enter our airports and board our airplanes,” Gottheimer told federal budget officials last week.


Sherrill has blamed the administration of her predecessor, Phil Murphy (D), in addition to Idemia because the problem started when he was governor. Sherrill took office in January.


Murphy spokesman Mahen Gunaratna said Friday that Murphy was unaware of this issue before Sherrill brought it to light this week.


The registration matter has drawn national attention, including criticism from President Donald Trump. The Trump administration is suing New Jersey over the state’s refusal to hand over unredacted voter roll information. U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has alleged that more than 35,000 noncitizens are registered to vote in New Jersey.
Dana DiFilippo contributed.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Warren County eyes slaughterhouse as solution for NJ’s road-weary livestock farmers
description: New Jersey's livestock farmers often travel hours for meat-processing, because of a statewide lack of USDA-approved slaughterhouses.
text:
New Jersey's livestock farmers typically travel hours out of state to take cattle, poultry and other animals for meat-processing, because of a statewide lack of facilities approved by the USDA to butcher and package meat for individual sale. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)Third-generation farmer Chad Muckenfuss raises cattle, pigs, and chickens on his sprawling farm in Medford, continually rotating livestock around 120 acres in a regenerative approach that keeps both the animals and the pastures healthier than factory farming.
It’s a model that has kept the Muckenfuss family farm successful, with a steady stream of customers devoted to organic meats. There’s only one problem.
“All of my meats are processed two-plus hours one-way over in Pennsylvania,” he said.
New Jersey has no slaughterhouse certified by the U.S. Department of Agriculture where the state’s livestock farmers can get animals butchered for individual cuts, a shortcoming that forces farmers to haul them long distances to out-of-state facilities that are so backlogged many have monthslong waits.
Industry advocates are trying to change that, with plans to open a meat-processing center in rural Warren County by late 2028.
But it has been slow going.
More than a decade ago, Rutgers University researchers warned of a “sharp decline” in slaughter plants since the mid-20th century and its economic toll especially on smaller livestock farmers. In 2019, New Jersey agriculture officials landed federal funding to study the feasibility of creating a centrally located regional processing facility or on-farm processing and inspections. And Warren County commissioners, calling in a 2021 resolution for a slaughterhouse to be sited there, noted the county’s status as the state’s top livestock producer and warned the absence of a processing plant was “unsustainable.”
Joe Labarbera, director of the agriculture and economic development program at Warren County Community College, blames the poky progress on “a cultural misunderstanding” about agricultural development. Public officials at every level of government have prioritized preservation and lost focus on supply-chain economics, he charged.
“They’re saving the farmland, but they’re not saving the farmer,” Labarbera said.
But some state officials who support the Warren County proposal are working to change that.
Sen. Doug Steinhardt (Hal Brown for New Jersey Monitor)
Sen. Douglas Steinhardt (R-Warren) introduced three bills last month that would speed up permitting, expand the workforce, and create tax incentives for slaughter plants and other projects that support agriculture.
New Jersey Agriculture Secretary Ed Wengryn anticipates construction will be underway within the next 18 months.
“This is really critical for our livestock industry,” Wengryn said.
 A decades-long decline
Suburban sprawl gobbled up so many agricultural acres in the Garden State since the 1970s that the U.S. Department of Agriculture in 2011 named New Jersey the nation’s leader in farmland loss.
As farms disappeared, so did their support industries like slaughterhouses.
Policymakers scrambled to preserve farmland, permanently protecting about 250,000 acres in the past 45 years, even as the state auditor found the state should be doing more.
Ben Spinelli, executive director of the New Jersey Highlands Water Protection and Planning Council, agrees the state’s work is far from done. The state-created council, which protects natural resources and oversees development in a hilly and forested 1,300-mile stretch of North Jersey, supported the Warren County slaughterhouse proposal with a $150,000 planning grant in 2023.
“I believe that we have come to the end of the decline of agriculture in New Jersey, and we’re in a place where agriculture is going to rebound,” Spinelli said. “Now we have to take a look and see where the opportunities are to bring back not just the farmers and the farming, but the support industries that make what they do possible.”
Vegetables, soybeans, and fruits may be New Jersey’s biggest agricultural commodities, but more than 24,000 cattle graze on Garden State farms, according to USDA data. Farmers here also raise hogs, chickens, turkeys, and other animals for their meat.
The USDA listed about 45 slaughter plants and markets in New Jersey in 2021, the most recent data available, but most were rendering plants (that handle animal bones and other byproduct after meat is cut), bulk butchers (that don’t cut and package for individual sale), and specialty services (like halal butchers).
Chad Muckenfuss is a third-generation farmer who must haul his animals more than two hours from his farm in Medford to meat-processing plants in Pennsylvania, because New Jersey has no USDA-approved slaughterhouses that butcher meat for individually packaged sale. (Photo courtesy of Michael Paras Photography)
With no in-state slaughter plant to take his animals for individual cuts, Muckenfuss treks his cattle to a butcher in Nazareth, Pennsylvania, and his poultry to a plant in Gettysburg. The trips stress the animals, add time and costs that ultimately inflate meat prices for customers, and require scheduling that can impact his whole year and beyond, he said.
“I have to commit to all of the animals that I’m going to process a year in advance with these processors, because they’re so backed up,” he said. “But the flip side of that is, we had a very harsh winter this past winter, so most of the cattle lost a little bit of weight. In order to meet my deadlines, I can’t just magically have them gain weight, so I have to cancel reservations that I had. And you only get a certain number. Once you give up slots, it’s very difficult to gain them back again for the following year.”
The butchers’ backlog means that Muckenfuss and other livestock farmers often have limited cuts for sale. Customers who try to order Muckenfuss’ meat online sometimes “just see ‘out of stock,’ and it could be out of stock for four months,” he said.
In Hillsborough, such challenges drove Lima Family Farms to take the unusual step of opening its own private USDA-inspected slaughterhouse on site in 2023.
“During Covid was when we decided that we needed to open our own facility, because if they were closed down, we couldn’t get our animals in. And our customers still wanted the meat,” said Abigail Blanchard, who manages the farm’s store. “Now the animals don’t have to leave the property, which is great for them.”
But that’s a solution out of reach for many farmers, because it’s expensive. The USDA requires inspectors to have their own office and bathroom on site and to observe processing from start to finish.
Muckenfuss hopes the public’s growing concerns about the path meat takes before it appears in store refrigerator cases will spur change.
“‘Buy local,’ and the pushback on lab-grown meats is a real driver for people wanting to know where their meats come from. It is becoming more and more of a political agenda item, as opposed to before, where everyone was like, ‘Well, if they got to drive to Pennsylvania, then let them drive to Pennsylvania,’” he said.
He supports the Warren County plan but also thinks the industry needs multiple slaughterhouses around the state.
Cows graze on pastures at the Medford Cattle Farms in South Jersey. (Photo courtesy of Chad Muckenfuss)
 From litter to livestock
In Warren County, the proposal known as the Northwest Jersey Processing and Innovation Center may be closest to completion, with a site identified, partnerships cemented, and seed funding secured.
Still, even those who welcome the center have voiced environmental, cost, and other concerns.
The 21-acre site, where the old Covanta trash incinerator and recycling plant operated for 30 years in Oxford, has contaminated soil that requires remediation. That’s underway, said Jason Hahn, a spokesman for Reworld, formerly known as Covanta.
Funding uncertainties also have held up development.
Construction will cost $12 million, Labarbera estimated. That is not yet funded.
The center last spring landed $980,000 in federal funding, earmarked for Warren County Community College to expand programs to train butchers and food sanitation workers and buy instructional equipment. That’s an annual grant for four years, totaling close to $4 million, Labarbera said.
And one of the bills Steinhardt introduced would provide $3 million in state funding to further expand vocational training. Industry insiders say a longstanding labor shortage in the meatpacking industry, which historically has relied on immigrant workers, is likely to worsen as the Trump administration carries out its mass deportation mission.
Who ultimately will own the site and center also has proven controversial. The county owns the site and plans to donate it to the community college, with the commissioners passing a resolution in April to do so despite objections from residents about smell, traffic, foreign laborers, and cost.
Commissioner Jason J. Sarnoski shared some residents’ concern about removing the property from the tax rolls and voted against the resolution, saying he supported the plan in concept but opposed giving away publicly owned property.
“It is an asset and giving away an asset is not in the best fiscal interest of the taxpayers and not the best fiscal interest of the county,” Sarnoski said.
Labarbera told the New Jersey Monitor that such an “obsession with rateables” does not serve the broader economy well.
“Anytime you try to do anything in New Jersey, you come up to this combination of a fight over rateables and a fight over ‘Well, we don’t want this in our town.’ Almost like a town is an HOA instead of a town,” Labarbera said.
He expects the critics will quiet down as they learn how the slaughterhouse will help New Jersey’s livestock farmers.
The center is expected to handle 6,000 animals in its first year and as many as 17,000 by its fourth year, employ 55 people, and train the next generation of meat-processing professionals, he said. He envisions the college eventually opening satellite slaughter plants elsewhere in the state, with an overarching goal of growing the industry.
“This is bigger than just a meat processing plant,” Labarbera said. “This is truly a benefit for the entire state of New Jersey. This is going to give New Jersey a sustainable local supply chain that is going to be able to withstand economic disruptions, power surges, and pandemics.”

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Critics call for more details about Stratos data center in Utah’s west desert
description: Critics of the Stratos data center are pushing for more details on the plan and criticizing the rapid pace of early approvals for the project.
text:
The sun rises over a part of Hansel Valley, in Box Elder County, near the proposed Stratos Project, a massive data center planned for 40,000 acres of land, on Thursday, May 28, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)Rhonda Lauritzen returned earlier this month to the beach on the northern tip of the Great Salt Lake where she splashed around as a kid. But this time, she was surrounded by dry mud, with no water in sight. 
Lauritzen brought reporters to Monument Point as she and other critics made their case against the proposed Stratos data center in the neighboring Hansel Valley. They wanted to see more than the lake, though, including information on potential environmental costs and which company would move in. The rapid rollout of the project backed by celebrity investor Kevin O’Leary of TV’s “Shark Tank” was also top of mind.  
“The lack of transparency makes me insane,” Lauritzen told Utah News Dispatch. “I mean, that is not what we stand for as a society in America, in Utah, it’s not how we should be doing business, and it just feels like that pendulum has swung so far that maybe it finally swung far enough to wake people up.”
Rhonda Lauritzen and her brother Val Anderson are pictured near Monument Point in Box Elder County on July 13, 2026. They brought a large photograph of their father, taken in the same area decades ago. (Annie Knox/Utah News Dispatch)
As more data centers have cropped up across the country, they’ve brought up concerns including rising power bills and water contamination, transforming the concept of artificial intelligence from something abstract to a topic of discussion at the kitchen table, said Christabel Randolph, associate director of the nonprofit Center for AI and Digital Policy, based in Washington, D.C.
“And at the same time, it’s a real transparency and democratic governance issue,” Randolph said. “People want to know why their leaders are approving these projects when folks are not sure what they’re getting in return.”
In Box Elder County, a citizens’ group has gone to court to pursue a referendum allowing voters to undo the county’s approval.
Stratos developers say the project would bring an initial $30 million to the county and a permanent 2,000 skilled jobs, higher than the 50 jobs data centers typically provide, according to a 2024 Virginia legislative audit of the industry in that state. 
In terms of water, backers say the project wouldn’t draw directly from the Great Salt Lake and would use two kinds of cooling systems to keep servers from overheating: a closed-loop system circulating liquid and air-based cooling. 
They’re also seeking water rights for more than 13,000 acre-feet — enough to supply 26,000 households per year — saying those rights are attached to the land they’re buying. But they contend the data center would use less water than the ranchers there do now. 
Abandoned buildings are pictured at Locomotive Springs on Thursday, May 28, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)
Lauritzen, a resident of neighboring Weber County, who with her brothers runs a business extracting minerals from the lake for use in supplements, said she has concerns the data center’s water consumption will actually be higher. 
“We’re adding to an ecosystem that’s already beyond crisis,” she said. 
Utah lawmakers are doing their own research. At the state Capitol in May, a natural resources panel voted to study impacts from data center development on water, wildlife and air quality  ahead of the 2027 legislative session, though they didn’t name Stratos and haven’t analyzed the issue publicly yet. 
This is the first year Utah is requiring large data centers to report their water use to the state, but the numbers will be reported to the public in the aggregate under HB76. The law allows data centers to raise claims of business confidentiality to keep their information from being broken out individually.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In April, the data center proposal cleared an initial round of approval from Utah’s Military Installation Development Authority, or MIDA. Hundreds protested 10 days later at a meeting of the three-member Box Elder County Commission, which did not take public comment before it gave unanimous support to the project, while others have converged on the Utah Capitol in opposition. 
Rhonda Lauritzen speaks during a rally at the Utah Capitol against the 40,000-acre Stratos data center in Box Elder County. (Annie Knox, Utah News Dispatch)
In response to outcry across the state, Gov. Spencer Cox signed an executive order he said would raise the bar for how Utah evaluates data center proposals, noting they need permits tied to air and water quality. And O’Leary made a concession, halving the project size in response to demands from Senate President Stuart Adams, who had earlier voted to advance it as chair of the MIDA board. 
MIDA, for its part, is pledging a transparent process, to include the creation of a Box Elder County development review committee. The authority said through a spokesperson that the project’s developers would carry out every environmental test required by the state and federal government. 
But an attempt to put a referendum on the ballot and a separate lawsuit filed against MIDA by the left-leaning Alliance for a Better Utah have complicated its path forward. 
“Out of respect for the referendum process and litigation, MIDA is paused on Stratos,” the authority’s spokesperson, Kristin Kenney Williams, said in a statement. 
Adams went on to lose his legislative seat in the Republican primary, a stunning political upset for one of Utah’s most powerful politicians. But as the political dust settles, it’s still not clear exactly how and when Utahns will learn more about the evolving plan. 
Adams had announced early in June that a new source of information on the proposal was on its way, saying “to ensure transparency and public accountability, a centralized public-facing website will be created in coordination with state agencies, so Utahns have access to project information, review materials, environmental analyses and updates as policymakers do throughout the process.” 
While the state hasn’t put up a new portal, Stratos developers have launched their own website aimed at sharing information with the public, but haven’t committed publicly to any schedule of updates. O’Leary Digital did not respond to a request for comment from Utah News Dispatch.
Rhonda Lauritzen and Ben Abbott of Grow the Flow speak with journalists at a stock tank in rural Box Elder County on July 13, 2026. (Annie Knox/Utah News Dispatch)
After a Utah State University professor warned in May of the “extreme” heat the project and its gas power plant could generate — raising temperatures by upward of 20 degrees at night — Stratos backers and Utah Gov. Spencer Cox rejected those estimates as inaccurate. 
Ben Abbott, executive director of conservation group Grow the Flow, said he questions why the developers didn’t fill the information gap first by releasing their own numbers and a plan to manage the effects. 
“This kind of rollout really harms public trust and makes it difficult to do things the right way,” Abbott said.
