title: State officials say Idaho’s wolf population dropped by about 100 wolves to 1,129
description: Idaho’s wolf population decreased to an estimated 1,129 animals in 2025 as state officials work to reduce the population through expanded hunting and trapping, Idaho Department of Fish and Game officials said this month. Statewide, the wolf population is down by an estimated 106 wolves compared to the estimated 2024 wolf population of 1,235. Overall, […]
text:
State officials in Idaho say the wolf population is down and they are trying to reduce it further through aggresive hunting and trapping. File photo courtesy of Eric Cole/U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service)Idaho’s wolf population decreased to an estimated 1,129 animals in 2025 as state officials work to reduce the population through expanded hunting and trapping, Idaho Department of Fish and Game officials said this month.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Statewide, the wolf population is down by an estimated 106 wolves compared to the estimated 2024 wolf population of 1,235.
Overall, the state wolf population has been declining since 2020, when state officials estimated more than 1,650 wolves lived in Idaho. 
 



 Idaho’s estimated wolf population

May 2025: 1,129
May 2024: 1,235
May 2023: 1,333
May 2022: 1,211
May 2021: 1,592
May 2020: 1,688
– Source: Idaho Department of Fish and Game
 



Idaho Department of Fish and Game Wildlife Program Coordinator Cory Mosby said officials believe the wolf population is decreasing because of aggressive hunting and trapping.
“Our wolf population is decreasing statewide, and that is very much an intentional effort by the department,” Mosby said during a July 16 Fish and Game Commission meeting. 
Mosby also said the number of livestock killed and injured by wolves is also trending downward. 
Ghost wolves: As Idaho aims to reduce its wolf population, advocates worry counts aren’t accurate

While the wolf population is going downward, state officials want to see it reduced even more.
Over the past five years, the Idaho Legislature and the Fish and Game Commission have expanded hunting and trapping seasons and expanded the allowable methods used to kill wolves in an effort to further reduce the wolf population down to about 500 animals, state officials have said. 
“In our plan, our objective is to reduce the statewide wolf population to around 500 animals,” Mosby said during the July 16 meeting. “That’s like our ultimate marching orders goal.”
Wolves are a native species that were killed off and driven to the point of local extinction in Idaho and the U.S Rocky Mountains by the 1930s through widespread poisoning and trapping. The U.S. government reintroduced wolves to Idaho and Yellowstone National Park in 1995 and 1996 using wolves captured in Canada, leading to one of the most successful and controversial wildlife recovery stories in American history. 
Following a series of legal battles, wolves were removed from the Endangered Species List in Idaho in 2011, and Fish and Game opened a hunting and trapping season to reduce the number of wolves. 
Wolf populations and the methods for estimating wolf populations are closely scrutinized by some wolf advocates who worry wolves are disappearing and have questioned the accuracy of previous methods Idaho used to estimate its wolf population, the Sun previously reported. 
 How does Idaho come up with its wolf population estimate?

Because wolves live in remote areas and can be difficult to observe closely, state officials estimate the wolf population every year rather than physically count each animal. 
Over the last couple of years, Fish and Game officials have changed the way they estimate the state’s wolf population and when they time the estimate. Now, officials use a method that involves taking genetic information from a tooth from each wolf killed in Idaho and using it to help estimate the number of new wolves born each year and the statewide wolf population, the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. The new method produces a wolf population estimate for May of the previous year.
That’s a change. Through 2023, officials used a series of trail cameras to produce a population estimate for August of the previous year. 
 



  Further reading: Howl, 30 years of wolf reintroduction in Idaho

For more on the history of wolves in Idaho, check out Howl, a longform written series and podcast by the Idaho Capital Sun and Boise State Public Radio.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: ​He fled gang violence. Now this ICE detainee in Aurora tries to avoid deportation.
description: Rudy Villeda Mejía has his own roofing business, a wife and three stepchildren in Washington, near the state’s border with Canada.  He has never been charged with a crime. He entered the U.S. without authorization for a second time in 2010 after he was kidnapped by a violent cartel in Mexico, and has been in […]
text:
Rudy Villeda Mejía, pictured holding his granddaughter, fears deportation back to his native Honduras due to violence he faced in the country. He has lived in the U.S. since 2010. (Photo courtesy of Mabel Shaffer)Rudy Villeda Mejía has his own roofing business, a wife and three stepchildren in Washington, near the state’s border with Canada. 
He has never been charged with a crime. He entered the U.S. without authorization for a second time in 2010 after he was kidnapped by a violent cartel in Mexico, and has been in the U.S. since then, according to a notarized personal statement Villeda Mejía submitted with his visa application, which Newsline reviewed. 
Villeda Mejía attended routine check-ins with immigration officials in Seattle for more than a decade. But U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrested Villeda Mejía at the Denver International Airport on March 30, and he has since been in custody at the ICE detention center in Aurora. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“They just took him in. They didn’t tell him why. They didn’t say he’d done anything wrong. He has no criminal history. They just took him and they detained him,” Henry Hollithron, Villeda Mejía’s attorney, said. 
ICE has “a lot of discretion” when it comes to taking people under its supervision back into custody, but there are certain rules they must follow, and Hollithron said those procedures were not followed when ICE arrested Villeda Mejía. 
“It’s not that they didn’t have the legal authority to detain him, it’s that the way they did it didn’t follow the right procedures,” Hollithron said. 
Courts have denied multiple attempts to get Villeda Mejía released from custody, and his application for a T visa, which is designated for victims of human trafficking, is pending with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services. To get approved for a T visa, the applicant has to physically be in the U.S., Hollithron said, so if Villeda Mejía is deported, the process is cut short.
“The T visa is really his only lawful pathway to … stay with his family. There’s really nothing else,” Hollithron said. “And he can’t do anything through his family unless he stays outside the U.S. for 10 years.” 
Previous attorneys Villeda Mejía worked with never advised that he should apply for a T visa and made several mistakes while filing paperwork in his case, according to Hollithron and Villeda Mejía’s family members. Hollithron, who took on his case after he had already been detained earlier this year, filed an application for a T visa for Villeda Mejía at the start of July. 
Villeda Mejía has attested to immigration authorities that he was kidnapped and held hostage. Court records acknowledge that after two men in Mexico helped him cross the border he was held for ransom for six months in the U.S. and that his family reported this to police in Washington.



Quotation







They just took him in. They didn't tell him why. They didn't say he'd done anything wrong. He has no criminal history. They just took him and they detained him.


– Henry Hollithron, Rudy Villeda Mejía's attorney


A May court order from California blocked ICE from detaining immigrants with pending T visa applications, along with other visas for crime victims. But Villeda Mejía is still in ICE custody, and the Department of Homeland Security said he will remain in ICE custody pending his deportation. 
“He has received full due process,” an unnamed department spokesperson said in an email to Newsline. The Denver ICE Field Office did not answer questions about Villeda Mejía’s arrest, his visa application or plans to release him from detention or deport him. 
Family and business struggling
Mabel Shaffer, Villeda Mejía’s wife, has hip displacement, and he takes care of her full time. Since he has been in ICE custody, she has worked to keep their business afloat, while doing her best to care for herself with the help of loved ones. Walking for too long causes extreme pain for her, and she struggles to put on socks and shoes by herself. 
“There’s a lot of things that Rudy does, and he takes care of me, but it’s been very hard on me,” Shaffer said. “Our family is completely stressed out. I’m a mess.”
Shaffer met Villeda Mejía through a mutual friend in 2011 and they started dating shortly after in 2012. They got married in 2014, and she said “he’s been a really good stepfather to my children.”
“My kids basically grew up with no other figure, so he was a good example to them,” Shaffer said. 
Shaffer came to Colorado to visit her husband over the Fourth of July, and she said “he’s a wreck. I’ve never seen him so badly.” He was moved to a newer part of the ICE detention facility in Aurora, and Shaffer said he isn’t able to go outside for fresh air frequently. He’s concerned about contracting illnesses in the detention center, and Shaffer said he’s lost weight because there are not enough food options. 
Rudy Villeda Mejía runs a roofing business in northern Washington that has struggled since U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrested him in March. (Photo courtesy of Mabel Shaffer)
Villeda Mejía calls Shaffer to speak with her several times a day, she said. Those calls cost money, but Shaffer said he tries to give her advice to help her manage their business on her own. She’s worried about telling customers that her husband is in ICE custody, too, because she has had negative reactions from some people who she told. 
Villeda Mejía builds custom metal roofs, and he is the only person at this company with the specialized skills to manage certain parts of their jobs, Shaffer said. The company has not been able to complete many of the jobs they otherwise would with Villeda Mejía leading them, Shaffer said. 
“Nobody can replace Rudy,” Shaffer said. 
The business is struggling to repay loans for new equipment the company purchased, Shaffer said. Her husband is not a flight risk because of how much he has invested into his family, business and community, she said. 
“Since he’s been incarcerated, the business has been hurting a lot,” Shaffer said. “I’m trying to keep the employees with their job, but it really is getting more challenging as the time goes by because he’s been incarcerated for going on four months.”
History of violence
Court orders related to his case, the notarized personal statement from Villeda Mejía, Hollithron and family members offered details of his immigration history and why he left his native Honduras.
Villeda Mejía grew up surrounded by gang violence in Honduras. He remembers walking by the house of one of his school teachers when he was about 10 years old and seeing the teacher’s severed head. Gangs repeatedly tried to recruit him, and they threatened him as he continued to refuse. He ultimately decided that his “life would not be safe” if he stayed in Honduras and he left in 2007. 
Colorado health officials still unable to investigate tuberculosis case at ICE detention facility

When Villeda Mejía first entered the U.S. in 2007, after traveling from Honduras through Guatemala and Mexico, he was sick, dehydrated and malnourished from the trip. Border Patrol agents detained him and ordered he be removed from the country. 
Villeda Mejía expressed fear of returning to Honduras and awaited a conversation with an asylum officer for a “credible fear” interview. That interview never happened, and Homeland Security officials pressured Villeda Mejía to sign a request to end the credible fear process, though he later testified that he did not know what he signed at the time. 
Signing that document resulted in a final order of removal that prohibited Villeda Mejía from returning to the U.S. for five years. He went back to Honduras and received emergency medical treatment. 
He attempted to reestablish himself in Honduras, but violence continued to follow him. Villeda Mejía worked at a computer repair shop, and in October 2009, gang members came in and demanded he repair their phones. While repairing the phones, Villeda Mejía found and unintentionally deleted videos of the gang members “killing and hurting people while dressed like officers from the Honduran authorities,” according to his personal statement. The gang members threatened him at gunpoint and demanded he restore the videos, which he did. 
Villeda Mejía and his cousin attempted to relocate to a different part of the country, but gang members found and beat them. He left the country again, traveling through Guatemala to Mexico. 
In the summer in 2010 in Mexico, two armed men approached Villeda Mejía and told him they could help him get documents to work legally in the U.S. He followed them to a car and they drove him to an unknown location, and soon after demanded Villeda Mejía share contact information for his family. When his family did not answer after two phone calls, they beat Villeda Mejía.
“The third time, they got through and shouted down the line, ‘We took him yesterday, and if you don’t pay, we’ll send him back in pieces!’” Villeda Mejía said in his personal statement. “I suffered many indignities at their hands, though they did receive some money from my family.”
After “endless days” in captivity, Villeda Mejía got into a car with a driver and the two men who initially approached him. The car drove for several hours, and they eventually reached the southern border of the U.S. A Border Patrol official waved the car through. 
“That was how I last entered the United States — I have not left this country since then,” Villeda Mejía said. 
Hollithron said Los Zetas cartel members trafficked Villeda Mejía into the U.S. before they held him for ransom, making him a victim of human trafficking and eligible for a T visa. The men brought Villeda Mejía to an abandoned house and continued to beat him and hold him captive after his family did not answer requests for money.

Have a news tip?


CONTACT US



“The mistreatment continued every day. I could not sleep for the sounds of women weeping and men crying out in pain that never seemed to fade,” Villeda Mejía said. “Since I was constantly held in the dark, I have no idea how long I spent there.”
Eventually, they blindfolded Villeda Mejía and put him in another car. He thought they were going to kill him. The car drove for a long time, and then they told him to get out of the car and “not to speak of what had happened.” 
“They warned me that they would keep track of me always,” Villeda Mejía said. “Then, they told me to walk straight forward and not to go left or right, else they would shoot me.”
He kept walking and ended up at a mall. A family gave him some coins so he could call his family, and Villeda Mejía’s family told him that they paid the Los Zetas cartel $3,000. His father reported what happened with the cartel to police in Washington, who sent the information to Homeland Security. 
“To this day, I am still experiencing the after-effects of my ordeal with Los Zetas,” Villeda Mejía said. “I find it very difficult to trust anyone, cannot be in a room with the lights off, and have a lot of nightmares. I have also been diagnosed with Bell’s Palsy as a result of what I went through.”
Attended every check-in
Villeda Mejía moved to Washington and began to build a life. He met and married his wife. He started a business. In 2014, ICE detained him and reinstated the initial removal order against him. He was held in ICE detention for about six months and was released on a $5,000 bond.
Certain options for Villeda Mejía, like legal residency through his wife, who is a U.S. citizen, are off the table because of the paper he signed the first time he came into the U.S. 
“Because he was ordered removed and he came back, even if involuntarily, he came back without permission, so that pathway is cut off,” Hollithron said. 
An immigration judge denied Villeda Mejía’s requests for protection in 2016, and his appeal of that decision was also denied in 2017. ICE ultimately released Villeda Mejía from custody and required that he check in at the Seattle Field Office periodically. Subsequent motions to reopen his case were all denied. He attended every check-in from August 2018 until April 2025. He did not make his next scheduled check in April after he was detained at the Denver International Airport, where he had a layover flying home from a trip visiting family on the East Coast.
The next step is for Hollithron to file a motion asking Judge Regina Rodriguez with the U.S. District Court of Colorado to reconsider her denial of Villeda Mejía’s habeas corpus petition — a legal mechanism that challenges wrongful detention — because she did not consider the legality of how ICE arrested and detained him in the first place. Some judges have issued orders that say ICE’s noncompliance with rules around detaining someone justify the person’s immediate release, Hollithron said. 
“Separately from whether he can be removed to Honduras or not, is ICE, they didn’t follow the procedures. If they want to detain and deport him, they have to follow the rules, just like they expect the people they are targeting to follow the rules,” Hollithron said. “And if they don’t, then they should not benefit from their breaking of the rules.”
Rodriguez on July 17 denied a separate request to pause Villeda Mejía’s deportation while his attorney appealed her denial of his habeas corpus petition. That means he could still be deported at any time.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Fifty for 150: Katharine Lee Bates writes ‘America the Beautiful’ following 1893 visit to Pikes Peak
description: Poet Katharine Lee Bates spent the summer of 1893 teaching English at the Colorado Summer School at Colorado College in Colorado Springs, on a leave of absence from Wellesley College in Massachusetts. By that time, she was already a published poet and author of works including the novel “Rose and Thorn” and contributions in newspapers […]
text:
A view of Pikes Peak in El Paso County, photographed by George Beam in the 1920s. (Photo Courtesy of Denver Public Library Special Collections, GB-5272)Poet Katharine Lee Bates spent the summer of 1893 teaching English at the Colorado Summer School at Colorado College in Colorado Springs, on a leave of absence from Wellesley College in Massachusetts. By that time, she was already a published poet and author of works including the novel “Rose and Thorn” and contributions in newspapers such as The New York Times, The Atlantic Monthly and the Boston Evening Transcript. 
 


This story is part of Colorado at 150. Each Fifty for 150 story focuses on an event that helped define Colorado over 150 years of statehood. Newsline is publishing one Fifty for 150 story every weekday in reverse chronological order until the sesquicentennial, Aug. 1, when the final of 50 stories, about the declaration of statehood, will appear.



Bates, then 33 years old, wrote the start of the poem that would become “America the Beautiful” while on a trip to the summit of Pikes Peak, one of Colorado’s many peaks that soar above 14,000 feet. Indigenous people referred to the mountain as Tava-kaavi or “Sun Mountain.”
Later, Bates remembered of that ascent that the group had to abandon their wagon near the top and finish the route with mules. Nowadays, travelers can drive, hike or ride the cog railway to the top of the mountain and rest at the visitor’s center.
“I was very tired. But when I saw the view, I felt great joy. All the wonder of America seemed displayed there, with the sea-like expanse,” Bates wrote.
Bates published the poem two years later in the nationally-circulated magazine The Congregationalist and revised it at least twice in the early 20th Century. Eventually, the poem was set to the tune of the 1882 song “Materna,” written by Samuel Augustus Ward.
For over 100 years, people have sung the iconic song, which includes the first stanza:

O beautiful for spacious skies,
For amber waves of grain,
For purple mountain majesties
Above the fruited plain!
America! America!
God shed His grace on thee
And crown thy good with brotherhood
From sea to shining sea!

title: Lack of access to adequate healthcare impacts Alabama infant mortality rates
description: Alabama’s infant mortality rate improved in 2024, but access to adequate healthcare impacts outcomes for babies in their first year of life.  According to data from the Alabama Department of Public Health, the state’s infant mortality rate was 7.1 babies per 1,000 live births in 2024, reflecting the rate of infants who died within their […]
text:
Sierra Edgio talks about her birth experience as Ramona crawls on the carpet at the Alabama Birth Center Wednesday, April 15, 2026 in Huntsville, Ala. One reproductive health provider said that birth centers, and access to them, is one way to reduce Alabama's infant mortality rate. (Eric Schultz for Alabama Reflector)Alabama’s infant mortality rate improved in 2024, but access to adequate healthcare impacts outcomes for babies in their first year of life. 
According to data from the Alabama Department of Public Health, the state’s infant mortality rate was 7.1 babies per 1,000 live births in 2024, reflecting the rate of infants who died within their first year of life. That was down from 7.8 deaths per 1,000 births in 2023, which was a seven-year high.
State Health Officer Dr. Scott Harris wrote in a letter to state lawmakers in the Fiscal Year 2025 Perinatal Report that the maternal and infant health crisis is not unique to Alabama.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Lack of access to care, closure of labor and delivery services, poverty, poor nutrition and chronic disease play significant roles in the health of mothers and infants,” he wrote. “With the purpose to improve, promote and protect health, it is essential that we address the factors that contribute to maternal and infant poor health outcomes.”
Alabama infant mortality rate, and locations of hospitals that offer delivery services. (ADPH)
Some of the counties with the highest infant mortality rates do not have an active delivering hospital, according to the ADPH data. There were 41 counties in Alabama without an active delivering hospital in 2024, and there were 42 active delivering hospitals elsewhere in the state.
According to the University of North Carolina’s Sheps Center, nine rural hospitals have closed in Alabama since 2009. Only 30% of the state’s rural hospitals have labor and delivery units, leaving many expectant parents to drive long distances for care. Providence Hospital in Mobile closed its labor and delivery services at the end of June.
While the infant mortality rate has been on a downward trend nationwide over the past 50 years, it has been more mixed in Alabama. Harris said reducing infant mortality is challenging, but important work, in an interview after the report was released earlier this month.
Alabama’s infant mortality rate has fluctuated over the last decade, according to data from the Alabama Department of Public Health. (ADPH)
Alabama’s infant mortality rate has fluctuated over the last decade while the national average has been on a downward trend. (ADPH)
“We want legislators and then their constituents to understand the importance of the work we do around infant mortality and keeping moms and babies safe. Alabama consistently ranks low nationally in how well we do with that, but it’s not because we aren’t trying,” Harris said. “We have a lot of tremendous people who are doing great work, but it’s really difficult to overcome a lot of the barriers that people have in our state, and we just want our legislature to understand that.”
The leading causes of death for infants in 2024 were congenital anomalies, preterm births and low birth weight (LBW), and bacterial sepsis. The three accounted for 42.5% of infant deaths in 2024. Racial disparities were observed in the top two leading causes of infant death, according to the report. About 74% of babies who died from congenital anomalies were white, and about 65% of babies who died from preterm and LBW were Black. 
Robin Marty, executive director of WAWC Healthcare, said in an interview that losing access to labor and delivery services means losing access to prenatal care.
“We are not getting the follow-up care that babies need in their first year in order to make sure that they have healthy lives,” Marty said. “That’s the inherent problem: when you lose hospitals, you lose those doctors as well. Once you increase the burden of a mother being able to get to a pediatrician, a mother being able to get into an OB/GYN for their prenatal care, a mother being able to get the follow-up care that they need and get all of those appointments that they need, that’s how you get low birth rates. That’s how you get people who go into premature labor, and that’s how you get infants that are dying at birth or within just a year of their birth.”
WAWC used to provide abortion services, but now it provides prenatal and pregnancy services, contraceptives, STI/STD testing, gender-affirming care and annual exams. 
In western Alabama, there were two inactive delivering hospitals in 2024 in Greene and Clarke counties. The infant mortality rates in the region range from 4.8 deaths per 1,000 births in Monroe County to 31.1 deaths per 1,000 births in Wilcox County. Some counties in the region did not report data. 
A 2023 report from March of Dimes, a nonprofit, identified 22 Alabama counties as “maternity care deserts,” most of which were in the western part of the state. 
“We have moms who have difficulty with transportation to get care. We have many counties that just don’t have providers that are available,” Harris said. “We have a lot of people who can’t afford to get the care they need. We have people who just haven’t been educated on how to keep themselves healthy, and how to have a healthy pregnancy and how to take care of their baby very well.”
Infant mortality rates for Black Alabamians remain disproportionately high. The infant mortality rate among white Alabamians was 5.4 deaths per 1,000 live births in 2024. For Black Alabamians, the rate was 11.8 per 1,000. In 2023, the rates were 5.7 and 13.1 deaths per 1,000 births, respectively.
Black babies make up about one-quarter of Alabama’s births, but more than 40% of its infant deaths. (ADPH)
Rep. Marilyn Lands, D-Huntsville, said in an interview that Alabama should consider a different approach when caring for pregnant patients.
“I think there’s a lot that can be done with looking at the role of doulas and midwives and the scope of practice for nurse practitioners,” she said. “I’m really encouraged by the community health model.”
Huntsville Hospital, a non-profit community hospital, in June awarded $600,000 total to 11 local non-profits that aim to improve overall health outcomes across the region, according to a press release. 
According to the Perinatal report, incorporating “evidence-based efforts will help address factors impacting health outcomes such as access to healthcare, geographical disparities, lack of quality education, poverty and unemployment.”
“The big difference I think is that we’re when you have a low birth weight or a preemie, and this is a population that, because of lack of prenatal care, but also lack of preventative healthcare and all of the other isms – lack of food, lack of clean water – that is why we are seeing lower lower birth weights and also early early births,” Marty said.
Solutions
Elisabeth Nussel, clinic manager, talks about the resources available at the Alabama Birth Center Wednesday, April 15, 2026 in Huntsville, Ala. (Eric Schultz for Alabama Reflector)
The report also included suggestions for the Legislature for the future, like continuing the Perinatal Report program and increasing the number of autopsies performed on maternal deaths. The last Maternal Mortality Review done by ADPH was released in 2021. It found that 78% of the reviewed deaths were preventable.
Marty said that the Legislature and ADPH should do more, including “get over whatever their issue is with birth centers.”
“That is the number one thing that they can do. And once that is released, then that would allow the opportunity to be able to open up the whole area, quite frankly, to being able to have more access to healthcare,” Marty said.
ADPH and birth centers in the state have been in a legal battle for years because the department wants to regulate the centers – which provide an option between home and hospital birth – as it does hospitals. 
A Montgomery County judge ruled last week that the centers can keep operating despite a ruling earlier this year subjecting them to the regulation after Harris sent the centers cease-and-desist letters in June. 
Alabama birth center licenses still valid despite appellate court ruling, says Montgomery judge

Lands, who often sponsors reproductive care-related legislation, said in an interview that incorporating midwifery and doula care, and community-based care could help close the care gap in rural areas.
“I think we really have to get creative and rethink the way we’re delivering prenatal care and taking care of pregnancy and newborns,” Lands said. “I think we need a new model. This one size fits all that we’ve been offering here is not working for us.”
Lands sponsored the House version of a 2025 law that allows pregnant people to be eligible for Medicaid, which sunsets in 2028. Marty said she was frustrated that the access to health insurance was not mentioned in the report.
According to a 2025 memo sent to Alabama providers and hospitals from the Alabama Medicaid Agency, providers and insurance determiners have to complete a training and sign a waiver with the agency in order to become a “qualified determiner” of presumptive eligibility for pregnancy. A message seeking comment from the Alabama Medicaid Agency was left Friday.
“There is no mention of the fact that actually training doctors to recognize or training healthcare providers to recognize that this is a person who could be qualified be able to get them their care as quickly as possible and get them into Medicaid as quickly as possible,” Marty said. “That would save lives, and that is not mentioned at all.”

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Lee signs onto Trump data center cost protection pledge as local communities push for regulation
description: Gov. Bill Lee last week joined 22 Republican governors in signing onto President Donald Trump’s “Ratepayer Protection Pledge,” a voluntary agreement to hold companies responsible for the costs of building, maintaining and powering data centers.  The Trump administration has publicly touted the pledge as sparing taxpayers from tax and electricity rate hikes t[...]
text:
Billionaire Elon Musk's xAI supercomputer is in a predominantly Black Memphis neighborhood already affected negatively by environmental pollution. (Photo: Karen Pulfer Focht for Tennessee Lookout)Gov. Bill Lee last week joined 22 Republican governors in signing onto President Donald Trump’s “Ratepayer Protection Pledge,” a voluntary agreement to hold companies responsible for the costs of building, maintaining and powering data centers. 
The Trump administration has publicly touted the pledge as sparing taxpayers from tax and electricity rate hikes tied to data centers, even as communities across Tennessee and the U.S. push back on plans for the massive data infrastructure projects in their own backyards.
Tech companies including Google, Meta and OpenAI have also signed onto the pledge, which positions data center expansion as essential to the nation’s future.
“America’s continued economic and technological leadership depends on reliable, large-scale data center infrastructure built here at home,” the pledge says.
On Friday, Lee posted a message of thanks to Trump for introducing the pledge.
“Tennessee has shown we can lead the nation in innovation while protecting hardworking families from higher utility bills, & we’re grateful for your leadership to advance policies that strengthen our economy & secure America’s future,” Lee posted on X.
There may be an appetite among voters for ratepayer protections with more teeth, according to Sarah Hunt, president and CEO of Rainey Center, a Washington, D.C.-based nonprofit public policy research organization.
“Only 9% of voters that we polled had even heard that these tech companies had voluntarily signed onto this pledge that the White House had put together, and 61% of voters, after we tell them about it, want to see Congress make the Ratepayer Protection Pledge binding law,” Hunt said during a July Infrastructure Summit hosted by the Tennessee Chamber of Commerce and Industry.


The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency has declined to set nationwide environmental standards for data centers, instead leaving regulatory decisions to states and local governments. 
Tennessee lawmakers this year passed a law stipulating that owners of data centers that require at least 50 megawatts of power must pay for any infrastructure upgrades needed to produce the electricity the data center demands. Sen. Brent Taylor, a Shelby County Republican and the law’s senate sponsor, said the law is meant to protect ratepayers from power bill increases.
But the law has some caveats: if the infrastructure upgrades benefit other ratepayers or follow normal rules that apply to all large electricity customers, utilities can help data centers cover the cost. 
The law alternatively allows data centers to power themselves using equipment like gas-powered turbines — without state or local oversight — raising concerns from environmental groups and community coalitions who say these turbines pollute the air and emit continuous sound. Data centers may also purchase power from independent producers that operate outside of public utilities.
Tennessee lawmakers did not pass six other bills introduced this year that would have set up guardrails for data centers, ranging from registration and permitting requirements to mandatory reporting on water, electricity and fuel use.
Multiple local governments across the state have instituted moratoriums on data center project approvals while they create regulations for the growing industry.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Proposed North Dakota pig iron plant to turn Minnesota mine waste into steel, a first for US
description: This is the first in a two-part series about North Dakota projects that would process Minnesota mining materials. Coming tomorrow, read about a potential nickel processing facility. CALUMET, Minn. – Enormous piles of iron-rich waste sitting dormant in Minnesota are about to see movement for the first time in decades, soon heading hundreds of miles […]
text:
Structures from a defunct mining operation stand on the Hill Annex Mine State Park in Calumet, Minnesota, on July 13, 2026. Calumet Reclamation proposes to reclaim the iron waste and transport it to Minot, North Dakota, for processing. (Photo by Peyton Haug/For the North Dakota Monitor)This is the first in a two-part series about North Dakota projects that would process Minnesota mining materials. Coming tomorrow, read about a potential nickel processing facility.
CALUMET, Minn. – Enormous piles of iron-rich waste sitting dormant in Minnesota are about to see movement for the first time in decades, soon heading hundreds of miles west to North Dakota.  
North American Iron plans to develop a 2,400-acre site near Minot to produce pig iron, an essential ingredient in steel-making. The operation, which could produce 2 million metric tons annually, would be the first of its kind in the country and aims to boost domestic production.
Jim Bougalis, CEO and founder of North American Iron and sister company Calumet Reclamation Co., said high tariffs and global conflict, coupled with North Dakota’s interest in the project, added to its momentum. 
The facility is slated to bring 650 permanent jobs to the Minot area.
“This is one of those projects that adds an economic pillar to our city and region,” said Mark Lyman, economic development specialist for the Minot Area Chamber. “It being so brand new adds diversification to our economy.”
Iron to feed the country for ‘centuries’
The Mesabi Iron Range, famous for its mining activity, encompasses over 100 miles of northeastern Minnesota, where industry and population has ebbed and flowed drastically for nearly 150 years, ramping up when the price of ore does and downturning when it falls. 
Because America’s steel-ready pig iron is imported from other countries, the Trump administration’s aggressive tariff policies have made it expensive to import from major producing countries — namely Brazil, Ukraine and Russia. The military depends heavily on the material to build things like warheads, submarines and aircrafts.  
Jim Bougalis, CEO and founder of North American Iron and sister company Calumet Reclamation Co., holds unprocessed ore at the Calumet Reclamation offices on July 13, 2026. (Photo by Peyton Haug/For the North Dakota Monitor)A closeup view of mining waste from Calumet, Minnesota, that Calumet Reclamation proposes to reclaim and transport to North Dakota. (Photo courtesy of Calumet Reclamation)Ore travels on Canadian National Railway Company cars through the Mesabi Iron Range in Minnesota on July 13, 2026. Iron-rich waste in Calumet, Minnesota, will travel by rail approximately 500 miles to North Dakota for processing. (Photo by Peyton Haug/For the North Dakota Monitor)
Bougalis grew up on the range in Hibbing, just down the road from Calumet where his company holds mineral leases for millions of tons of iron-rich waste sitting on 20 square miles. 
Minnesota has enough iron to feed the country for centuries, according to Bougalis, who claims there are approximately 3 billion tons sitting on the surface of the range. 
Stockpiles dating back to the second World War stretch city blocks and stand like small mountains, some over 300 feet tall. Soon, the waste will be railed nearly 500 miles to Minot.
The project is being touted as a low-impact way to domestically produce iron, not only because it will put to use idle waste, but because it will be processed using newer technology that emits far less carbon than traditional processing. 
In essence, the rock or “feed stock” is crushed and made into preconcentrate, material that resembles a pile of wet sand. That process takes place in Minnesota before hitting the rail to North Dakota. 
When it reaches the pig iron plant, the material is then concentrated into a finer sand or dirt-like substance before transforming into small iron pellets to be later used for steel.
A site rendering shows the proposed North American Iron pig iron plant planned for northeast of Minot. (Courtesy of North American Iron)
Pig iron factories have historically involved workers shoveling coal into huge blast furnaces to burn oxygen off the iron, turning ore into liquid and emitting carbon dioxide in the process. It’s among the most intensive parts of production. 
The facility going up in Minot, however, will use a lower-temperature chemical process to remove the oxygen from the iron ore without turning it into liquid. The highly mechanized system has both less risky working conditions and fewer emissions, reflecting how technological advancements have changed the industry. 
Instead of using coal to refine the ore, the facility will use the hydrogen found in natural gas, which emits water vapor, not carbon dioxide. 
The company is working with the Energy and Environmental Research Center at the University of North Dakota to explore the potential for underground carbon dioxide storage at the site, Bougalis said. No applications have been filed so far for carbon sequestration wells, and planning materials submitted to state environmental regulators don’t include that process.
Minot’s new neighbor
The project was initially proposed for Underwood, North Dakota, but is now planned for industrial land northeast of Minot near the Air Force base. Renderings show the tallest structure standing more than 250 feet, a height that rivals the North Dakota Capitol. 
It will recycle city waste water, not drinking water, using a closed-looped system, Lyman said. A heavy film will be sprayed over the ore in Minnesota to minimize dust as it travels. 
A major component of the planned site is using natural gas produced in western North Dakota. WBI Energy is proposing the Minot Industrial Pipeline, an 87-mile project to bring up to 250 million cubic feet per day of natural gas from Tioga, according to the North Dakota Pipeline Authority. A WBI spokesperson said the project is still under development and the final scope is subject to customer commitments, regulatory review and final project approvals. The pipeline would require approval from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission.
The pig iron plant also will involve construction of a 300-megawatt natural gas-fired power generation facility at the Minot site, according to Bougalis.
“The opportunity to keep natural gas in the state and use it to the benefit of a new industry is a win all around,” Lyman said.
Reclaimed ore, high prices mean Minnesota iron could head to North Dakota

The 650 jobs added to Minot will include high-paying jobs, company leaders say. 
When it comes to finding workers, Calumet Reclamation plans to start recruiting locally with North Dakota universities and the Minot Air Force Base. It will then turn its efforts national before handing off recruitment to a third party for building an immigrant workforce, if necessary, according to Bougalis. 
Lyman of Minot said the city has plenty of housing to accommodate the incoming workforce. Peak construction will entail up to 4,000 jobs. 
“I don’t think we’re in some housing crunch that’s unsolvable, even with a couple thousand employees. But still, we’re thinking about that. We’re already talking with property developers,” he said. 
Why North Dakota? 
Access to surplus power, quicker permitting and existing infrastructure makes it cheaper to build a factory in North Dakota than in Minnesota, Bougalis said. 
He said North Dakota has also become one of the project’s biggest investors, putting in $7 million from the Clean Sustainable Energy Authority and just over $2.6 million from the Department of Commerce. 
North American Iron proposes a pig iron plant in this area northeast of Minot, North Dakota. (Photo by Jacob Orledge/North Dakota Monitor)
Northwest Landowners Association Chairman Troy Coons said the group doesn’t have an official stance on the project, but he hopes the development adequately addresses environmental and landowner impacts on the front end.
He noted that industries often come to North Dakota for processing because Minnesota regulations are more strict. 
The Minnesota Department of Natural Resources is conducting an environmental review known as an environmental assessment worksheet. Once that becomes public, which is anticipated this fall, that will prompt a 30-day public comment period, according to a spokesperson. After that, the department will evaluate whether a more rigorous environmental impact statement is required, the department said.
Company proposes to upcycle Minnesota iron mine waste in central North Dakota

In North Dakota, regulators are evaluating an application for an air quality permit, said Karl Rockeman, deputy director of the Department of Environmental Quality.
Together, various aspects of the operation — from the gas-powered energy generation to the iron roasting machines — will be considered a “major source” of potential air pollution under the Clean Air Act, meaning the company will have to demonstrate its emissions are below a certain threshold and monitored regularly, Rockeman said.
The department’s Division of Solid Waste also will evaluate the project, Rockeman said.
Both reviews require a 30-day public comment period, neither of which have happened yet. Rockeman said the company could also need a permit for wastewater disposal, but that plan is still being developed. 
The company’s application for an air quality permit can be found on the department’s public portal. 
Calumet Reclamation and North American Iron expect permitting to be completed this fall, with construction expected to begin around 2027 and production commencing in 2029.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Courts order North Dakota to pay landowners’ legal fees in two lawsuits
description: A judge this month awarded North Dakota landowners attorney fees in a lawsuit against the state over a property rights law found to be unconstitutional. The ruling means the state could owe nearly $975,000 in legal costs to the landowners and groups behind three related court challenges filed since 2019.  “We are grateful that the […]
text:
Bismarck attorney Derrick Braaten updates landowners on the status of pore space litigation against the state of North Dakota on Feb. 2, 2026. (Photo by Jacob Orledge/North Dakota Monitor)A judge this month awarded North Dakota landowners attorney fees in a lawsuit against the state over a property rights law found to be unconstitutional.
The ruling means the state could owe nearly $975,000 in legal costs to the landowners and groups behind three related court challenges filed since 2019. 
“We are grateful that the court recognized not only the merits of our case, but also the substantial time, effort, and expense required to defend our property rights,” Kurt Swenson, a landowner in Oliver and Mercer counties, said in a statement.
Swenson is the lead plaintiff in a lawsuit challenging the North Dakota Industrial Commission’s decision to grant permits for Summit Carbon Solutions’ proposal to inject carbon dioxide gathered from five states into underground storage in North Dakota. 
Summit permit for CO2 storage voided as second judge finds North Dakota law unconstitutional

The storage involves injecting carbon dioxide deep underground into small cavities called pore space for long-term storage in order to receive federal tax credits. But some landowners have challenged the constitutionality of the North Dakota law, which allows the Industrial Commission to authorize the use of pore space without landowners’ consent. These opponents argue the state’s actions violate their property rights.
South Central Judicial District Judge Jackson Lofgren agreed. He ruled earlier this year the law was unconstitutional because it did not guarantee “just compensation,” determined by a jury, to be paid to the landowners for the use of their pore space.
This month, Lofgren went a step further and ruled the landowners who filed the lawsuit can recover about $429,000 in attorney fees and legal costs from the state. 
“Families should not have to spend years and significant resources fighting the State simply to keep what is already theirs. The ruling confirms that when the government overreaches, there can be real consequences,” Swenson said. 
South Central Judicial District Judge Jackson Lofgren presides over a trial to determine the constitutionality of North Dakota’s ban on gender affirming care for minors on Feb. 3, 2025. (Mary Steurer/North Dakota Monitor)
Derrick Braaten, a Bismarck attorney representing Swenson and other landowners in the case, said it was important that Lofgren ruled the Industrial Commission was not “substantially justified” in issuing the storage permits to Summit. 
“What the judge is saying is, it’s not just unconstitutional. It wasn’t even a close call,” Braaten said.
This is the second time in eight months that a district court judge ruled the law was unconstitutional and the state is responsible for paying the attorney fees and legal costs of the people who challenged it. 
Northeast Judicial District Judge Anthony Swain Benson first declared the law to be unconstitutional in December of last year, reaching a similar legal conclusion as Lofgren later did, in a case brought by the Northwest Landowners Association and North Dakota Farm Bureau. That case challenged the law itself, rather than the permits issued to Summit. 
Benson ordered the state to reimburse the Northwest Landowners Association and North Dakota Farm Bureau approximately $278,000.
Both cases are being appealed to the North Dakota Supreme Court. If the Supreme Court overturns the district courts’ decisions, the roughly $707,000 the state has been ordered in attorney fees and legal costs would also be reversed. 
“We’re going to be challenging the attorney fees awards and appealing them as part of our broader appeal of the case,” the Attorney General’s Office said in a statement.
North Dakota judge rules in favor of landowners, finds law unconstitutional

Lofgren’s decision to award attorney fees in the case was supported, in part, by his observation that the Legislature had the opportunity to correct the law’s “constitutional defects.” The judge wrote that a reasonable interpretation of a related court case, resolved in 2022, would lead to the conclusion this law was unconstitutional. 
The Northwest Landowners Association previously challenged a 2019 law that excluded pore space from the definition of land and allowed the pore space to be used for oilfield operations, such as injecting carbon dioxide or disposing of saltwater, while prohibiting the surface owner from asking for payment. 
The North Dakota Supreme Court ruled the law was unconstitutional in 2022. Benson, the district court judge in that case as well, ordered the state to reimburse the landowners association for about $266,000 in attorney fees.
After the latest district court rulings, Rep. Todd Porter said lawmakers will likely wait until the Supreme Court definitively settles the dispute before taking any further action. 
Rep. Todd Porter, R-Mandan, speaks during a meeting of the Emergency Response Services Committee on Feb. 25, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
“The law is not in effect, and so there really isn’t anything to do until the Supreme Court comes out with their ruling,” Porter said.
Porter, R-Mandan, has been the chair of the House’s energy committee for more than a decade. He said the 2009 law at issue was an attempt to tackle a complex subject during the brevity of an 80-day legislative session. 
Porter said it is possible the Legislature may not consider any changes to the law until the 2029 legislative session, if the Supreme Court confirms it is unconstitutional, depending on the timing of the decision. The next legislative session begins in January and typically ends by early May.
“They will tell us what we did wrong and what we did right,” Porter said. “That sometimes will make us go back to square one and start over and create an even better law that meets the muster of what the court has decided.”
North Dakota Monitor reporter Jacob Orledge can be reached at jorledge@northdakotamonitor.com.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Beard talks priorities, pivot from Nebraska primary election to Nov. 3 faceoff
description: Editor’s note: This is the third in a three-part series with Nebraska gubernatorial candidates about their pivot from the May 12 primary election to the Nov. 3 general election. LINCOLN — Rick Beard knows the uphill climb he faces to be elected Nebraska’s next governor but feels his third-party status and ideas for a state-run medical […]
text:
Rick Beard of Omaha, the Legal Marijuana NOW nominee for Nebraska governor, meets with voters at a developmental disabilities community listening event on April 30, 2026, in Lincoln a couple weeks before the May 12 primary election. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)Editor’s note: This is the third in a three-part series with Nebraska gubernatorial candidates about their pivot from the May 12 primary election to the Nov. 3 general election.
LINCOLN — Rick Beard knows the uphill climb he faces to be elected Nebraska’s next governor but feels his third-party status and ideas for a state-run medical cannabis program to generate new tax revenue could appeal to voters.
In a one-on-one interview with the Nebraska Examiner a few weeks after the May primary, Beard, the gubernatorial nominee for the Legal Marijuana NOW party, outlined his top priorities if elected: legalizing strong medical cannabis and industrial hemp programs, getting corporate and political action committee money out of the state and taking a more serious, in-depth look at data centers, including a pause on development and mandated closed-loop cooling systems.
Beard, a wine professional and private chef, will face Republican Gov. Jim Pillen of Columbus and former Democratic State Sen. Lynne Walz of Fremont.
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen of Columbus, a Republican at center, is running for reelection against former Democratic State Sen. Lynne Walz of Fremont, left, and Rick Beard of Omaha, the nominee for the Legal Marijuana NOW party. (Photos courtesy of the candidates/campaigns | Nebraska Capitol photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
The trio could also face former State Sen. Brett Lindstrom of Omaha, an ex-Republican and now registered nonpartisan who announced a signature campaign to appear on the Nov. 3 ballot. His deadline is Aug. 3, in one week.
Of why Beard is the right choice, he said he understands working-class issues and has the “most realistic, solid, viable plan” to help Nebraska. Still, he recognizes the hard path for third-party candidates and sees 2026 as his shot to share his ideas and make a difference.
“If there’s any year that a third party is going to stand out and shine,” Beard said, “I think that this is the year more than any other year that we’ve had in the past.”
State-run medical cannabis program
Beard said he woke up a couple of days after the May primary with his “big idea” to mitigate and avoid the fears of politicians worried about “big cannabis,” “bad players” or cartels. He proposed that the state runs “everything” around medical cannabis, such as hiring farmers, buying facilities and overseeing land.
“All along the way, we make the money, we make all the profit and we make the taxes,” Beard said.
Commissioners on the Nebraska Medical Cannabis Commission during an April 13, 2026, meeting. From left, Commissioners Bud Synhorst of Lincoln, Jim Elworth of Nebraska City, Lorelle Mueting of Gretna (interim chair) and J. Michael Coffey of Omaha. All but Mueting also serve on the Nebraska Liquor Control Commission. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
The idea stems from a current regulatory system he says is set up to fail with onerous regulations and “astronomical” or “unrealistic” fees more stringent than in the liquor industry.
“I feel that the intention of the [Medical] Cannabis Commission is to prevent this whole thing from happening, which they’ve been doing a very good job of so far,” Beard said.
The voter-created Medical Cannabis Commission consists of three governor-appointed members of the Liquor Control Commission and up to two more at-large appointees.
Pillen has appointed all current members and solicited applications for one vacancy. He has praised the commission for enacting strict guidelines at his request to further his goal to provide narrow access to the medicine and prevent it from spilling into recreational use.
Former State Sen. Lynne Walz of Fremont, the Democratic nominee for Nebraska governor, left, and Rick Beard of Omaha, the Legal Marijuana NOW nominee for Nebraska governor, attend a developmental disabilities community listening event on April 30, 2026, in Lincoln, a couple weeks before the May 12, 2026, primary election. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Beard said it’s an “election-year tactic” for the commission to appear as if it’s moving forward when regulations would actually make it “impossible” for the program to succeed.
Pursuing a state-run program might require more legislation or a constitutional amendment, Beard noted, but he estimates doing so could generate $100 million in new tax revenue each year, up to $500 million when everything is up and running.
‘Changes the game’
Asked whether he would pursue recreational marijuana, Beard said he would like to keep it medical because that’s what Congress, and now the U.S. Department of Justice, offers protections for. However, he said Nebraska’s program needs to be “compassionate.”
Rick Beard holds up the release of a new wine in Murphys, California, in 2018. (Photo courtesy of Rick Beard)
Beard said Nebraska would not get the upward of $500 million in annual revenue without a “compassionate” program that gives “nearly full access to everybody” with a doctor’s note, “not to where you have to be dying.”
“As long as an adult doctor gives you a recommendation, from this state or any other state, I feel that our citizens should be allowed to use it compassionately,” Beard said.
He said smoking cannabis is also necessary for some people to get needed relief. Current state regulations prohibit the sale of smokeable or vapor products.
The state could face a deficit as high as $1 billion, combining a $200-million-plus deficit through the current fiscal year, ending June 30, and initial projections for the following two years. Lawmakers will need to tackle that shortfall in the 2027 legislative session that begins in January.
Beard said the state must eliminate tax breaks for corporations and Nebraska’s “ultra-rich” and must not turn away federal dollars.
“We can continue to be preyed on for our natural resources, underpaid labor and billionaire tax breaks, or we can join together and put an end to this absurdity,” Beard said.
Beard said Nebraska could also double its biofuel production using hemp while doing so in a cleaner way that uses less fertilizer and water and also helps clean the soil and reduce nitrates. He said the new industry could generate millions more and help keep young people in the state.
Rick Beard sits on a tractor in Murphys, California, in April 2019 and talks about tractors with a young child. (Photo courtesy of Rick Beard)
He said hemp-grown products could also help housing by being cheaper to make.
“We’re just pissing away so much money, and we’re falling behind while other states move forward with money and progress and reform,” Beard said.
Beard said the increased revenue would also be critical in addressing property taxes.
“It really changes the game as to what cannabis can do for our state financially to where we’re really talking about fixing roads … and the actual ability to reduce property taxes,” Beard said.
He continued: “I don’t honestly believe that the other candidates have a powerful plan for Nebraska finances like this.”
Working with the Legislature
One potential 2026 ballot measure could complicate Beard’s ideas around medical cannabis. The proposal, from the Respect Nebraska Voters campaign, would increase the threshold to change voter-approved laws — including laws around the legalization and regulation of medical cannabis — from 33 of 49 state lawmakers to 40 of 49 state senators. Supporters turned in signatures by the July 3 deadline and await verification to be placed on the Nov. 3 ballot.
Some advocates of the successful 2024 campaign around medical cannabis have urged caution and warned that doing so could lock in “gridlock” should any legislative changes be needed. In 2025, for instance, an advocate-backed bill failed to garner a simple majority, let alone 33 votes.
Pillen talks priorities, pivot from Nebraska primary election to Nov. 3 faceoff

Beard said he is “all for” the Respect Nebraska Voters proposal that “protects the will and vote of the people.” Whether it’s a state-grown, state-sold and state-operated system or a regulatory licensing, testing and oversight system, he said he wants to ensure access to medical cannabis.
However, Beard said, the question is whether people can “save” the voter-approved laws from “damage” inflicted by legislative inaction and guidelines from the Nebraska Medical Cannabis Commission, or whether another petition or constitutional amendment would be needed.
“When we have fewer than 100 people dismantling the vote of 2 million people, we need this to protect us,” Beard said.
Should Beard continue to face executive branch or legislative pushback, he said he could go back to his original idea to pursue a 2028 ballot measure or constitutional amendment.
In the meantime, Beard said he would deploy a lesson he says he learned from Pillen: lead with executive orders and executive action.
“I don’t know why, when I’m governor, why I can’t do that,” Beard said. “I think that if they want to oppose it with these kinds of powers and these kinds of techniques, I think that we can make it happen with these same kinds of powers and techniques.”
Beyond working around hemp and cannabis, Beard said he doesn’t foresee needing to drive action in the Legislature from the Governor’s Office. Pillen has been among governors who have taken a more active role in pushing their legislative priorities.
‘Committed to rising above’
Beard has not yet filed a finance disclosure committee with the Nebraska Accountability and Disclosure Commission, which is required if he raises or spends more than $5,000.
That’s by design, Beard said, as he has refused to take corporate or PAC money and doesn’t want to take money from voters.
“It’s a difficult uphill push without money, but at the same point, what am I going to do?” Beard said.
Walz talks priorities, pivot from Nebraska primary election to Nov. 3 faceoff

Even if he had funds, he said it would likely lead to negative campaigning and an expectation that he uphold the interests of his donors. He said that’s holding back his opponents.
“It just kind of really takes the honesty out of politics and out of deciding who we elect,” Beard said. “I’m hoping through our campaign that by not taking the money, people realize our purity and our intent to represent the people more than represent corporations or the interests of PACs.”
Since taking office in 2023, Pillen has raised more than $12 million and had more than $9.5 million in his campaign account by mid-June. In the last year, Walz raised nearly $1.5 million, with almost $675,000 in her campaign account by mid-June.
By Sept. 1, Beard will need to select a running mate, and he said he’s on the search for someone who will “have some brilliant ideas” and perhaps bring qualities he doesn’t, such as a little more political experience, a legal background or a more agricultural, rural-based view.
Beard said that if given the chance, he “absolutely” would debate his opponents. He said that’s important for Nebraskans to see candidates interact and speak and assess them accordingly.
“I am truly not Democrat. I am truly not Republican,” Beard said. “I find heavy faults with both of those parties, and I’m committed to rising above that.”
