name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Conservationists worry Endangered Species Act changes could threaten recovery efforts
description: Conservationists credit the Endangered Species Act for the red-cockaded woodpecker’s limited rebound, but they fear a Trump administration proposal could erase that progress as well as other efforts to protect threatened animals.
text:
The red-cockaded woodpecker seeks out mature longleaf pine trees to build its home. (Renee Bodine/USFWS)The continuous rattle of a red-cockaded woodpecker’s bill against a pine tree used to be a much more common sound throughout Louisiana forests. The plucky bird makes its home by burrowing into the hearts of longleaf pine trees, and the sound of its repeated efforts to make a home for its young was once nearly ubiquitous across the region.
Longleaf pine ecosystems historically spanned hundreds of thousands of miles in the Southeast. Today, they’ve been reduced to only 3% of that area, largely the result of logging and development. As a result, woodpecker populations have dwindled dramatically. 
Conservationists credit the Endangered Species Act for the species’ limited rebound, but they fear new Trump administration policy could erase that progress as well as other efforts to protect threatened plants and animals. 
The slow comeback
Red-cockaded woodpeckers were once abundant, with their historic range extending from as far south as Florida to as far north as New Jersey.  
The woodpeckers live in clusters, anywhere from two to eight birds in one nest. Its numbers dwindled to their lowest point in the 1960s, with only 10,000 birds or about 1,500 to 3,500 clusters scattered among increasingly isolated portions of pine forests, according to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service.  
Scientists estimate the species’ numbers had dropped 99% from what they were at the time Europeans first settled in the U.S. 
In 1973, the red-cockaded woodpecker was among the first species to receive federal protection when Congress approved the Endangered Species Act. The landmark law protected listed animals from actions that either kill them directly or destroy their habitat. 
“Protecting habitat is a key part of the Endangered Species Act,” said Karrigan Börk,
a law professor and Endangered Species Act expert at the University of California, “It’s been on the books since the act itself was passed in the ‘70s.”
The red-cockaded woodpecker has rebounded somewhat from its dire lows. As of 2020, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service estimated there were around 7,800 clusters, representing anywhere from two to five times the numbers from the 1960s. The agency used this population increase as justification to change the woodpecker’s status from endangered to threatened in 2024. 
But legal experts and conservation biologists worry about how a new federal rule could affect the red-cockaded woodpecker and other imperiled species. 
Red-cockaded woodpecker in flight, (Martjan Lammertink/U.S. Forest Service)
What does ‘harm’ mean?
The U.S. Department of Interior announced in July it would no longer consider habitat destruction as direct harm to a species. This goes directly against the conclusions of conservationists who work to bring species back from the brink. 
“We cannot avoid extinction without protecting habitat,” said ​​Vicky Meretsky, a professor at Indiana University’s School of Public and Environmental Affairs. “You can’t save a species that is becoming homeless without providing a home.”
Merestky worked for years with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to revive numbers of the California condor, which had fallen to 22 birds in 1982. Habitat loss was among the factors that caused the species, which now numbers more than 600, to nearly go extinct. 
Meretsky said it is impossible to separate habitat protection from endangered species protection.
“Well over two-thirds, probably closer to 80% of species, have habitat loss as at least one of their major reasons for endangerment,” Meretsky said. “It has been the leading cause of endangerment for a very long time.” 
While the red-cockaded woodpecker is still known as a success in conservation terms, its comeback is slow in comparison to other species. For example, the once endangered bald eagle now numbers more than 400,000 across North America, according to the Fish and Wildlife Service. 
Louisiana’s state bird, the brown pelican, was gone entirely from the state federal before protections were put in place. The USFWS estimate for the species now reaches 650,000 birds when taking into account its entire range from the U.S. to Central America and the Caribbean.  
The red-cockaded woodpecker’s recovery struggles are, in part, because of how severe its habitat problems are. They are also extremely territorial and don’t migrate, making the search for suitable habitat competitive even in the best of circumstances. 
Longleaf pine forests are found in Southeast, Southwest and Central Louisiana, with the biggest concentration in the Kisatchie National Forest. All areas have seen the impact of logging and development, and longleaf pines take nearly 60 years to mature enough for a woodpecker to find it suitable for a home. The birds seek out the oldest, sturdiest trees, ideally free of sap and infected with red heart fungus, which softens the wood enough to allow for easier nest building. 
Biologist retrieves red-cockaded woodpecker chicks from a nest for banding and data collection near Fort Polk, Louisiana, May 26, 2022. (Ian Fischer/USFWS)
Conservation confusion
The Fish and Wildlife Service, with help from the U.S. Forest Service, works to conserve the species by building nesting boxes and undertaking programs to grow other native trees such as slash and loblolly pines. These trees don’t take as long to mature as longleaf pines, and the birds will sometimes use them to nest.
In Louisiana, private landowners can enter into agreements with the Louisiana Department of Wildlife and Fisheries and federal wildlife officials to preserve habitat for red-cockaded woodpeckers. Called the Safe Harbor Program, landowners commit to management activities that enhance, restore or maintain habitat for the birds. In return, they get official assurance from the state and federal agencies that there won’t be increased restrictions on the use of their land if conservation efforts attract more red-cockaded woodpeckers. 
“There’s a whole bunch of safe harbor agreements across the country that have that same structure and that provide that same protection for the landowner,” Börk said, adding that they became common under the Clinton administration to promote conservation on private lands.
Property is surveyed when a landowner agrees to enter the program to assess how many red-cockaded woodpeckers already live there. When a base number is reached, landowners are responsible for maintaining at least that count. But if more woodpeckers move into the area, the landowners can remove their nesting trees and habitat without any consequences. They just have to give state or federal officials 60 days written notice so the agencies can attempt to relocate the affected woodpeckers. 
Börk said changing the definition of harm under the Endangered Species Act could render these programs ineffective. 
“If the way this administration is interpreting harm is to mean that habitat destruction doesn’t actually kill the species … those landowners don’t need that safe harbor protection anymore, because they can just go out and cut those trees down anyway,” he said.
“This is actually going to result in a lot more confusion,” Börk added.
The rule change fits into a larger scheme of Trump administration actions to roll back protections for the environment and wildlife long respected under the law, he said. 
“This is a slapdash move by the administration that doesn’t have a lot of clear thought behind it,” Börk said. “This is part of the administration’s very broad effort to break as many things as quickly as possible, in terms of environmental regulation, in hopes that some of it will stick.”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: First responders, military personnel endure mental health challenges. Summit promotes ways to help.
description: The call for help came late on a frigid January night in Indianapolis. A car had crashed into a retention pond with a family trapped inside. Indianapolis and Lawrence police officers rushed to the scene, where they found the vehicle 15 feet from shore and beneath 10 feet of icy water. The officers, setting their own […]
text:
The nation's active duty military service members and veterans are at significantly higher risk than civilians of PTSD, depression, substance abuse disorders and suicidal thoughts. (Getty Images)The call for help came late on a frigid January night in Indianapolis. A car had crashed into a retention pond with a family trapped inside.
Indianapolis and Lawrence police officers rushed to the scene, where they found the vehicle 15 feet from shore and beneath 10 feet of icy water.
The officers, setting their own safety aside, entered the water to rescue a father and his two children. The children survived, but the father was lost.
The officers’ courage was remarkable, but calls to respond at a moment’s notice to life-threatening emergencies are routine and often traumatic for police, firefighters and emergency medical personnel.
The stress of responding in the face of danger and the cumulative trauma of witnessing tragedy after tragedy can exact a heavy toll — first responders are five times more likely to suffer from post traumatic stress disorder and depression than other Americans.
Our nation’s active duty military service members and veterans also are at significantly higher risk than civilians of PTSD, depression, substance abuse disorders and suicidal thoughts.
To help promote healing and wholeness among first responders, military personnel and veterans, this year’s Indiana Mental Health Roundtable Summit, hosted in partnership with the Sagamore Institute, will focus on supporting those who serve our communities and our nation on the frontlines of danger.
The summit, on Aug. 7 at the JW Marriott in Indianapolis, will bring together mental health professionals, lawmakers, nonprofit leaders, military veterans and first responders to discuss the challenges and the opportunities for strengthening the mental health of the men and women who serve and protect.
Goals for the summit include:

Educate mental health professionals, frontline responders, service members and state and local leaders on the mental health issues that affect those who serve.
Promote conversations across sectors on mental and behavioral health insights relevant to veterans, police, EMTs and firefighters.
Showcase solutions and innovations that are improving mental health outcomes for those who serve, with guidance on leveraging those practices in Indiana.
Explore state and federal policies that shape how Indiana and the nation support the mental health of those who serve.
Equip participants with resources to strengthen the mental health of first responders, military personnel and veterans.

Registration for the summit is still open but closes Wednesday. Please join us in supporting the mental health of those who answer the call to serve.
On our worst days they give their all — walking into fires, standing against violence, delivering life-saving medical care, defending our nation.
Their sacrifices come with a high price. We need to ensure they have the support they need after the crisis ends.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Once again, national Democrats are making a primary mistake
description: It is clear in hindsight, and clear to many at the time, that the choice to sideline New Hampshire in the 2024 Democratic presidential primary process was designed to spare President Joe Biden from scrutiny over his ability to mount a vigorous reelection campaign. South Carolina was chosen to go first. As New Hampshire, following […]
text:
A "Write-In Joe Biden" campaign sign sits in a Portsmouth snow bank. (File photo by Hadley Barndollar/New Hampshire Bulletin)It is clear in hindsight, and clear to many at the time, that the choice to sideline New Hampshire in the 2024 Democratic presidential primary process was designed to spare President Joe Biden from scrutiny over his ability to mount a vigorous reelection campaign. South Carolina was chosen to go first.
As New Hampshire, following state law, held its primary first anyway, there was a farcical super PAC effort by Biden surrogates to win the write-in vote here without Biden campaigning. As that succeeded, the New Hampshire delegates were seated at the Democratic convention.
Now it seems clear that New Hampshire will be passed over again by Democrats, based on the premise that it is not diverse enough, in favor of South Carolina or Nevada. The former would be a very strange proving ground. Biden got only 43.4% of the South Carolina vote in 2020 as he went on to win nationally. There is just one Democrat in the state’s seven-member House delegation. The state legislature has been Republican since 1998.
Nevada is also a peculiar political ecosystem. It was there that President Donald Trump, as a candidate, unveiled his June 2024 “no tax on tips” proposal, which Kamala Harris parroted at a Nevada rally two months later, and that led to a four-year suspension of taxes on tips in the federal budget reconciliation bill that passed last year.
If Nevada goes first, a successful Democratic candidate will have to appeal to the critical bloc of Culinary Workers Union members, which could shape his or her remaining campaign in ways that may not appeal to the broader nation. It reminds me of the ethanol pledge that “The West Wing” so well depicted presidential candidates Arnold Vinick and Matt Santos struggling with at a Corn Growers Expo in Iowa.
There is no such organized group to pander to in New Hampshire. And yet, for those who might suggest our state lacks the diversity to go first, I would ask what one’s definition of diversity is. Isn’t age a demographic? New Hampshire has the nation’s second-oldest population. Nationally, according to the U.S. Census Bureau, “From 2020 to 2024, the older population grew by 13.0%, significantly outpacing the 1.4% growth of working-age adults (ages 18 to 64), while the number of children declined by 1.7%.”
By 2034, U.S. sales of adult diapers are projected to exceed baby diaper sales. Our aging population is going to place a strain on safety net programs like Medicaid and Medicare, and New Hampshire would be a great place to hone a message to senior voters. After all, according to the trustees of the Medicare Hospital Insurance trust fund, it will be insolvent by 2033. Kind of a big deal.
There are an estimated 4 million tipped workers in the country. In contrast, in 2024 data showed that 43.3 million U.S. citizens who are 65-and-older voted, easily the biggest age demographic to vote. It might be somewhat important for a Democratic candidate to win over these older voters, given that Trump won them 51-47% over Harris.
Treating New Hampshire as flyover country would also be taking for granted a state where Republicans have a lock on state government and the presidential vote isn’t a given. Had Al Gore won New Hampshire in 2000, Florida would have been immaterial. Although Hillary Clinton lost the electoral college in 2016, she nearly lost New Hampshire too — carrying it by only a 47.6%-47.2% margin over Trump.
Finally, the retail politics required to win the New Hampshire primary, instead of just pouring money into a major media market like Las Vegas, has made for more nimble candidates in both political parties. It would be a shame for national Democrats to devalue that tradition. And it would be a big loss to the civic experience of Granite Staters.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Two former governors: Party labels belong in elections, not on the Kansas Supreme Court
description: Americans’ trust in the judiciary and the justice system is eroding at every level. From the U.S. Supreme Court to state courts across the country, polls show sharply declining public confidence in courts as trustworthy institutions. The response from many special interest groups and politicians has been to try to politicize these institutions further, and [[...]
text:
Two Kansas governors, one from each party, unite to voice skepticism about an effort to change the Kansas Supreme Court. (Getty Images)Americans’ trust in the judiciary and the justice system is eroding at every level. From the U.S. Supreme Court to state courts across the country, polls show sharply declining public confidence in courts as trustworthy institutions.
The response from many special interest groups and politicians has been to try to politicize these institutions further, and the next front is state supreme courts, starting here in Kansas.
Across the country, there is a growing effort to turn judgeships into elected positions, allowing billionaire political donors to flood judicial races with money and to treat the bench as just another prize to be won in our increasingly polarized society.
We believe this is the wrong solution. And we say this as two former governors of Kansas from different political parties, where the state has used a better model — the gold standard for others to follow — to select the judges who sit on our state’s highest bench.
For years, Kansas has selected supreme court justices through a nonpartisan, merit-based process. A diverse nominating commission — with representatives from every corner of the state — evaluates individuals on their qualifications and recommends three candidates to the governor. The governor then appoints from that list. Once appointed, Justices face periodic statewide retention elections, giving Kansans a vote on who continues to serve on the bench.
Kansas voters created this merit-based system after the “Triple Play” scandal, when a state Supreme Court seat was handed out as a political favor.
The merit-based system works. We have seen it work, because it allowed us to appoint capable, independent justices who served Kansans well. And we have fought for it together. In 2016, well-funded special interest groups launched a coordinated effort to remove nearly every justice standing for retention — not because those justices had failed in their duties, but because they had ruled in ways that powerful outside groups disliked. Back then, we came together to make the case to Kansas voters that this was exactly the kind of political pressure the system was designed to resist. Voters agreed, and the effort failed.
Now many of those same forces are back, better organized and better funded, pushing once again to put billionaires and dark money special interests in control of our Supreme Court. In less than two weeks, Kansans will vote on whether to keep the merit-based system or replace it with partisan judicial elections. We are  confident voters will reject the attempt to overhaul the state’s Supreme Court.
Our courts are not just another institution. They are the last firewall against partisanship and special interest influence in a world increasingly defined by both. When legislatures are gridlocked or controlled by powerful interests, when independent agencies are politicized, when elections themselves are disputed, courts are where Americans go. The courthouse is the place where every Kansan should stand on equal footing with the most powerful interests. That only works if those judges got there on merit, not by money or political loyalty.
In states that do elect their state supreme court justices, hundreds of millions of dollars now pour into judicial elections. Outside groups and individual billionaire donors have made capturing state courts a strategic priority. We should be doing everything we can to shield our courts from that pressure.
This is not a partisan argument. A judiciary that can be bought is dangerous to everyone, regardless of party. When judges owe their seats to donors and party bosses, the rule of law becomes contingent on who holds power.
Every Kansan needs the courts to be the backstop of our political system that produces fair, independent rulings, and every one of us deserves to know that the judge across the bench got there because they were the best qualified, not the best funded.
Kathleen Sebelius served as Governor of Kansas from 2003 to 2009 and as U.S. Secretary of Health and Human Services from 2009 to 2014. Bill Graves served as Governor of Kansas from 1995 to 2003. name: Maryland Matters
title: Canceled federal grants hit teen pregnancy prevention in Baltimore, rural counties
description: The federal government's abrupt termination of teen pregnancy prevention funding last month means the loss of more than $3 million to Maryland programs, which are trying to see if they can still offer young people programming for without federal support.
text:
The Maryland Department of Health says that canceled federal grants will impact efforts to reduce teenage pregnancy in rural school districts. (Photo by Tony Anderson/Getty Stock image)The federal government’s abrupt termination of teen pregnancy prevention funding last month means the loss of more than $3 million to Maryland-based programs, which are scrambling to see if they can still offer programming for young people without federal support.
The Maryland cuts were part of about $68 million in grant funding awarded under the federal Teen Pregnancy Prevention Program that was eliminated by the Trump administration, three years into the five-year program. The government claimed that 53 out of 67 programs were normalizing sexual activities for teens.
Funding affected included $1.4 million allocated for teen pregnancy prevention efforts with the Maryland Department of Health and $1.8 million for the Baltimore City Health Department.
“The Department is evaluating the potential impacts of the federal government’s decision, as well as how MDH can continue to best serve the health and well-being of Maryland teenagers,” according to a recent email from the Maryland Department of Health.
The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services did not respond to requests for comment or provide examples where Maryland’s or Baltimore’s use of those grant dollars promoted sexual activity for minors.
Some groups in Maryland welcomed the decision to terminate the funds. The Maryland Family Institute said the gran program supported a curriculum that may have been used to “introduce minors to concepts that are wholly inappropriate,” such as “anal sex, abusive pornography, abortion without parental consent, and transgender ideology.”
Federal health agency cancels most of its teen pregnancy prevention grants

“Indecent is one word to describe them; immoral is another,” said Jeffrey Trimbath, president of the Maryland Family Institute, in a written statement Monday. “These programs have shown little effectiveness and have become tools for the sexualization of Maryland’s children.”
But pro-abortion groups and public health researchers say that comprehensive sex education efforts have contributed to significant reductions in teen pregnancies since the 1960s, along with other factors. When the Teen Pregnancy Prevention Program started in 2009, the teen birth rate was 39.1 births per 1,000 females aged 15-19. By 2024, the rate had fallen to 12.7 per 1,000, with preliminary data for 2025 indicating further reductions.
“Look at the data,” said Robyn Elliott on behalf of the Women’s Law Center of Maryland. “Teen pregnancy is at the lowest rates that it has been at in many, many years…. These programs, along with other efforts to support teens in making their own healthy choices – we should continue that, not pull back.”
Maryland’s teen birth rate in 2024 was 10.9 live births per 1,000 females ages 15-19, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, below the national average. It’s the lowest teen birth rate in the state since at least 2014, when the state’s teen birth rate was 17.8 per 1,000mand has been on a downward trend since.
Last year, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services issued new parameters around how the grant funding could be used.
“The policy reaffirms the Teen Pregnancy Prevention Program’s core mission: to reduce teen pregnancy through medically accurate and age-appropriate programming, not to promote harmful ideologies, risky sexual activity for minors, or other content outside the scope of the program,” HHS said at the time. “Program materials are expected reflect the immutable biological reality of sex, not radical gender ideology, and may not promote anti-American ideologies such as discriminatory equity ideology. Programs with such unauthorized content are not eligible for federal funding.
That effort to limit the scope of the grant program was struck down by the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia.
The Trump Administration issued a similar policy change in 2026, and terminated the 56 grant programs in the process.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Baltimore health officials and the state health department each received a notice on June 26 that their five-year grant funding would end, cutting off the funding two years early.
City health officials believed they were in “good standing” with federal officials and “maintained routine communication with federal project officers.”
“The department received no advance notice or opportunity for discussion before the termination,” the Baltimore Health Department said in a recent email. “As a result, the remaining grant funds are no longer available to the City.
Those funds would have been used to engage 11,500 youth and 11,500 adults in comprehensive teen pregnancy prevention education, according to city health officials.
“This grant supported initiatives to improve adolescent health among Baltimore City youth through evidence-based public health strategies recommended by the federal government,” the department said. “Funding facilitated the implementation of evidence-based programs for individuals aged 15-24 across three primary settings: classrooms, clinics, and communities.”
As for the Maryland Department of Health, the remaining $1.4 million in grant funding would have continued teen pregnancy prevention and sexually transmitted infection reduction efforts in six rural counties, working with the Johns Hopkins University Center for Adolescent Health, local health departments, local education agencies, universities and clinics to do so.
“Funding would have supported the expansion of evidence-based programs and systems-level efforts,” the state health department said in a recent written statement, “including Youth Advisory Boards, as well as the provision of technical assistance and professional development, to achieve program goals.”
Maryland is one of more than two dozen states affected by the sudden termination of those grants.
A group of progressive organizations and county governments filed a lawsuit against the Trump administration this month, arguing that the new protocols for the grant funding do not align with the statutory purpose of the Teen Pregnancy Prevention Program decided by Congress back in 2009 to use “medically accurate and age appropriate programs” that have “been proven effective through rigorous evaluation.”
“The Trump-Vance administration’s repeated attempts to terminate proven evidence-based programs and spread misinformation to teens have real consequences for young people’s futures,” said Skye Perryman, president and CEO of Democracy Forward, which is leading the lawsuit.
“This is a backdoor, ideologically-driven effort disguised as education, defying Congress’s clear directive that these grants support medically accurate, age-appropriate, evidence-based programs. An overwhelming majority of Americans believe young people should receive honest, inclusive sexual education,” Perryman said.
Elliott, who analyzes Maryland health policy, says that the terminated grants are another attempt to block access to reproductive healthcare services and education.
“The teen pregnancy prevention program has a lot of basic education and things like that, but it also has a component of letting teens know about birth control,” she said. “This particular program, when we combine it with all the other movements they’ve made to block birth control access … this is just one of those steps.”

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Tattoo parlor sues SC over 22-year-old law requiring distance from churches
description: Tiny Zaps, a New York tattoo shop, says the law violates the First Amendment's guarantee of self-expression.
text:
Tattoos done by Tiny Zaps included in a legal filing arguing South Carolina laws about tattoo parlors violate the First Amendment right to self-expression. (Photo courtesy of Tiny Zaps)COLUMBIA — Whether tattoo parlors have a constitutional right to ink near churches and schools is the central question of a federal lawsuit challenging a decades-old state law.
South Carolina became the second-to-last state in the nation to allow tattooing in 2004, following only Oklahoma. The law legalizing the practice set parameters, including that parlors needed to stay at least 1,000 feet away from any nearby churches, schools and playgrounds, and no artist could tattoo on the neck, face or head.
In a lawsuit filed last week in federal court, a tattoo shop and two people who want to get inked are arguing those rules violate the First Amendment right of self-expression. The state Department of Public Health and attorney general’s office, named as the defendants, have not yet filed responses.


“Whether artwork appears on canvas, paper, or skin, the Constitution protects both the artist’s right to create it and the customer’s right to receive it,” the lawsuit reads.
Tiny Zaps, a New York City-based tattoo parlor, wanted to hold a pop-up parlor at a hotel in downtown Charleston, similar to events the business does across the country, owner Sam Kelly told the SC Daily Gazette on Thursday.
“I think it’s a really fun, young, vibrant city and just had a hunch it would be a good fit for Tiny Zaps,” Kelly said. “I think people in Charleston would be happy to have our services there.”
He started looking into the state laws to make sure the event would meet all the required health codes, only to realize he couldn’t hold the event at all because the hotel was within 1,000 of a church.
In the Holy City, getting out of the required distance from a church is very difficult, Kelly said.
“I looked at a map and was like, ‘Oh, yeah, that’s why there’s not a single tattoo shop in downtown Charleston,’” Kelly said.
The shop also wanted to offer small behind-the-ear tattoos, which are very popular but illegal in the state, Kelly said.
Joshua and Stephanie McDonald, a couple from Fountain Inn, are also suing for the right to get tattoos on their heads and necks. Where someone gets a tattoo should be a decision between them and their artist, Kelly said.
“To have to limit that and take it off the table for some rule that, to us, doesn’t seem to have anything to do with the health and safety and sanitation of tattooing just seems pretty off to us,” Kelly said.
Kelly is happy to follow requirements in place for health and safety reasons, he said. But, like the distance from churches, “it seems like there’s no real rhyme or reason for it, other than an outdated stigma around the craft of tattooing,” he said.
Once seen as an “underbelly, niche counterculture,” Kelly said, tattoos are becoming more common and socially accepted.
In a 2023 Pew Research Center survey, nearly one-third of people said they had at least one tattoo. Having ink was most common among women and people in their 30s and 40s, according to the survey.
“I think people of all ages, all walks of life, get tattoos for different reasons,” Kelly said. “Tattooing, at the end of the day, is just a medium.”
South Carolina has close to 200 tattoo parlors, according to the state health department. Still, people sometimes have to travel to another city, or another state, to get the work they want, Kelly said.
“They should be able to get this service in their city,” Kelly said.
Legislators have filed bills for years that would change the laws, but none have gained any traction.
Since his 2022 election to the Statehouse, Rep. Brandon Guffey has repeatedly sponsored bills that would allow churches to sign off on having a tattoo parlor nearby, change the prohibition on head tattoos and let parlors also do piercings or sell artwork.
The Rock Hill Republican has many tattoos, including three on his arm memorializing his son, the victim of a sextortion scam who died by suicide in 2022.
“One of the ways I wanted to honor my son was to get his birthmark done, and I shouldn’t have to drive to Charlotte to get it done,” Guffey said.
Guffey sees the law as government overreach, since it tells businesses where they can and can’t operate, he said.
Opening a liquor store is easier than opening a tattoo parlor in the state, despite many people sharing moral objections to the two, he added.
“I just think it’s a dumb law, the way South Carolina wrote it,” Guffey said. “It keeps us from having tattoo artists like there are in many other states.”
Although tattoo artists have struggled with the law for years, many don’t have the funds or resources to bring a legal challenge, Kelly said.
Plus, federal court opinions seem to signal a shift in what judges consider covered under the First Amendment, said Dean McGee, an attorney for Pacific Legal Foundation working on the case.
The South Carolina Supreme Court in 2002 ruled the First Amendment does not cover tattoos, which were then illegal in the state. But more recent cases, such as a 2023 U.S. Supreme Court decision protecting website designers’ rights to self-expression, opened up the possibility of a different outcome, McGee said.
“The Supreme Court has rejected the idea that just because someone is doing something professionally doesn’t mean they’re not engaging in protected First Amendment speech,” McGee said.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Pro-data center group launches in Georgia to try to win over critics
description: An organization that represents the data center industry is trying to get Georgians to think of the electricity-hungry facilities more favorably. Connected Georgia and its parent organization America Connects recently established a state presence when they created a website on June 15 and a YouTube channel the next week, where the organization published a 30[...]
text:
The QTS data center complex under development in Fayetteville, Georgia, US, on Thursday, Oct. 17, 2024. A new data center industry group is embarking on a Georgia-focused publicity campaign to improve public opinion of data centers in the state. Photographer: Elijah Nouvelage/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesAn organization that represents the data center industry is trying to get Georgians to think of the electricity-hungry facilities more favorably.
Connected Georgia and its parent organization America Connects recently established a state presence when they created a website on June 15 and a YouTube channel the next week, where the organization published a 30-second ad that has garnered over 2 million views in about four weeks.
“From homes to hospitals to businesses, Georgia’s data centers are unlocking a smarter power grid for our communities,” the YouTube ad says.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The rampant growth of data center construction in Georgia has spurred intense statewide outrage at local government meetings where zoning decisions are being made. 
A wave of bipartisan bills was introduced and debated during the 2026 legislative session, from proposals to enact a statewide moratorium or claw back tax incentives aimed at attracting the massive facilities to the state. But none of these bills reached the governor’s desk.
Outrage over surge of data centers in Georgia inspires wave of bipartisan bills

Protestors recently packed a Marietta City Council meeting to speak out against a data center proposal that was approved last year. Last week, nearly 1,000 people confronted OpenAI and local officials after the company known for ChatGPT announced it would build a $20 billion data center in Effingham County. 
And some candidates for office have tapped into the anger in their campaigns. 
It’s unclear at this point how far the group will go in promoting data centers in Georgia, and Josh Levi, the head of the Data Center Coalition, a nonprofit organization that advocates for data centers, did not address their plans in a statement for this story. Levi is one of only three people listed on federal tax filings for America Connects, the parent organization behind Connected Georgia. All three are or have been associated with the Data Center Coalition.
The Data Center Coalition is an association representing some of the biggest names in the data center industry, such as Amazon, Google and Microsoft. The coalition’s representatives have testified against a bill aimed at regulating the facilities in Georgia that ultimately stalled this year. The organization has hired two lobbyists at the state Capitol over the last years but has not spent money on lobbying activity, according to Georgia Ethics Commission data.
In neighboring North Carolina,  the group spent $367,272 on an advertising campaign in the state, according to NC Newsline, which is the Georgia Recorder’s sibling newsroom. Connected Georgia does not appear to have filed any contract with the Federal Communications Commission for a similar campaign in Georgia. Levi did not address questions about its specific campaign plans for the Peach State.
In a statement, Levi said that Connected Georgia’s goal is “to inform Georgians about the benefits of data centers.”
“Through Connected Georgia, the industry seeks to better explain the role of data centers to the public — including how they operate, why they are important to our daily lives and the 21st Century economy, as well as information about the industry’s responsible usage of water and its commitment to paying for the energy it uses,” Levi said.
But Mark Woodall, a lobbyist for the Sierra Club of Georgia, said he believes that data center skepticism and opposition from the public won’t die because of a publicity campaign. He described the effort as an attempt to slow down or prevent potential regulations or policies that have been successfully enacted in other states, pointing to a recent one-year moratorium on data center construction approved in New York and Virginia’s new tax on the electricity data centers use.
“The Data Center Coalition is trying to put lipstick on a pig,” Woodall said. “Nobody believes these people. It doesn’t matter how much money they spend. Nobody’s going to believe them.”
Woodall also pointed to the recent pushback against the massive OpenAI data center project in Effingham County, saying that “there’s one thing that independents, Democrats, and Republicans agree on: they all hate data centers.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: ‘It puts special education back 50 years.’ Ohio advocates concerned over recent federal changes.
description: Ohio special education advocates fear recent changes to the U.S. Department of Education will cause confusion, delays, and a loss of service to students.  The Trump administration announced in June it will move the Office of Special Education and Rehabilitative Services to the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, and the Office for Civil […]
text:
Ohio school children in a classroom. (Photo by Morgan Trau.)Ohio special education advocates fear recent changes to the U.S. Department of Education will cause confusion, delays, and a loss of service to students. 
The Trump administration announced in June it will move the Office of Special Education and Rehabilitative Services to the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, and the Office for Civil Rights to the U.S. Department of Justice. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The special education office is responsible for making sure states follow the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA), a federal law that ensures students with disabilities have access to a free and appropriate public education. 
The civil rights office investigates complaints from students and families.
Dee Marks sits on the Member Organization Council, an arm under the governing board of the Ohio Coalition for the Education of Children with Disabilities.
“For special education in Ohio, it means the process of children with disabilities getting their needs met just got significantly more complicated,” Marks said.
“There’s significant fear that it’s going to degrade the programs and services that have historically been provided under IDEA to the point where students with disabilities will no longer be educated to the level that the law dictates that they should be educated to.” 
About 14% of Ohio students receive special education services, said Jennifer Webb, past president for the Council for Exceptional Children’s Ohio chapter. 
“It puts special education back 50 years to when we were diagnosing and trying to fix kids versus identifying them to give them the services they need to help them learn the best,” said Webb, chair of the teacher education programs at Malone University, a private university in Canton. 
This move also creates a stigma that students with disabilities are viewed as having a medical need first, instead of being viewed as a student first, Marks said. 
For example, she talked about students with disabilities who are blind. 
“You have specialized needs, but all of those needs are focused on education … that student navigating the education building, accessing the curriculum, making sure that it’s in braille or audio so that that student has access,” Marks said. 
She wonders if the focus would now be a medical first model under HHS. 
“It becomes less about them getting access to the education and more focus on that student who’s blind, which then becomes a big concern that that student might be segregated because they’re different,” Marks said. 
Robyn Linscott, director of education and family policy at The Arc of the United States, agrees. 
“Moving IDEA oversight into HHS pushes students with disabilities toward a medical model, where disability is treated as a diagnosis to manage instead of a natural part of human life,” she said in a statement. 
“When that mindset drives education decisions, students are more likely to be segregated, underestimated, or treated as separate from the school community.”
The U.S. Department of Education will continue to be in charge of the statutory responsibilities over special education as required by federal law, but this shifts the day-to-day operations to HHS. 
“It adds another layer of complexity because two departments are involved, and one is still going to have the ultimate responsibility for this other department underneath it, but then how does a parent of a child with a disability who has an issue navigate that?” Marks asked.  
She also wonders how HHS will be able to support students’ educational needs. 
“The Department of Education has, for decades, been in charge of special education, and all of a sudden they just carve special education out, send it to Health and Human Services, and they’re not qualified to handle that programming,” she said. 
This move further shrinks the U.S. Department of Education as President Donald Trump works to fulfill his campaign promise to dismantle the department. 
The Education Department had announced 10 earlier interagency agreements, or IAAs, with HHS, Labor, Interior, State and Treasury, which transfer several of Education’s responsibilities to those agencies.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio governor candidate suggested consolidating universities. Economists think it’s a bad idea.
description: Republican nominee for governor Vivek Ramaswamy in March said that consolidating Ohio’s public universities would make higher education better and more affordable. The strong consensus of economists surveyed on the topic this month said such a move would reduce the number of graduates in Ohio and reduce economic output. They split on whether it would […]
text:
Ohio Republican candidate for governor Vivek Ramaswamy. (Photo by WEWS.)Republican nominee for governor Vivek Ramaswamy in March said that consolidating Ohio’s public universities would make higher education better and more affordable.
The strong consensus of economists surveyed on the topic this month said such a move would reduce the number of graduates in Ohio and reduce economic output. They split on whether it would even save any money.
Amid a backlash, Ramaswamy is now backing away from his call. 
“I think that we have too many duplicative programs in our universities,” Ramaswamy told a Strongsville audience earlier this month, according to Cleveland’s WEWS. 
He later added, “I want every region to have the best higher education institutions available for people in (every) region. But not every university needs to offer every program.”
Vivek Ramaswamy said Ohio should shut down ‘subpar’ universities. Then came the backlash.

Ramaswamy said something quite different  in a March 27 column in The Columbus Dispatch. He cited Ohio’s aging population and declining enrollment, and referred approvingly to the fact that Georgia eliminated nine public universities between 2011 and 2018.
He wrote that as governor, he would “identify where missions overlap, where enrollment collapse has made independence untenable, and where administrative functions can be unified without harming students.”
The result, he said, would “create a more competitive, increasingly affordable and rightsized higher education system for taxpayers and students.”
A panel of Ohio economists surveyed by Scioto Analysis wasn’t sold on the argument. None believed it would help the Ohio economy in the long run.
Asked whether they agreed that, “Reducing the number of universities in Ohio would reduce long-term economic output in the state of Ohio,” 11 agreed and four were uncertain. 
None said they thought cutting the number of public universities would increase economic output.
Most of them work for public universities, so a little bias in their favor might be inherent. But Kevin Egan of the University of Toledo made a straightforward argument for why cutting public universities cuts economic output.
“On average college graduates earn more reflecting their extra value to the economy,” he wrote in the comment section of the survey. “Closing any local public university will reduce some local commuters from attending college and thus will reduce valuable workers to the economy in the long-term.”
On the other hand, Curtis Reynolds of Kent State University said the economic benefit of public colleges in Ohio might be blunted because Ohio’s leadership doesn’t do a better job of making the state attractive to young professionals.
“I am less confident about this for one simple reason: Ohio struggles to keep the college graduates that we create,” he wrote. “If the state cannot keep college graduates, then producing college graduates may matter less (from the perspective of the state).”
Reynolds didn’t mention the issue, but when CNBC earlier this month ranked Ohio its Top State for Business, it ranked it 18th for quality of life. And one thing it could have dinged Ohio on is an abortion ban passed by Republicans in the state’s gerrymandered legislature. It was later overturned by voters, but legislative Republicans continue to try to restrict abortion rights.
“And with surveys showing a sizable percentage of younger workers would not live in a state that bans abortion, we factor reproductive rights in this category as well,” CNBC said of its quality-of-life scoring.
The Ohio economists overwhelmingly agreed that getting rid of public universities would cut the portion of Ohioans who get college degrees. Twelve said it would and two were uncertain.
“It will reduce the number of bachelor’s degrees and eventually reduce the number of graduate degrees as well,” said Charles Kroncke of Mount St. Joseph University.
Ramaswamy was famously part of incoming President Donald Trump’s “Department of Government Efficiency” before making an early departure.
Run by Elon Musk, another billionaire with no government experience, DOGE promised to cut waste and save taxpayers $2 trillion. 
The ramshackle effort caused widespread chaos and fired people who often had to be rehired. It saved vastly less than promised — and by some estimates, it even ended up costing taxpayers billions.
While Ramaswamy said his college-consolidation plan would save Ohioans money, the economists didn’t seem to believe the matter was so clear-cut.
Six said it would save money, six said it wouldn’t and two were uncertain.
Even some of the economists who said consolidation would save money questioned the wisdom of doing so.
“It would save money for the state in the short run but would be penny wise and pound foolish in the long run,” said Bob Gitter of Ohio Wesleyan University. “Education is one of the primary functions of government.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Should Ohio freeze utility rates for a year?
description: Earlier this month, Ohio state Rep. Desiree Tims introduced a bill to freeze utility rate increases in Ohio for the next year. Tims’s bill comes in a time of increasing concern about affordability. According to the Energy Information Administration, the residential price of electricity per kilowatt hour in Ohio grew 29% from 2019 to 2024. […]
text:
An electricity meter. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current).Earlier this month, Ohio state Rep. Desiree Tims introduced a bill to freeze utility rate increases in Ohio for the next year.
Tims’s bill comes in a time of increasing concern about affordability. According to the Energy Information Administration, the residential price of electricity per kilowatt hour in Ohio grew 29% from 2019 to 2024.
Utility prices are an element of family budgets where the state has a clear lever for controlling costs. 
Since electricity companies are regulated entities, they negotiate with the state public utilities commission to set prices for their ratepayers. The state has the ability to freeze these prices for a year if it wishes to do so.
In a lot of ways, this sort of policy change is like a sales tax holiday, which the state of Ohio has embraced in the past, or a gas tax holiday, which legislators have bandied about recently to offset gas price increases endured by Ohio in the wake of the U.S. war with Iran. 
It represents a temporary suspension of a cost for ratepayers to provide relief in the short-term.
In the short term, a utility freeze would help low-income households. 
According to the United States Department of Energy, the average low-income household in Ohio spends about 11% of their income on utilities compared to 3% for a median-income household and 1% for a high-income household. 
While a utility freeze would be less targeted than an earned income tax credit, it would likely disproportionately benefit low-income households.
Energy insecurity can lead to unsafe health outcomes for households.
 As many as 1 in 10 U.S. households report keeping their household temperature at an “unsafe” level due to energy prices. 
A utility freeze could help households stabilize their finances without forcing them to cut back on heating or cooling their homes. 
Stability in energy prices could even lead to stabilization in home environments that could have spillovers into educational outcomes, like what we’ve seen with federal energy assistance programs.
While low-income households spend a larger percentage of their income on energy, evidence from the Energy Information Administration suggests the highest-income households consume energy at nearly twice the rate of the lowest-income households. 
This means upper-income households could be saving twice as many dollars from a utility rate freeze as low-income households, reducing the inequality impact.
The biggest problem with a rate freeze is that it could lead utilities to defer maintenance of existing infrastructure, which could impact reliability of electricity service and grid modernization efforts.
 This could lead to more blackouts, especially as growth in energy demand is leading to more users taxing the power system.
Ultimately, this policy represents a bet that utility increases over the next year will not be used for essential maintenance, efficient grid modernization, or reliability upgrades that outweigh the short-term benefit the freeze would have for household incomes, especially for low-income households. 
If Rep. Tims is right, this could mean better outcomes for households at little cost to the public. 
If she is wrong, the short-term benefits would come at the cost of a quicker degradation of the grid, which means more blackouts and could lead to higher costs in the long run. 
While there is part of me that wants to see if her bet is correct, there is another part of me that thinks a more targeted policy, like an earned income tax credit expansion, would achieve the same boost to household income without the potential costs to the grid. 
We’ll see if the General Assembly has an appetite for either.
