name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Latest Pa. budget provides support for nursing homes, but work remains
description: Nursing homes got a slight boost under the latest state budget, but say more support is needed for the critical industry.
text:
A physical therapist guides a nursing home resident through an exercise. (Photo by Whitney Downard/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)Providers caring for the commonwealth’s fastest-growing population got a little relief in Pennsylvania’s latest spending plan, securing guaranteed minimum funding for nursing homes. 
“I would say the General Assembly and the governor heard us loud and clear and I believe they absolutely came through on this,” said Garry Pezzano, the president and CEO of LeadingAge PA. 
For decades, a state budgeting maneuver known as the Budget Adjustment Factor, or BAF, reimbursed nursing homes below the cost of care. Regulators would determine payments depending on dollars allocated under the state budget, often at a rate that left operators shorthanded. 

Pa. long-term care providers call for more state dollars and predictable funding


In a budget that neglected to tackle looming policy questions, lawmakers chose not to eliminate the BAF, a long-time goal for providers, but opted to set a floor at 86% — above the current 79% — starting in 2027.
Over the next two years, nursing homes will receive an additional $162 million through the state formula, with a federal match of $215 million. Having a minimum gives facilities greater flexibility to budget, making their income more predictable, Pezzano said. 
“The fluctuation of the floor can be tremendous, and it’s something that happens on a quarterly basis,” he added. “Imagine what that does with your ability to forecast, to budget, to develop programs. You (now) know that at least you can count on that 86% of your allowable costs (being) covered.”
In a rapidly aging state, the fifth-oldest in the country, the need for long-term services is only growing. The number of residents over the age of 84 is expected to triple by 2050, but capacity is shrinking as nursing homes close or decertify beds.
Inadequate funding — especially through Medicaid, which funds care for more than 70% of nursing home residents — was just one of three roadblocks for operators identified by LeadingAge, alongside workforce shortages and consumer preferences. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The General Assembly also declined to revisit staffing ratios or tackle delayed Medicaid approvals, all items on LeadingAge’s wishlist. 
“We’ve got priorities now for continued momentum,” beyond steady funding, Pezzano continued. “I would say that we lobbied just as hard to reform staffing ratios and that didn’t happen.”
 Not enough nurses

The long-term care sector struggles to recruit and retain qualified staff amid a nationwide nursing shortage exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic. 
“Attracting people is a real priority, and we really need to work better together to attract people to see that there is really meaningful work, satisfying work to be done in long-term care,” said Pezzano.
One method would expose high school students to the field, allowing juniors and seniors to earn school credit while working in a facility — Senate Bill 116, which creates that pathway, passed the chamber unanimously in February.
Sen. Dave Argall (R-Schuylkill) speaks at a Capitol rally on June 2, 2026 while Rep. Mike Schlossberg (D-Lehigh) looks on. (Photo by Whitney Downard/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
In addition, Sen. David Argall (R-Schuylkill) authored two more measures  to shore up long-term care staffing, both of which have passed the chamber. Senate Bill 114 would allow students to take a certification exam “upon completion of relevant coursework,” while Senate Bill 115 offers an “alternative competency exam” as a replacement for potential hires who might not have a high school diploma or GED. 
All three proposals  have LeadingAge’s support and await action in the House. 
Pezzano said “overly prescriptive” staffing ratios added to the difficulty, setting minimum requirements for patient care using a formula based on hours worked, types of licensed staff and the number of residents. Operators chafed at the requirements under a national version, which proponents say would improve care, and the federal government reversed course late last year.  
Cheila Martinez, a former certified nursing assistant and now housekeeper at Spruce Manor in Reading, said quality resident care “depends on the entire nursing home team,” from nurses to laundry staff. 
“When any part of that team is short-staffed, residents feel the impact and workers burn out,” Martinez continued in a statement sent through her local union. 
As an SEIU union member, Martinez and others pushed for the updated reimbursement “because resident care requires much more money to stabilize the workforce,” saying her local contract gives workers the right to bargain over new public funding. 

The budget invests $2.5 million into the Nursing Shortage Assistance Program, which are grants that help offset student loans for nurses hired by hospitals, potentially growing the pool of qualified providers. The program, which launched last year with a $5 million investment, hasn’t yet allocated funds.

“I’m lucky to work at a Saber facility, where workers and management have built a strong partnership that works together to improve care and job standards,” she added. “But not every nursing home operator is like Saber.”
She called for the legislature to pass an accountability measure like the one proposed by Rep. Dan Frankel (D-Allegheny), which doesn’t yet have a bill number. The accompanying memo focuses on transition periods between operators and owners, and requires state approval before new companies take over. 
However, Martinez’s union seeks more emphasis on accountability to make sure staffing ratios are enforced. 
“We will also continue to work hard to improve the ownership and operator regulations so that Pennsylvanians can trust their state taxpayer dollars are going where they belong,” she concluded.
 Beyond institutional care

Long-term care encompasses more than nursing homes, which are the most expensive and intensive version of care. The budget barely touched pay for home health visits — a long-time goal for advocates — but did include a rate increase for Living Independence For the Elderly (LIFE). 
The LIFE program had 8,446 unique participants as of last summer, but growth has been stagnant despite the state’s aging population. 
Pezzano, whose organization represents LIFE operators as well as skilled nursing facilities, called the program a “value-based solution” that allows individuals to age at home but still have access to certain health services. 

State-funded senior programs in Pa. see opportunity in federal rural health dollars


“This program really is the most cost-effective way to care for people. It costs a fraction of what it costs to stay in a nursing home,” said Pezzano.
Families who might not know about LIFE or other homecare options might use a nursing home as “a default setting,” Pezzano continued. 
“People don’t want to think about getting older, and the absolute last thing you want to think about is being older and not well. So people put it off, and then individuals and their families are forced to make really important decisions under duress because there isn’t a plan for it,” he added.
The program received  a 3.9% increase, equal to $7 million. A proposal from Sen. Dan Laughlin (R-Erie), Senate Bill 482, tries to spread awareness about LIFE by requiring more organizations to share information with Medicaid enrollees. 
LIFE, home health and skilled nursing facilities were all part of one larger interconnected “ecosystem,” continued Pezzano, noting that housing shortages complicate care as well as delayed Medicaid approvals. 
“We have really been deliberate in introducing the whole concept of needing to look at aging services as an ecosystem,” he said. “We’re very sensitive to the fact that it’s not just about advocating for skilled nursing facilities. Because what you do in skilled nursing facilities will impact LIFE, will impact home health, homecare.”

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Corruption by Another Name (Part II)
description: In announcing closure of the Everglades immigration detention center known as “Alligator Alcatraz,” Gov. Ron DeSantis said the notorious facility — denounced as inhumane by civil rights groups — was always meant to be only temporary until more permanent detention centers could be secured, and federal officials now have that capacity. “Alligator Alcatraz fulf[...]
text:
New College of Florida is located in Sarasota. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)In announcing closure of the Everglades immigration detention center known as “Alligator Alcatraz,” Gov. Ron DeSantis said the notorious facility — denounced as inhumane by civil rights groups — was always meant to be only temporary until more permanent detention centers could be secured, and federal officials now have that capacity.
“Alligator Alcatraz fulfilled the role that it was designed to serve,” DeSantis said. “Today it now has zero detainees. It has helped remove many, many dangerous people from the street and get them out of not only the state of Florida, but the United States of America.”
 


Corruption by Any Other Name (Part I) 


DeSantis said he was proud of what his administration had accomplished.
“We stood this up,” he said. “We surged critical resources. We built critical infrastructure. We were able to manage very complex operations, and we were able to execute the mission when called upon efficiently.”
These comments are vintage DeSantis, a staged response to his deliberately inhumane decisions as he tries to save face. He may tout efficiency, but despite being open for less than a year, Alligator Alcatraz will likely turn out to be the single most expensive immigration detention center in the history of the United States, critics assert.
CBS New Miami reports that financial analyses by its journalists indicate that operating the detention camp in the Everglades and Baker County cost as much as $3,571 per detainee each day, more than 20 times the national average. Critics have decried these massive, no-bid contracts which drew more than $1 billion in taxpayer dollars away from essential state health, food security, and housing programs.
A recent Miami Herald investigation estimates that while misusing more than $1 billion on the detention camps, he guided taxpayers’ dollars to between 55 and 83 companies owned or operated by political allies, friends, and donors.
Over a year, DeSantis repeatedly dipped into Florida’s Emergency Preparedness and Response Fund — described by Democratic and other critics as a slush fund — to finance his anti-immigrant operation, circumventing regular channels and ignoring checks and balances.
Since 2023, DeSantis manipulated the process by waiving more than 24 state laws and regulations and extending the 60-day emergency more than 20 times. All to pave the way to erect “Alligator Alcatraz,” the detention camp on land sacred to the Miccosukee Tribe. Critics are deeply concerned that there has been no accountability to the legislature or the public and everything was conducted in secret.
 Human cost
DeSantis’ vanity project came at a tremendous human cost. He boasts that his agents have seized almost 22,000 undocumented immigrants. Hundreds disappeared into the detention network, all dehumanized and mistreated.
Amnesty International paints pictures of cruelty and despair. Human beings forced to endure calamitous living conditions: trapped in cages; no AC in sweltering heat; overflowing toilets; and routine flooding during severe weather.
When it comes to the public’s money, DeSantis and most of those in the political class act as if the supply is infinite and that he has the right to use it for projects that harm the very people they purport to serve.
 Sea change
Also of widespread concern is DeSantis’s use of taxpayers’ money to subvert higher education while enriching his MAGA buddies, as well as the manner in which he has hijacked higher education.
“This is a conservative capture of Florida’s public higher education,” said Robert Cassanello, a University of Central Florida history professor who is president of the United Faculty of Florida union. “It’s all ideological, and politically driven.”
As the Florida Tributary’s Michael Vasquez reports, DeSantis has used an army of loyalists to build a conservative higher-ed empire.
“With only a year left in office, Gov. Ron DeSantis has a limited window of time to wield power in Tallahassee. But on college campuses across Florida, DeSantis continues to expand his army of political loyalists — both college presidents and university trustees, who are poised to dominate for many years to come, no matter who is elected governor in 2026,” Vasquez wrote.
“As a result, higher education could become DeSantis’ enduring political legacy. And the governor’s final year in office will provide still more opportunities to push academia in a conservative direction.
Vasquez reports the DeSantis’ hijack is “intertwined with the conservative Heritage Foundation … which authored the controversial Project 2025 blueprint to guide the Trump administration’s efforts to reshape Washington.”
“With President Donald Trump term limited as well, aligning with Heritage could benefit DeSantis politically in the future,” Vasquez explained. “This Heritage-inspired sea change has outraged alumni and the communities surrounding Florida’s college campuses, some of whom view DeSantis’ allies as interlopers — many of the leaders DeSantis has installed have no previous connections to the schools they now run, limited experience in higher education, or live out of state. Those limitations have not stopped these new leaders from burrowing deep into the universities’ affairs, according to public records obtained by The Tributary, from micro-managing the materials presented in individual classrooms to replacing signs on bathrooms.”
 Well-placed allies
Guided by the Heritage Foundation, DeSantis, Christopher Rufo, and a coterie of far-right allies on the boards of trustees and elsewhere in the higher education firmament have engineered the changes.
DeSantis has forced out progressive and forward-thinking university presidents and replaced them with men and women carrying the anti-Black, anti-woman, anti-LGBTQ+ banner. They willingly manipulate curricula, erase Black history, dismantle DEI and affirmative action programs, and impose a cold, sterile, far-right conservative syllabus across campuses.
Meanwhile, allies on trustee boards engineered exorbitant paydays for each president installed at public state universities.
The takeover began when DeSantis and his allies dismantled New College of Florida. Since 2023, former House Speaker and close DeSantis ally Richard Corcoran has run the Sarasota university. His base salary is $699,000, while his total annual compensation frequently exceeds $1.2 million, including perks like an $84,000 housing stipend, a $12,000 car allowance, and lucrative performance/retention bonuses.
In February, he received a $200,000 bonus performance award for the third year in a row and that was followed by another $600,000 bonus days later for an “accrued retention payment” for continuing “uninterrupted service” for the past three years.
He is feasting at the public trough despite New College having a student population of fewer than 700.
Former Lt. Gov. Jeanette Nuñez was named sole finalist during the search for president of Florida International University. She’d served as interim and was voted in as permanent last summer. Nuñez has an annual base salary of $925,000 as part of her five-year contract and she is eligible to receive annual performance bonuses of up to $400,000.
Former Education Commissioner Manny Diaz Jr. was ensconced as president of the University of West Florida with a lavish a total annual compensation package of $946,040. This includes a $674,000 base salary, up to $107,840 in annual performance-based incentives, a $60,000 housing allowance, a $14,000 car allowance, and an $89,000 retirement supplement.
As has become commonplace in this process, Diaz was approved in a single-candidate competition — despite clear rules intended to require “more than two” finalists for trustees to consider.
Diaz has been a chief architect of the state’s retooling of public higher education with support from both DeSantis and members of the conservative Heritage Foundation.
Phoenix columnist Diane Roberts captures the greed with which these people operate.
UF trustees chair Mori Hosseini, a real estate magnate, rules the University of Florida the way DeSantis has operated in the Sunshine State, she writes: “No part of the university is free from his influence. He pushed UF’s distinguished College of Medicine to hire the state’s science-challenged surgeon general. Now UF pays Dr. Joseph Ladapo more than $300,000 per year — not that he does anything so pedestrian as actually teach classes.”
Few of those in DeSantis’ orbit aren’t enjoying exorbitant paychecks at the public’s expense, Roberts added.
“A trustee who hasn’t been identified had a hand in arranging an adjunct gig at UF’s law school for Florida’s attorney general [James Uthmeier]. The average pay for an adjunct professor is between $3,000-$7,000 per course. Uthmeier’s getting $100,000 for two hours of instruction per week.
“The AG doesn’t see the problem.”
Uthmeier recently staged an event to announce a statewide audit: He wants to “combat public corruption” and root out “bribes, kickbacks, conflicts of interest, evidence of money being spent on special interests, personal interests, personal gain,” Roberts wrote.
Critics have not taken all this lying down. Students, faculty and labor unions have fought back against the corruption of the process, several have filed lawsuits, but DeSantis and crew have sidelined or ignored detractors and continued on their merry way.
The profound hostility that Florida’s politicians have towards universities and their insistence on using ideological purity tests to choose their leaders not only “makes Florida look stupid,” as Roberts points out, but it is also jeopardizing the futures of the next generation.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Child neglect is vast in CT and DCF may not be so bad
description: If DCF is measured by the breadth of child neglect and abuse in Connecticut, the agency might seem to be an almost miraculous success.
text:
Beating up on Connecticut’s Department of Children and Families is easy and politically satisfying. Child neglect and abuse are rampant and worsening in the state and are beginning to overwhelm the agency’s social workers again, if not yet quite as much as the staff was overwhelmed when it was under federal court supervision from 1991 to 2022.
Connecticut’s Hearst newspapers quantified the problem the other day, reporting that the deaths of 62 children in the state since January 2025 came under DCF investigation and the circumstances of about 20 of the children had been reviewed by the agency in some way before they died.
Distressingly, neither DCF nor police have yet offered an explanation of the circumstances around one of those deaths, that of a 3-year-old Manchester girl who was struck and killed by a car as she crossed a thoroughfare unaccompanied at about 4:30 in the morning on June 10. Apparently she is to be officially forgotten.
Three days later Gov. Ned Lamont reminded Connecticut that the government has arranged for free meals to be available to all children at various locations throughout the state while schools are on summer recess. As for getting the children to the free meals and back home, the program makes the big assumption that, unlike the Manchester girl, they have competent adult supervision.
It’s not DCF’s fault that Connecticut has thousands of households not competent to take care of their children. Many of these households are fatherless; many are headed by people with mental illness or a drug, alcohol, or gambling addiction, or people who are undereducated and whose ability to make a living doesn’t match the child-raising responsibilities they undertook. Inflation and the rising cost of housing, a large part of which is ever-increasing property taxes — the rising cost of government itself — may keep them from ever getting out of the hole they dug for themselves.
DCF social workers review such circumstances knowing that no children should have to live where household competence is marginal and their health and safety are at risk. But the social workers also know that removing children from such homes risks psychological harm to them and political harm to the agency. The social workers soon learn that their judgments are easily questioned — that they may always be damned if they do and damned if they don’t.
It’s not a happy job and many tire of it quickly, just as many teachers in Connecticut’s impoverished cities and inner suburbs are demoralized by the misbehavior of their unparented students and the difficulty of keeping order in their classes. These teachers become eager to leave for positions in towns with better-parented students and higher pay.
It is often said that DCF is broken, and investigation of its most troubling cases typically finds negligence or bad judgment. But if DCF is measured by the breadth of child neglect and abuse in Connecticut, the agency might seem to be an almost miraculous success.
For a good indicator of that neglect and abuse is the rate of chronic student absenteeism in the state’s schools. About 17% of students meet the chronic threshold, missing 10% or more of their classes. That’s about 83,000 students who are neglected at home if not abused too. Chronic absenteeism in the cities, which have more poverty, more danger to children, and a disproportionate number of DCF cases, is closer to 25% or even 30%.
Twenty fatalities in a year and a half in a population of at least 83,000 neglected children constitute a fatality rate of less than three-tenths of 1%, or two-tenths of 1% per year.
Until Connecticut is ready to remove tens of thousands of neglected children from deficient homes and put them in group homes, modern orphanages, or ready otherwise to address the social disintegration being engendered by the excesses and perverse incentives of the welfare state, how much better can a child-protection agency fairly be expected to do — if it can even keep finding people willing to try to deal with it?
Chris Powell has written about Connecticut government and politics for many years.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Let’s have democracy funds throughout CT
description: Before the next election cycle, cities and municipalities across Connecticut should join Seattle, New York, and other local democracies in building “democracy funds.”
text:
After the first half of Donald Trump’s second term, Democratic voters across the country, including Connecticut, have been skeptical of the influence of money in politics. 
Voters have seen that politicians subject to the whims of super PACs are less likely to defend the interests of the people in their governance. And when politicians do not deliver on popular policies, voters lose trust in the ability of our political institutions to reliably and successfully govern.

Richie George

In Maine, 75% of voters approved a ballot initiative that would limit the amount of contributions from individuals and entities to super PACs to $5,000, effectively eliminating super PACs from the state. Dinner Table Action, a conservative organization dedicated to fostering “limited government,” sued the state, and now a key case, led by the campaign finance reform nonprofit Equal Citizens, will be heard by federal judges and may head to the U.S. Supreme Court. 
 While debates over the future of super PACs are held in courtrooms, everyday citizens can act now to renew American democracy. Change is possible through public financing programs at the state and local levels. 
In Seattle, residents participate in the Democracy Voucher Program  created after a citizen-led initiative, called “Honest Elections Seattle,” passed a suite of campaign finance reforms in November 2015. Those reforms also included limits on campaign fundraising and lobbying, added penalties for violations of election law, and instituted new reporting requirements for candidates’ and their families’ finances. 
As of March this year, the Seattle Ethics and Elections Commission distributes four $25 “Democracy Vouchers” to each resident who may assign a voucher to a candidate and thus donate to their campaign. The Democracy Vouchers are funded by property taxes, costing the average property about $13 a year. The candidate may use their Democracy Voucher to finance campaign activities, instead of cozying up to wealthy donors or super PACs. 
 This electoral program combats distrust in political institutions by directly involving citizens in the campaign finance process. After ten years of implementing the program, campaign donors are   more representative   of Seattle in terms of race, income, age, and geographic location. Voter engagement and the diversity of candidates have also increased. The Democracy Voucher Program has reinvigorated Seattle’s democracy.  
“Most of the people who heard of the program supported it,” said Cindy Black, former Executive Director of Fix Democracy First, a Washington nonprofit dedicated to democratic strengthening. “And when we explained what the program was to people who didn’t know, they supported it.” 
Closer to home, New York City’s Campaign Finance Board manages the Matching Funds Program, helping candidates rely on the city’s residents for small-dollar donations instead of super PACs and special interests. Candidates voluntarily participate in the program, and the program matches small contributions from New York City residents up to $2,000 in public funds per eligible contributor. Notably, Mayor Zohran Mamdani funded his campaign through New York’s Matching Funds Program, and many other legislators and government officials have been elected through the program.
 As a student organizer and registered voter in New Haven, I was elated to discover that New Haven has a “  Democracy Fund  ,” and it is the only municipality in Connecticut to have such a fund. New Haven’s Democracy Fund uses appropriations from the Board of Alders and citizens’ donations to publicly fund mayoral candidates. By accepting public funds, these candidates agree to abide by limits on campaign donations and expenditures: they must not accept more than $400 from individuals or a town committee, they cannot accept contributions from political committees or businesses, and they must not spend more than $400,000 in a primary election or a general election. If they abide by these restrictions and obtain at least 200 small donations of at least $5, they will receive up to $125,000 in public matching funds and a public financing grant of $25,000 for both the primary and general elections. 
 Current Mayor of New Haven Justin Elicker is a Democracy Fund   recipient  . And as of this year, the Fund has celebrated two decades of operation. 2027 will be the first election cycle when mayoral, city/town clerk, and alder candidates will run for four-year, instead of two-year, terms. New Haven’s Democracy Fund will likely be crucial in financing a busy field of candidates.  
 Before the next election cycle, cities and municipalities across Connecticut should join Seattle, New York, and other local democracies in building “democracy funds.” They encourage citizen involvement in campaign financing and ensure candidates are responsive to citizens’ demands. This ensures candidates represent voters instead of big moneyed interests. With political will and smart budgeting, municipalities like Hartford, Stamford, and Waterbury can fund these initiatives. At the state level, it would ensure that Connecticut adequately represents   all   people’s interests. 
 To transform Connecticut’s democracy, we must transform how we fund the campaigns of our representatives. 
Richie George lives in New Haven.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico Democratic lieutenant governor candidates tout experience, vision in final plea
description: Four Democrats made their final pitches to party members to join Deb Haaland on the Nov. 3 ballot as the party's lieutenant governor candidate.
text:
Four candidates vying to become the Democratic candidate for New Mexico lieutenant governor made their closing statements July 25, 2026, to the Democratic Party of New Mexico’s State Central Committee. Clockwise from top left are Public Lands Commissioner Stephanie Garcia Richard, state Sen. Harold Pope (D-Albuquerque), Toni Pinedo and Geoffrey Luehring. (Screenshots from virtual SCC meeting)Four candidates vying to become the New Mexico Democratic Party’s lieutenant governor nominee made their closing arguments Saturday to the party’s State Central Committee, which is tasked with electing a candidate to run alongside Democratic gubernatorial candidate Deb Haaland.
The Saturday meeting marked the culmination of a roughly month-long campaign since Secretary of State Maggie Toulouse Oliver, who previously won the Democratic party’s nomination in the June primary election, dropped out June 18 due to health reasons.
The SCC met virtually for about 20 minutes Saturday to hear from each of four candidates seeking to replace Toulouse Oliver and join Haaland on the ticket ahead of the Nov. 3 general election. 
The roughly 500 SCC members will now cast votes, using a ranked-choice voting system, until 5 p.m. Wednesday. The Democratic Party of New Mexico expects to announce a winner Thursday. 
The candidates — Public Lands Commissioner Stephanie Garcia Richard, state Sen. Harold Pope (D-Albuquerque), Geoffrey Luehring and Toni Pinedo — each spoke for roughly four minutes in their final appeals to the SCC before voting began. 
Garcia Richard, who spoke as more than a dozen supporters stood behind her, touted her experience fighting for public lands across eight years as land commissioner, as well as her collaboration with Haaland when Haaland was federal Interior Secretary under former U.S. President Joe Biden. Haaland has endorsed Garcia Richard to be her lieutenant governor. 
“We’ve worked together for years,” Garcia Richard told the SCC. “Deb trusts me to do this job, and I can promise you there will be no daylight between the governor and lieutenant governor.”
Pope, who is New Mexico’s first-ever Black state senator, lost to Toulouse Oliver in the primary. He described himself as an anti-establishment Democrat whose political success resulted from a commitment to working-class voters and hard work, not “powerful connections.”
“I know there’s been an endorsement in this race, but this vote belongs to you,” Pope told the SCC. “No endorsement can cast your vote. No political leader can replace your conscience. Only you can decide what kind of leadership our party will put before the people of New Mexico.”
Luehring, of Albuquerque, said his non-political background would make him well-suited to join Haaland on the ticket. New Mexicans don’t need another politician as lieutenant governor, he said, but instead need a “ground-level force” that would implement Haaland’s “high-level vision.” 
“Secretary Haaland has more than enough political experience for everyone running. We don’t need another politician sitting beside her, doing the same thing,” he said.
Luehring wore a T-shirt emblazoned with a photo of pop icon Britney Spears and the phrase “Gimme More,” the title of one her 2007 hits. He later explained that the shirt was a “subtle hint that we should expect more from our government.” 
Pinedo, the final candidate to speak, is an Indigenous advocate from Gallup. She said she decided to jump into the race out of concern for homeless youth across the state and hopes whomever the SCC elects makes finding housing and resources for troubled young people a priority. 
“You better pick the right one,” she said. “And you better pick the one that’s gonna actually work for everybody, not because that’s your name on a poster.”

name: VTDigger
title: An insurance card is not an appointment
description:
Vermont's healthcare debate keeps arguing over who pays. The real crisis is that regulators are already deciding who gets seen — and calling it cost control instead of rationing.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  An insurance card is not an appointment.
text:
This commentary is by Matt Swenson, who is the founder of Omnidex Solutions, a risk diagnostics company. He lives in Vermont.
Vermont’s healthcare debate has spent a decade stuck on the wrong question. The political class argues about who should pay the bill. Patients are asking something simpler: Can I actually see a doctor?
Insurance is not care. Coverage is not capacity. A promise from the government does not create a primary care appointment, a hospital bed, a nurse or an operating room. Yet Montpelier keeps tightening its grip on the money while patients have fewer real options every year.
Call it what it is. The Green Mountain Care Board is a rationing authority, whether or not anyone in Montpelier has the nerve to use the word. It sets hospital budgets, caps revenue and increasingly dictates what hospitals can build and offer. For fiscal year 2026, the board denied $94.5 million in revenue Vermont hospitals had proposed, most of it aimed at the University of Vermont Medical Center.
The board has its defense. Regulators accused the UVM Health network of shipping Vermont healthcare dollars to New York to cover losses at its New York hospitals and said the network should cut administration, executive pay and traveling staff before touching patient services. Fine. Hospital executives have earned that scrutiny. But look at the arrangement: Regulators choke the money, administrators pick where the cuts land, and patients absorb whatever falls out of the fight. Nobody voted for that outcome, and nobody answers for it.
The pattern is already on the ground. In 2024, UVM Medical Center shelved a planned $130 million outpatient surgical center after the board approved a fraction of the revenue growth it requested — a facility meant to replace aging operating rooms and expand the exact surgical capacity Vermonters are waiting on. Vermont did not reduce the need for surgery that year. It reduced the ability to perform it.
That is rationing by spreadsheet, and Act 68 is about to make it law, pushing Vermont toward global hospital budgets: fixed annual spending targets, first for the larger hospitals, eventually for all of them. Global budgets look tidy because the numbers are set in advance. Illness doesn’t care what the number is. When demand outruns the approved figure, you get closed beds, dropped service lines, out-of-state transfers and longer waits.
There’s a quieter cost. Squeeze a hospital hard enough, and it stops practicing medicine and starts managing throughput. Patients get sent home minutes after surgery ends, nowhere near a safe margin for anesthesia recovery, because the bed has a quota. Surgery becomes drive-through. Recovery becomes your problem, at home. That is the Walmart model of healthcare: high volume, standardized product, minimum staffing, everybody processed on the average and nobody treated as a person. At least McDonald’s is honest about what it’s selling.
Vermont is building the machinery of single-payer without the payer: centralized financial control, politically set spending caps and the delusion that squeezing payment produces affordability without destroying access.
Canada is the warning label. Its system guarantees public coverage for medically necessary care, and Canadians wait anyway. In 2024, only 68% of hip replacements and 61% of knee replacements happened within the recommended six-month window, and only 69% of cataract surgeries within the recommended 16 weeks — even as Canada performed record surgical volumes. The clinicians are not the problem. Scarcity is. When government dominates payment and constrains capacity, rationing doesn’t go away. It moves from price to queue.
The asymmetric patient pays first — the patient whose illness refuses to match the average the budget was built on. Several interacting conditions, a strange diagnosis, a failed prior treatment, a need for one particular surgeon. Standardized pathways were never built for that person, and a budget-driven system has every incentive to push them aside. The asymmetric patient waits the longest, gets transferred the farthest and takes whatever the system has left over.

READ MORE

Better models exist. Switzerland covers everyone without a government payment monopoly: regulated basic insurance for all, subsidies for those who can’t pay. It’s expensive, but it proves the point Montpelier refuses to hear: Universal coverage does not require running every dollar through one public spigot. Kaiser Permanente proves the delivery lesson: Tying insurers, physicians, hospitals and records into one system genuinely cuts waste. But Kaiser also shows the trap. A closed network works right up until you need something it doesn’t have. Then coordination becomes confinement.
Take the coordination, refuse the captivity. Vermonters should hold enforceable rights to outside referrals and second opinions whenever timely care isn’t available in network. Take Switzerland’s regulated competition, refuse Canada’s payment monopoly.
And measure reform by access, not enrollment. How long for a primary care appointment? How many specialists take new patients? How many surgeries slipped? How many Vermonters had to leave the state for treatment?
Montpelier keeps mistaking control for reform. Past a point, controlling budgets controls care — and when the state caps capacity and patients have nowhere else to go, cost containment stops being accounting. It becomes rationing with better manners.
An insurance card is not an appointment. A balanced spreadsheet is not a cured patient.

name: VTDigger
title: Norwich sets $250 fee for short-term rentals
description:
The town planning commission said the regulations will protect the community against “adverse secondary impacts” from nonconforming rentals violating health and safety standards.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Norwich sets $250 fee for short-term rentals.
text:
Priscilla Vincent raises her hand with a question, at left, during a public comment period before the Selectboard at Tracy Hall on a proposed zoning bylaw to regulate short-term rentals in Norwich, Vt., on Wednesday, July 23, 2026. Planning Director and Zoning Administrator Steven True is at right. The Selectboard voted to approve the bylaw for a two-year period which will require owners of such accommodations to register the property, submit to an inspection, and pay a $250 fee. Photo by: James M. Patterson/Valley News

This story by Sofia Langlois was first published in the Valley News on July 23, 2026.
Homeowners offering short-term rentals in Norwich must now register with the town government and pay a $250 fee, based on interim bylaws adopted by the town selectboard.
“I think there are some people, there are some houses in town that that’s their business model, and you’re going to have to go and tell them that their business model is not viable anymore,” selectboard Chair Kimo Griggs said at Wednesday’s meeting.
The selectboard voted unanimously to approve the short-term rental bylaws for two years, effective immediately.
Planning commission chair Jaan Laaspere said there are three ways to come into compliance: Stop renting; register with the town and rent out the space for only a portion of the year so it passes as owner-occupied; or rent for a longer period, by month or year.
“It doesn’t take away their ability to make money on the property even if they don’t live there at all,” Laaspere said. “They would just have to switch to a monthly rent.”
The town planning commission said the regulations will protect the community against “adverse secondary impacts” from nonconforming rentals violating health and safety standards.
Vermont’s Department of Taxes defines a short-term rental as a dwelling room or unit rented out for fewer than 30 consecutive days and for more than 14 days per calendar year.
What’s not regulated is renting month to month or renting out a home for two weeks out of the year. “But if it’s on the 15th day, then you’re within the definition of a short-term rental,” said Steven True, the Norwich planning director and zoning administrator.
Norwich isn’t the first Vermont town in the Upper Valley to regulate short-term rentals. Others include Hartford, Woodstock and West Windsor. On the New Hampshire side, Hanover, Lebanon, Sunapee and Enfield also have short-term rental regulations.
With no previous mention of short-term rentals as an authorized use under the planning code, it was technically prohibited in Norwich. The new bylaws attempt to clarify what can be done to provide the service while complying with the town rules, Laaspere said.
Airbnb, which provides travel listings online, currently showcases several properties in Norwich available for visitors vacationing in the Upper Valley.
The selectboard held a public hearing on this matter a few months back, but feedback on the first proposal resulted in significant changes, which warranted a second hearing. Since then, the planning department has added fire safety language, defined owner-occupancy, and determined whether preexisting short-term rentals are exempt from the new rules.
The new ordinance is set to expire in July 2028. By that time, the town will revisit it and implement a replacement ordinance.
“The choice to make an interim, which means two years, was to be proactive, but not assume we knew everything for a long-term solution,” Laaspere said.

Norwich Planning Director and Zoning Administrator Steven True, right, answers questions from Selectboard members, from left, Brendan Classon, Matt Swett and Mary Layton during discussion at Tracy Hall in Norwich, Vt., on Wednesday, July 22, 2026, of new regulations for short-term rentals. Photo by: James M. Patterson/Valley News

The department decided it is not immune to the ordinance, considering that short-term rentals were technically never allowed. Norwich zoning regulations are set up to list allowed uses in each district. While bed-and-breakfasts and inns were on the list, short-term rentals were not, due to being a more modern trend, True said.
The application process gives the zoning administrator 30 days to consider approving a permit, which expires on Dec. 31 of the year it’s granted.
The lot must be owner-occupied — that is, the sole primary residence for the owner, declared for tax purposes annually on April 1.
The zoning administrator may inspect the property before issuing a permit or anytime after. The owner must provide contact information, a property map and a signed affidavit certifying building details, number of parking spaces, and health and fire safety compliance.
One standard for short-term rentals is to allow no more than two people per sleeping room, with at least 70 square feet of space in a single-person bedroom. There must be enough off-street parking to accommodate the maximum number of guests, and a visible house number and weekly garbage removal are required. Advertisements must also conform with regulations.
A permit request may be denied if it’s incomplete or if the town had revoked a previous permit, True said.
The enforcement process would begin when True hears reports of a possible violation from neighbors, he said. Then, he would investigate and have an informal conversation with the owners. “It’s all done in steps. And the informal portion is important,” True said of its effectiveness.
If the owner does not comply, a formal notice of violation would be issued. Across the state, there is commonly a $100 charge per day until the violation is corrected, True said. It’s up to the selectboard to enforce fines.
Application fees go into the town’s general fund, Treasurer Cheryl Lindberg said at the meeting.

name: Nevada Current
title: NV going 2nd. Or 22nd. Does it matter?
description: Nevada will go second on the 2028 Democratic presidential primary calendar, following South Carolina, a group of national party mandarins announced Friday. Apparently there’s still another step in the process, but all the kids who are following this seem to think that’s a mere formality and that the calendar is set. Nevada Democratic Party leaders […]
text:
(Photo by Joe Raedle/Getty Images)
Nevada will go second on the 2028 Democratic presidential primary calendar, following South Carolina, a group of national party mandarins announced Friday. Apparently there’s still another step in the process, but all the kids who are following this seem to think that’s a mere formality and that the calendar is set.


Nevada Democratic Party leaders had hoped Nevada would go first, arguing:


a) With its diversity and working class economy Nevada’s is about as representative of the contemporary United States as it gets, so no one is more qualified to give an early blast of momentum to a presidential candidate than Nevada Democratic voters, and


b) the Nevada Democratic electorate’s collective finger is on the nation’s collective political pulse, as evidenced by all those radically innocuous pro-business politicians Nevada Democrats vote for all the time, so — always and ever transactional first — Nevada will be sure to pick a plain vanilla winner yay! 


The validity of the first premise — and dubiousness of the second — aside, going first wouldn’t relocate the state any closer geographically to the East Coast political-media-industrial complex. Nevada likely wouldn’t be showered with the 24-7 “first-in-the-nation” attention historically bestowed on New Hampshire and Iowa in prior years, or that will be lavished on South Carolina in 2028.


Ever since Nevada became an early caucus state in 2008, it has been sort of a junior early state, never receiving the star treatment New Hampshire, Iowa, or South Carolina got. It doesn’t get polled as much. Except for the occasional goofy exception (Rand Paul), presidential primary candidates themselves have tended to treat Nevada with some indifference, not really looking Nevada in the eye, but over its shoulder at some state that’s cuter. The national political press doesn’t encamp in Nevada to cover the presidential race as a daily news story, but instead parachutes in on occasion to produce feature-style previews/overviews laced with gambling clichés. Nevada’s never really been viewed as a make or break state. 


And no, Joe Biden finishing second in 2020 after finishing third in Iowa and New Hampshire doesn’t mean Nevada counts; South Carolina and its living legend Democratic Rep. Jim Clyburn would have rescued Biden’s candidacy the week after Nevada’s 2020 caucus no matter where Biden had finished in the contest.


Speaking of Clyburn, earlier this week he turned to a baseball analogy and suggested to the New York Times that South Carolina would have more influence if it went not first, but fourth.


“I learned that the best batter on the team is the cleanup hitter. Fourth place. And so South Carolina will be OK continuing being the best batter on the team, the cleanup batter,” he said.


Meanwhile Nevada Democrats will go second, and hold a competitive early presidential primary for the first time. The hype and hoopla and nonsense that goes with being an early primary state (while not as intense and tiresome as perpetually being the smallest battleground state in the general election) should assure Nevada’s primary garners a much higher national public profile than the preposterous caucuses ever earned.


But that’s a low bar. Nevada’s moment in the spotlight will still be somewhat overshadowed, and the nation’s aforementioned campaign complex’s attention diverted, by two newly added looming early states, delegate-rich Michigan and Virginia. And Nevada’s impact on the Democratic nomination for president could end up being about the same by going second as it would be by going 22nd.
A version of this column was originally published in the Daily Current newsletter, which is free and which you can subscribe to here.

name: VTDigger
title: Then Again: When a mysterious killer stalked the men of Bristol
description:
Thirteen people abruptly sickened and died, and the cause proved to be a surprise. Some people laid blame on a state law.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Then Again: When a mysterious killer stalked the men of Bristol.
text:
A group of men pause to pose and enjoy a drink in a photo taken circa 1900-1910. In 1903, Vermont ended the longstanding statewide prohibition of the sale or consumption of alcohol for anything except “medicinal, chemical or mechanical purposes.” Replacing it was a “local option” law, whereby individual communities voted whether to ban alcohol within their boundaries. Photo courtesy of Lake Champlain Maritime Museum/Vermont Historical Society
The first signs of trouble were headaches, perhaps a bit of nausea, and mild stomachaches. The men might have shrugged the pain off as the price of a hard week of work. Or maybe they’d just had too much to drink.But the symptoms intensified. The abdominal pain became excruciating and was often coupled with dizziness, confusion, seizures and blurred vision. It was then followed by total blindness.The first deaths occurred Nov. 1, 1914. Two men from the town of Bristol, 60-year-old Samuel King and 55-year-old Fred O’Bryan, each seemingly having been in good health, died suddenly that morning. A phone call that afternoon announced the death of a third man under similar circumstances in the neighboring town of Lincoln. 
On Nov. 2, the morning newspapers reported the three deaths along with news that two other men were gravely ill. The afternoon papers reported the death toll had reached six. The following day, newspapers announced that the number of dead was now 12. All the victims were men, ranging in age from 24 to 70. The Rutland News declared ominously that “several more are very near death’s door.”  
By this point, authorities had already determined what was likely causing the wave of deaths. The symptoms and circumstances pointed unmistakably to alcohol poisoning. But instead of the grain alcohol that is in most liquor — typically made from barley, corn, rye and wheat — authorities were confident that all the victims had consumed wood alcohol, usually derived from scrap wood and paper, which can be lethal even in small doses.
Where the victims got the wood alcohol soon also became clear. As his symptoms worsened, O’Bryan disclosed that he’d recently purchased liquor from Don A. Bisbee, a trained doctor who had run a drug store in Bristol for the past 30 years. Other victims reported the same thing.
The mass poisoning occurred against the backdrop of Vermont’s “local option” system for regulating alcohol sales under which the state had operated for the past dozen years. Local option allowed voters to decide whether alcohol could be sold in their communities. 
The law, however, contained a loophole that was frequently exploited. Even in so-called dry towns, licensed pharmacists could legally dispense alcohol for “medicinal purposes” to patrons who presented a doctor’s note. But in Bristol in 1914, people couldn’t even take advantage of that loophole, since there were no licensed pharmacies in town. There was no legal way to buy alcohol locally. 
The public debated the role the state’s liquor laws played in the tragedy. The Bristol Herald reported that some people believed that “(i)f there had been an open saloon here the thirteen unfortunates would have been alive to-day.” Bristol being a dry town surrounded by other dry towns had forced drinkers to buy alcohol on the black market, they argued. The more common complaint expressed in Vermont newspapers, however, was that the public didn’t take liquor laws seriously enough. “(T)he sentiment in town is against an open saloon,” the Herald stated, “but willing to wink at illegal selling.”
‘Sorrow and weeping prevails’
It was apparently an open secret that Bisbee was not the only one in town breaking the law. “(Bristol) has long had a reputation for illegal selling of liquor,” reported the Enterprise and Vermonter newspaper of Vergennes, “and although the authorities have not been blind to the fact, so clever have the offenders been in eluding detection that the sale has gone on apparently with little cessation.”
Still, the authorities had occasionally nabbed offenders, including Bisbee. According to one news report, when Bisbee was caught in May of that year, he’d been heavily fined and lost both his pharmacy license and his right to practice medicine. Even this punishment didn’t deter him. Selling contraband was just too lucrative to resist. 

Left: A front page headline in the Nov. 3, 1914 edition of the Rutland News announces the rising death toll in the Bristol wood alcohol tragedy. Another man soon succumbed, bringing the total to 13 dead and many others stricken by the toxic drink. Right: Don A. Bisbee’s photo appeared in advertisements for his business selling trusses to relieve hernias, or ruptures, as they were then commonly called. Bisbee started the business after being pardoned and released from prison. Via Newspapers.com

“Saturday seems to have been the big day for laying in a stock of liquor and the drug store of D.A. Bisbee the place to get it,” the Enterprise and Vermonter wrote. The customers were men from Bristol and surrounding towns, many of them farmers, many of them poor.According to the paper, “(Bisbee) has not conducted a regular drug store, but carried a stock of patent medicines, fishing tackle, stationery, etc.” (Unlicensed pharmacies could sell nonprescription medicines, but nothing stronger.) “His specialty,” the newspaper continued, “seems to have been selling liquor on the sly.”
Bisbee was accused of selling wood alcohol mixed with burnt sugar and prune juice to give it the color of whiskey. After being arrested, Bisbee admitted selling alcohol from his store but said he’d had no idea the concoction contained lethal wood alcohol. Over the previous 30 years, Bisbee said, he’d purchased $100,000 worth of grain alcohol from the wholesale druggists J.L. Thompson & Sons of Troy, New York. 
As usual, the base alcohol he had doctored and sold that weekend had arrived from Thompson & Sons in a 10-gallon can marked “cologne spirits,” he said. “Cologne spirits” is a highly distilled alcohol made from grain or other fermentable sugar sources. It was not considered fit for human consumption and was typically used to manufacture perfume and cologne, but could still safely serve as a beverage base. Grain alcohol is almost entirely ethanol, a chemical compound the human body can tolerate in small doses. In contrast, wood alcohol is methanol, a highly poisonous compound. Tragically, the two compounds can easily be mistaken for each other, since they are both clear, flavorless and nearly odorless.
Bisbee was wracked with guilt. “They had confidence in me when they made the purchase,” he was quoted as saying. “They died thinking that ‘Doc’ had made a mistake. This is terrible.” 
Thirty of Bisbee’s customers were said to be seriously ill. With news reports warning that perhaps as many as 80 men had purchased alcohol from him that Saturday, the public anxiously awaited news of more deaths. In the end, the poisonous drink claimed only one more victim, bringing the total killed to 13.
“Sorrow and weeping prevails where but a few days ago there was life and happiness,” wrote the Bristol Herald, which reported on the many funerals.
Each death created a hole in the community, in a family, the Rutland News reported: “The wave of sudden and violent deaths which have swept the community leaves a train of helpless ones with no means of support, as nearly all of the victims were of the poorer families and many of them left aged mothers, or widows and small children.”
‘Those who died were my friends’
Autopsies confirmed that wood alcohol had caused the deaths, and chemical analysis found that various liquid samples at Bisbee’s store contained high levels of wood alcohol. After his arrest, Bisbee was jailed in Bristol but was soon moved to the county jail in Middlebury for his safety, because “feeling in town ran (so) high … the sheriff feared an attempt might be made to get at his prisoner,” the Orleans County Monitor wrote.
Prosecutors indicted Bisbee for causing four deaths — the ones most easily linked to him — and ultimately placed him on trial for only one of them, the death of 40-year-old Cyrus Curry of Bristol. That case offered an excellent chance of conviction: A local doctor could testify that he had attended Curry as he was dying and learned from the man that he’d purchased alcohol from Bisbee.
At his trial, held just two months after the incident, Bisbee admitted breaking the law by selling spirits, adding that he typically sold 4 or 5 gallons of alcohol a week. “But I certainly would not have sold the liquor if I had known it was wood alcohol. All those who died were my friends, some very personal friends.”

The Burlington Free Press announced the verdict in the wood alcohol trial on the front page of the Jan. 1, 1915 edition.

Jurors learned that when news of the deaths reached Bisbee, he apparently panicked and told a store clerk to destroy markings on the large can of alcohol. Fortunately for Bisbee, however, investigators found enough evidence (receipts and labels) to show that he had indeed ordered cologne spirits, not wood alcohol, from the wholesaler in Troy. Still, the prosecution argued, a man of his experience should have recognized that the wrong can had been delivered.
After a two-day trial, the jury deliberated for seven and a half hours before finding Bisbee guilty. The judge sentenced Bisbee to 12 to 15 years’ hard labor at the Vermont state prison in Windsor. Given that he was 63 at the time, Bisbee might have wondered whether he would ever leave prison. Nevertheless, he sought to clear his name. From prison, Bisbee sued J.L. Thompson & Sons, arguing it was the company’s mistake that had sparked the tragedy. In the spring of 1918, the company settled out of court and agreed to pay him $1,750. 
The settlement earned Bisbee more than just a valuable payout; it soon earned him his freedom. The next spring, largely due to Thompson & Sons’ implicit admission of responsibility, newly elected Vermont Gov. Percival Clement pardoned Bisbee, who had served four and a half years of his sentence. 
‘Blame should be divided’
Released from prison, Bisbee relocated to Rutland, where perhaps he hoped to enjoy a bit of anonymity. There he started a business selling trusses to patients suffering from hernias.
The Rutland News, however, killed that dream, alerting readers less than two weeks after his arrival that a “distinguished Vermonter” was living “incognito” among them. Several years earlier, the News reminded readers, Bisbee had been “much in the public eye by reason of the wholesale deaths in Bristol.”

A January 1915 headline in the Essex County Herald succinctly announces the sentence pronounced against Don A. Bisbee. Via newspapers.com 

The News had spotted an advertisement Bisbee placed for his truss business in the rival Rutland Herald, which Gov. Clement happened to own. The News found rich irony in the heading on Bisbee’s ad, which read “Watch Out. You are in Danger,” adding that “(t)he ‘Doc’ is considered an authority on this subject.” 
Bisbee’s name didn’t appear in the advertisement, but the News noted that his photo did. The image shows a mustachioed man relaxing in a rocking chair, with a cigar in one hand and a dog on his lap. So much for anonymity.
Bisbee took his business on the road, traveling around Vermont to fit people for trusses. He would announce his arrival in town with newspaper advertisements. For several years after the Rutland News story, he stopped using his photo with the ads and started using the slightly altered name “Dr. Alverton Bisbee.” 
Upon Bisbee’s release from prison, the Bristol Herald had come to his defense. “Bisbee has paid the penalty for the part he played in Bristol’s celebrated wood alcohol case, yet many condemn him for the entire job,” the newspaper stated. Given the settlement he had won, “the blame should be divided at least on a 50-50 basis between Bisbee and the John L. Thompson Drug Co.”
“We believe Dr. Bisbee is sincere in his desire and intention of living a better life,” the paper continued. “… We believe it will pay to give him a fair chance.”
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Then Again: When a mysterious killer stalked the men of Bristol.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Will Congress ban ‘mud dumping’ in Mobile Bay?
description: This article originally appeared on Inside Climate News, a nonprofit, non-partisan news organization that covers climate, energy and the environment. Sign up for their newsletter here. For decades, fishers, swimmers and environmental groups have complained that mud and silt from dredging operations in the Mobile Bay shipping channel have been smothering seag[...]
text:
The port city of Mobile, Ala., sits at the head of Mobile Bay and is a key link in shipping goods in and out of the U.S. (Lee Hedgepeth/Inside Climate News)This article originally appeared on Inside Climate News, a nonprofit, non-partisan news organization that covers climate, energy and the environment. Sign up for their newsletter here.
For decades, fishers, swimmers and environmental groups have complained that mud and silt from dredging operations in the Mobile Bay shipping channel have been smothering seagrasses, choking out oysters and clouding water that was once pristine.
Now those groups are one step closer to getting the practice of “thin-layer placement” in the sensitive estuary banned by federal law.
U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures, D-Mobile, says he has included an amendment in the Water Resources Development Act of 2026, or WRDA, that would ban the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers from using thin-layer placement in most circumstances.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“It essentially removes that option away from the Corps to dispose of dredged material,” Figures told Inside Climate News. “They can no longer just spray it across the bay.”
The WRDA is passed every two years to establish projects for the Army Corps to “improve the nation’s ports and harbors, the inland waterway navigation network, flood and storm protection, and other water resources infrastructure,” according to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee website.
The Corps has nearly completed a massive dredging effort to deepen and widen the Mobile shipping channel to allow larger ships to enter the Port of Mobile, a major artery for coal imports and exports.
Since the project began, however, complaints have come in steadily from fishers, residents and seafood organizations, including social media videos of Army Corps dredges spraying the spoil material across the bay.
William Strickland, executive director of the environmental group Mobile Baykeeper, said that level of sediment dispersal harms the local ecosystems that many people depend on for their livelihood.
“It clouds the water, doesn’t allow sunlight to reach the subaquatic vegetation or seagrass that it needs to grow,” Strickland said. “That sediment can land on our oysters and smother those. And generally, where they place it, we see a lot less life.”
The Corps says it aims to deposit 6 to 12 inches of sediment across the bay from dredging operations and considers that a beneficial use to the ecosystem.
“The material dredged from the federal navigation channel is natural sediment and a resource that should be managed intentionally,” Valerie Morrow, the Army Corps Mobile District dredge material program manager, said in a news release. “Thin-layer placement is an intentional placement practice that is a beneficial use of dredged material.”
Alabama passed a state law in February curtailing the practice, requiring that 70 percent of dredged material be used for beneficial use projects, and excluding thin-layer placement as beneficial use.
The bill now in Congress would further restrict the practice, with exceptions only for emergencies or where there is no timely alternative, Figures said.
This year’s version of the legislation advanced unanimously through the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and is awaiting a vote from the full House. Figures said “only [Speaker] Mike Johnson knows” when the bill might go before the House, but he expects the bipartisan bill would move quickly.
“This bill came out of committee with unanimous support, with no one voting against it, and so we anticipate something like this being able to work its way through and get on the House floor soon, but we don’t know exactly when that will be,” he said.
Figures said he “absolutely” expects the bill to pass in its current form, with bipartisan support in the Senate as well.
“We would not expect the language to change at all,” he said. “It’s something obviously that we discussed with other members of the delegation before we came up with the final language.”
U.S. Sen. Katie Britt, R-Ala., has also been a vocal opponent of the Corps’ practice of disposing of sediment by spraying it into the bay, and was credited with getting provisions promoting beneficial use of dredged sediment in the 2024 WRDA.
“We can do two things,” Britt said in a 2025 Senate Appropriations Energy and Water Development Subcommittee hearing on the Corps’ budget. “We can make sure that we have the economic engine that is the Port of Mobile, and we responsibly preserve our natural resources. It is imperative this dredged material could be used for habitat restoration, for beach nourishment, for wetland creation.”
Strickland, of Mobile Baykeeper, said the group is happy to see the bill advance with bipartisan support.
“There’s a ways to go, but we’re thrilled that we’ve got the language that we need in the bill, and that the community has come together to make it clear to our elected officials where they can work across the aisle,” he said.
In addition to the ban on “mud dumping,” Figures said the WRDA bill includes $50 million for several projects around his south Alabama district, which includes the port city of Mobile and multiple Black Belt counties dealing with challenging wastewater infrastructure issues.
The Black Belt is a crescent swath across rural south and central Alabama that once made up the heart of the state’s cotton industry. The area now struggles with severe economic stagnation, high poverty rates and significant infrastructure challenges.
“When you look across that region as a whole, as you know, many … suffer with a very unique issue of being in rural communities that don’t have public sewer hookups and that have soil concentrations at many of these homes that is not conducive to traditional septic systems,” Figures said. “That’s led to the issue of straight-piping, which is essentially running a sewer line out into the woods, which creates a number of health and environmental concerns.
“So this is something that will allow the potential for these resources secured through the Water Resources Development Act to be used locally to help address some of those issues.”

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: South Dakota runoff election spawns another reluctant ‘RINO’
description: Throughout my career in journalism, as an editorial writer and now as a columnist, I never seriously considered belonging to a political party. As an opinion writer, those political parties were subjects and sometimes targets but never any place I wanted to call home. My voter registration as an independent was something I wore like […]
text:
A sign stands alongside delegates seated at the South Dakota Republican Convention on June 27, 2026, in Rapid City. (Photo by Seth Tupper/South Dakota Searchlight)Throughout my career in journalism, as an editorial writer and now as a columnist, I never seriously considered belonging to a political party. As an opinion writer, those political parties were subjects and sometimes targets but never any place I wanted to call home.
My voter registration as an independent was something I wore like a badge of honor. If I was registered as an independent, I figured I could take shots at either party without being accused of favoritism. Whenever the subject of my voter registration came up, I told people I subscribed to the Groucho Marx philosophy that I wouldn’t want to belong to any club that would have me as a member.
That’s why it’s with a heavy heart and a certain degree of embarrassment that I confess that I am now a member of the Republican Party. It really wasn’t that tough to change my registration. It’s not like you have to get an invitation from the party in order to join or sign an oath pledging your loyalty. Just show up at the courthouse and fill out a form. I’ll admit there may have been some psychological trauma. I screwed up twice while filling out the form.
[Voter Guide: 2026 Republican governor nomination runoff Voter Guide: Runoff for Republican governor nomination.]
Of course my interest in joining the GOP is prompted by being able to vote in the Tuesday’s runoff for the Republican nomination for governor between Aberdeen businessman Toby Doeden and Gov. Larry Rhoden. Given South Dakota’s history of electing Republicans in statewide races, the winner of the runoff will likely be the state’s next governor.
As a newspaper editorial writer, a topic I returned to every two years was the Republican Party’s closed primary. It didn’t seem fair that, as a taxpayer, I got to pay for an election but not take part in it. After writing so many words about the need for an open primary, it seemed like it was time to lay down the pen, get off the sidelines and take action, no matter how disagreeable.
For its part, the Democratic Party welcomes independents and voters with no party affiliation to vote in its primaries. Every election year, that proves to be an empty offer. A Democratic primary in June is even more rare than a Democratic victory in November.
I’m not the only one making a political party change prior to the runoff. According to a recent South Dakota Searchlight story, since the primary, the Republican Party has gained at least 7,350 new members.
The influx of new members doesn’t seem to be welcomed by the party leaders. In another Searchlight story, state Republican Party Chairman Jim Eschenbaum said, “If you’re a Democrat, vote for Democrats. Work on your own party. Don’t sabotage our party. That’s what they’re doing.”
Eschenbaum seems to overlook the fact that independents and voters with no party affiliation outnumber registered Democrats in South Dakota. Eschenbaum calls this influx of new party members sabotage. Those new members will likely call it an attempt to have a say in the future of our state.
The political party Eschenbaum oversees has become a victim of its own success. Its membership has grown so large that it has spawned warring factions within the party. More traditional, small-government Republicans find themselves at odds with volatile “election integrity” enthusiasts whose agenda seems intent on proving that they are the most conservative members of the party.
One of our president’s favorite insults for those members of his own party who refuse to do his bidding is calling them RINOs — Republicans In Name Only. I may be a new member of the Republican Party, but make no mistake about it: I am a RINO.

name: VTDigger
title: ‘Fertile period’ in Rutland City 25 years ago served as backdrop for photographer’s surreal scenes of suburban life
description:
“It's important to make a picture in an actual place that means something,” said the photographer Gregory Crewdson.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  ‘Fertile period’ in Rutland City 25 years ago served as backdrop for photographer’s surreal scenes of suburban life.
text:
GREGORY CREWDSON, Untitled, 2002, Digital pigment print, image size 40 x 25 in. © Gregory Crewdson
Over the course of several weeks in the summer of 2001, photographer Gregory Crewdson captured unsettling and surreal scenes of American suburban life in a ranch-style home in Rutland. 
The series made in Rutland included pictures of a stunned Tilda Swinton looking toward the sky out of frame, with her hand gently resting on a car hood. One photo shows a weary Phillip Seymour-Hoffman drooping out of the driver’s seat of a car with a trunk overflowing with flowers. Another captures a slouched Gwenyth Paltrow hanging her head reflected in the mirror in a beige-toned living room. Yet another picture shows a distressed Julianne Moore in a nightgown perched on the edge of a bed. Crewdson also shot a forlorn William H. Macy sitting on a rainy eve in a garage brimming with sodden earth. 
The images created in Vermont featuring famous actors were part of Crewdson’s “Dream House” series, appearing in a spread in The New York Times Magazine in 2002, commissioned by Kathy Ryan, the magazine’s photography director for nearly 40 years. 
“It felt kind of magical in a way,” Crewdson said, 25 years on. “All these great actors in this ordinary home.”
GREGORY CREWDSON, Untitled, 2002, Digital pigment print, image size 40 x 25 in. © Gregory Crewdson
In addition to appearing in print, Crewdson’s photography is featured in permanent collections in several art museums including The Albertina in Vienna, Austria and The Guggenheim in New York, featuring photos taken in Rutland. 
He was drawn to the Marble City by its “timeless quality,” Crewdson said in an interview this month. He also seeks nondescript “yet compelling” places to photograph at twilight. Crewdson uses this lighting to “transform everyday life into some kind of mystery,” he said. 
“Rutland hit all those qualifications,” Crewdson, 63, from Brooklyn, New York, said. 
His series “Beneath the Roses,” shot across five years in the mid-aughts, also featured photos in Rutland, including a pregnant woman crossing the intersection of Merchant’s Row and West Street, a woman stepping out of a bronze Chrysler on a muddy lot into a puddle strewn with balloons, and scattered people caught in a daze by train tracks. The series also featured an image of actress Lauren Ambrose staring skyward standing by a gas station on State Street in Rutland.
“I think that a lot of his photographs have more meaning to the locals now because, you know, it’s right in their backyard,” Vermont filmmaker David Giancola said.
GREGORY CREWDSON, Untitled, 2003-2008, Digital pigment print, image size 57 x 88 in. © Gregory Crewdson
Crewdson first came to Rutland after renting equipment for photoshoots in the Berkshires from Rutland-based Edgewood Studios, an independent film company headed by Giancola. In that era of the early 2000s, Giancola directed films in the Rutland area such as the family drama “The Newcomers,” with then-aspiring actors Chris Evans, Paul Dano and Josh Peck and the science fiction action “Lightening: Fire from the Sky” with a young Jesse Eisenberg. 
During that time in the early 2000s, Giancoala said Edgewood Studios was “really cranking” out action, disaster and family films in Vermont, and had extensive equipment, stages, cameras, props housed in Rutland studio that Crewdson used for various shoots. Giancola said that the wide range of scenery in Rutland County, including mountains, lakes, quarries and industrial decay sets the stage for a variety of stories.
A Rutland-based actor and writer Sandy Gartner met Crewdson while working for Edgewood Studios, helping Crewdson cast for photos, and Crewdson asked her to be his production coordinator. Her first assignment was to construct a house frame for a shoot and she enlisted carpentry students from Stafford Technical Center in Rutland for the task, Gartner said. 
After aiding his photoshoots around the city, Gartner remembered her in-laws’ home in Rutland, which had been left untouched after their deaths.
“Something clicked,” Gartner said. “This is kind of like a ready-made set for him.”
GREGORY CREWDSON, Untitled, 2003-2008, Digital pigment print, image size 57 x 88 in. © Gregory Crewdson
Seeking out a cinematic look to his photographs, Crewdson agreed that the wood-grain, ranch-style home perched on a hill in the southeast side of the city looked like a preserved film set from the 1960s or ‘70s. He brought well-known actors into the home at the witching hour to inhabit his world, and tell the story in a single moment frozen in time. 
“I love how a still photograph has no beginning or no end,” Crewdson said. “In my pictures, there’s a sense that something just happened or is about to happen.”
Gartner recalled renting flowers from the local Home Depot for the shoot with Seymour-Hoffman and the Rutland City Fire Department hosing down background for the William H. Macy shot. She said Swindon was particularly “down-to-earth,” reciting a monologue for the crew for feedback. 
Gartner, who currently serves on the board of directors for Vermont Humanities and is the co- producing director of Vermont Actors’ Repertory Theatre, said that Vermont is still a haven for artists, with resources such as the Paramount Theater and Chaffee Art Center in Rutland. Still, Gartner said she witnessed the slow closure of arts and theater venues around Vermont due to financial constraints and the COVID-19 pandemic, such as the stage at the College of St. Joseph’s and JAG Productions in White River Junction. 
While still making films, Giancola has tightened operations at Edgewood Studios given the fast advancing digital technology. He said that nowadays, filmmakers can rely on phones, artificial intelligence and live interactive LED screens to make films, rather than expensive video cameras and set design. 
Giancola said that the early aughts were a “very specific, fertile period” for Edgewood Studios and for filmmaking generally, and remarked that smartphones have changed the way that artists relate to each other. “We spend a lot of time with technology and not with each other,” forgoing interactions that built trust needed for collaboration and artistic experimentation, Giancola said. 
Crewdson also continues to produce new work. He was recently featured in Rolling Stone magazine for taking the “perfect shot”  for the singer, songwriter Phoebe Bridgers’ upcoming tour, which has generated buzz for instituting a “phone-free” policy at concerts. The picture features a lone figure in a car driving through an empty, dilapidated street in Adams, Massachusetts at dusk. 
GREGORY CREWDSON, Untitled, 2003-2008, Digital pigment print, image size 57 x 88 in. © Gregory Crewdson
Crewdson said he feels aligned with Bridgers creatively in their shared fixation on “loneliness and mystery” in their art. Crewdson was not aware of the phone ban before the shoot, but did bring an analog phone booth to the street for the photograph, he said, capturing a time when making a phone call took more effort. 
Being present without a phone for the concert brings “intentionality” to the experience, Crewdson said, and he aims to bring a similar sense of purpose to making and viewing photographs.
In a digital world with ubiquitous images generated by AI, “it’s important to make a picture in an actual place that means something,” Crewdson said.
