text:
U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Birmingham) said people deserve stability, consistency and access to medical benefits at an April 17, 2025 press conference held by Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer. | Kyle DavidsonU.S. Rep. Haley Stevens of Birmingham now has Gov. Gretchen Whitmer in her corner as she sprints toward the finish line in the Aug. 4 Democratic U.S. Senate primary.
Whitmer’s decision to back Stevens over Dr. Abdul El-Sayed — who she beat in the 2018 gubernatorial primary — adds a powerful establishment Democrat to Stevens’ long list of endorsements. Recent polling has shown that Whitmer’s endorsement still holds sway in the state as her tenure as governor winds down which could move some undecided voters in the contest.
With a little more than a week until the primary, Whitmer on Friday said that Stevens shares her vision for a better Michigan.
“During my eight years as governor, we’ve faced tough challenges. But my north star has always been to get stuff done for Michigan. I know that’s Haley Stevens’ guiding light too, which is why I am so proud to endorse her for U.S. Senate,” Whitmer said in a statement and a video circulated by Stevens’ campaign. “With the great Gary Peters stepping down, Michigan needs an effective fighter to step up and deliver for our state in the U.S. Senate. That’s Haley Stevens.”


Whitmer also invoked key planks of Stevens’ campaign — Stevens’ experience serving as chief of staff on President Barack Obama’s auto rescue and her status as the most effective Michigan Democrat in Congress.
“Haley knows how to get things done for Michigan,” Whitmer said. “She’ll be ready to deliver on day one on manufacturing, lowering costs, and protecting our health care and Social Security. I’m thrilled to be endorsing her for U.S. Senate.”
Stevens said that Whitmer “has been a role model for so many Michiganders, myself included.”
“She’s led our state through some of our hardest challenges — always delivering for our manufacturing economy, our auto industry, and our workers,” Stevens said in a statement. “Governor Whitmer embodies what it means to be ‘that woman from Michigan’ and everything that makes our state so special. She’s authentically Michigan — and I could not be more honored to have her endorsement for U.S. Senate. Let’s go win!”

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: South Dakota universities’ Native American enrollment rises to pre-pandemic level
description: Native American student enrollment at South Dakota public universities has returned to its pre-pandemic level, according to a new report. Black Hills State University in Spearfish had 227 Native American students during the 2025-26 school year, up 49 from 178 the year before. That 28% increase was a major factor in the 6% systemwide growth […]
text:
A sign marks an entrance to Black Hills State University in Spearfish, South Dakota, on Aug. 28, 2024. (Photo by Seth Tupper/South Dakota Searchlight)Native American student enrollment at South Dakota public universities has returned to its pre-pandemic level, according to a new report.
Black Hills State University in Spearfish had 227 Native American students during the 2025-26 school year, up 49 from 178 the year before. That 28% increase was a major factor in the 6% systemwide growth in Native American students compared to the prior year. 
The university’s student body typically has the highest percentage of Native American students of the six institutions in the system. Urla Marcus, director of the Center for American Indian Studies at the university and a member of the Northern Cheyenne Tribe, said the recent numbers are a sign that new programs are working to recruit and retain more students.
Higher enrollment leads to a “ripple effect,” Marcus added.
“They can go back to their communities and make an impact, set that example that more people are attaining these degrees,” Marcus said.
In 2019, the Legislature required the South Dakota Board of Regents, which oversees the public universities, to develop programs aimed at increasing Native American student enrollment and retention. The board submits a report by July 1 each year detailing activities and progress made.


Systemwide, Native American enrollment decreased during the COVID-19 pandemic and stayed lower for several years afterward despite increases at some universities. 
The Native American percentage of the systemwide student body also dipped below 3% for several years but now stands at 3.2%. South Dakota’s overall population is 9% Native American.
Black Hills State’s latest increase pushed systemwide Native American enrollment to 1,155 — nearly reaching the 1,157 recorded in 2017. Native American enrollment increased this past school year by 16 students at South Dakota Mines and 15 at the University of South Dakota, but decreased by five at South Dakota State University, four at Northern State University and two at Dakota State University.
This is the first year since the pandemic that Native American enrollment decreased at South Dakota State. The university has played a significant role in increasing Native American enrollment within the South Dakota public university system in the last decade. President Barry Dunn, a member of the Rosebud Sioux Tribe, launched the Wokini Initiative in 2017 to recruit, retain and support Native American students. Enrollment of Native Americans at the university grew from 259 in 2017 to a peak of 329 in 2024.
Scholarships and financial aid awarded to Native American students across the state have nearly doubled since the 2022 school year, driven largely by a near doubling in Pell Grants and scholarships from institutions and private foundations.
Scholarships and financial aid awarded to Native American public university students in South Dakota have nearly doubled since the 2022 school year. Scholarship and grant aid totaled more than $11 million during the 2025-26 school year. (Courtesy of the Legislative Research Council)
Black Hills State has not yet recovered its own pre-pandemic Native American enrollment numbers, despite the recent gains. Students at the time of the pandemic, Marcus said, were “very cautious,” and many chose not to enroll outside tribal land, with some opting for tribal colleges instead. Those schools offered incentives that the university did not, such as tuition discounts and supplies.
Between 2015 and 2022, the latest data available from the National Center for Education Statistics, enrollment at Oglala Lakota College on the Pine Ridge Reservation fell by 189 students and at Sinte Gleska University in Rosebud by 103. Sisseton Wahpeton College on the Lake Traverse Reservation gained 55 students over the same period.
As the pandemic receded and tribal college incentive programs ended, Marcus said more students have shown interest in enrolling at Black Hills State. Marcus said the university’s location in the Black Hills, an area of historical and spiritual significance for several tribes, is a draw for students. The school has Native faculty and staff working with the center.
“Students see a lot of opportunities for them to grow and be successful,” Marcus said.
‘They saw the potential’: SDSU program boosts Native American success

In addition to more targeted recruiting efforts, Marcus said the center has strengthened or created new programs to support students, including mentorship and scholarship programs.
The Native Scholars program is in its third year. Students in the program regularly engage with advisers and the center’s administration, participate in cultural activities and mentor their peers. Graduates receive a stole and star quilt. The program graduated six students last spring and expects to graduate another 13 next spring.
The peer mentor program grew organically before being formalized in recent years, Marcus said. The center pairs upperclassmen with freshmen and sophomores who share similar fields of study and home regions.
“We have a lot of silent leaders in our center,” Marcus said. “These students have taken some years getting closer and closer to graduation. Younger students look up to them, ask them questions and allow upperclassmen to share what they’ve learned and what they’ve stumbled on.”

title: Environmental groups seek to block oil and gas drilling in Conecuh National Forest
description: Two environmental groups Thursday asked the U.S. Department of the Interior to prevent companies from drilling for oil in the Conecuh National Forest along the southern border of Alabama. The Center for Biological Diversity and the Alabama Ornithological Society alleged that the decision by the Department of the Interior’s Bureau of Land Management to open [[...]
text:
A lake in Conecuh National Forest. Environmental groups have filed an appeal to stop oil and gas drilling in Alabama’s Conecuh National Forest, saying it violates the Endangered Species Act. (U.S. Forest Service)Two environmental groups Thursday asked the U.S. Department of the Interior to prevent companies from drilling for oil in the Conecuh National Forest along the southern border of Alabama.
The Center for Biological Diversity and the Alabama Ornithological Society alleged that the decision by the Department of the Interior’s Bureau of Land Management to open about 2,000 acres of the national forest to oil and gas leases violated the Endangered Species Act and the National Environmental Policy Act.
“It’s appalling that the government is barreling forward to sacrifice the Conecuh National Forest to the oil and gas industry for profit,” said Lindsay Reeves, senior attorney with the Center for Biological Diversity in a statement. “Alabamians hike, camp and swim all across these public lands and it’s disturbing to see the Trump administration trying to turn them into frack fields.”
Messages seeking comment were sent to the U.S. Department of the Interior and the Bureau of Land Management on Friday.
The Bureau of Land Management in 2021 published a study on possible oil and gas activities for the Conecuh National Forest. Those findings were then used by the U.S. Forest Service to publish an Oil and Gas Leasing Availability Analysis in 2025 to determine whether parts of the forest would be closed off for oil and gas leasing.
The U.S. Forest Service in February opted to allow possible oil and gas drilling on all the land within the Conecuh National Forest.
The environmental groups argue that the Bureau of Land Management’s decision violates the Endangered Species Act because the agency did not consult with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service about the potential impact of allowing oil and gas drilling for endangered species living within the forest, relying instead on what it called a “deficient consultation” drawn from a 2004 impact study.
“This biological assessment contains one single, generic paragraph about the impacts that leasing 81,300 acres of national forest would have on nineteen threatened and endangered species – ranging from insects to mammals to mussels and fish – that occupy entirely different habitats on the Conecuh, as well as the federally-designated critical habitat of seven species,” the filing says. “No individual species impacts are discussed.”
Nine endangered species residing within the forest have been added since the 2004 study, according to the filing, including the Escambia map turtle, the Choctaw bean, the fuzzy pigtoe and two freshwater mussel species.
The filing also alleges that the Bureau of Land Management did not consider a host of factors when it only used the findings from the U.S. Forest Service study, such as noise pollution, changes to air quality from vehicle traffic,  water usage and groundwater drawdown.
The filing states that an impact study is needed for the forest.
“On a statewide scale, it supports a disproportionately high percentage of Alabama’s fish and mussels,” the filing said of the Conecuh National Forest. “It has significant national and global importance for biodiversity, particularly of fish, turtles, mollusks, and crayfish.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: In Hazlehurst public schools, students with disabilities lose out on required help
description: Cyntra Catchings, 8, enjoys time with his grandmother Cynthia Catchings, 55 of Hazlehurst, at Chautauqua Park in Crystal Springs, Tuesday, June 2, 2026.
text:
Audio recording is automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story.
HAZLEHURST — Cyn’tra sat in the back of his third-grade reading class at Hazlehurst Elementary. A worksheet lay before him: blank. He seemed confused, looking around at classmates, who were writing responses, and at the teacher. The teacher repeated the questions and provided hints and tips. 
The 8-year-old was easily distracted. He gave up after slowly reading through the questions.
“He required extensive support,” wrote Vonnie Byrd, his assistant principal, after observing Cyn’tra in class. “He appeared confused and looked around the room.”
District contractors, officials and employees performed five similar observations, six behavioral, psychological and skill-based tests, a review of Cyn’tra’s developmental history and an interview with his guardian. They noted details such as his ADHD diagnosis, the type of medicine he takes and why. He also struggles to sound out words and make sense of them on the page. The documents detail how he is generally collegial with other students and behaves well. They also noted concerns such as a time when he threw a tantrum and his behavior escalated to the point where he was taken to the emergency room. 
Cynthia Catchings, 55, of Hazlehurst and her 8-year-old grandson Cyn’tra Catchings at Chautauqua Park in Crystal Springs on Tuesday, June 2, 2026. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
Then Hazlehurst City School District officials dropped Cyn’tra from special education services. They gave no clear reason why.
The department’s decision was “devastating,” said Cynthia Catchings, Cyn’tra’s grandmother and guardian. 
The boy’s academic performance has dropped from B’s and C’s to D’s and F’s, she said.  
Catchings’ situation isn’t hers alone. Other Hazlehurst special education staff, parents of students with disabilities and advocates say the school district has not provided services required under federal law. They have filed more than a dozen pages of complaints with the Mississippi Department of Education and the Hazlehurst district’s central office in the last three years. 
Unresolved complaints and repeated violations of federal law are some reasons why the state might take over the district this school year. The agency also cited the district in December and March for operating a special education department that was unresponsive to parent concerns and lacked documentation of meeting students’ needs.
School board President Paul Rhodes declined to comment in light of pending litigation. 
District leadership has changed since the state education agency cited Hazlehurst schools for violating the rights of students with disabilities. Cloyd Garth, who was superintendent when the district was cited, did not respond to repeated requests for comment in regards to complaints from within the department during his tenure. He left his post on June 8, and school board members would not say whether he resigned or was fired. 
The district is also advertising for a new special education director. District officials did not respond to a request for comment on special education director Andrea Vasser’s employment status.
“I don’t know why they want him to fail,” Catchings said of the district cutting support services for Cyn’tra. “I don’t have any support from the school. They always say no child left behind, but we are both left behind: the parent and the child.”
Outcomes for students like Cyn’tra have reached a new low in Hazlehurst. The graduation rate for students with disabilities dropped from roughly 58% in 2023-24 to less than a third in 2024-25. 
State regulators note that dozens of students with disabilities aren’t getting required support
Under a new mandate from the U.S. Department of Education to provide written monitoring reports to districts, the state agency took additional steps to hold Hazlehurst public schools accountable for violating the civil rights of students with disabilities. In March, state officials notified Garth that investigators found poor oversight and no plans on how to help some students with disabilities.
Hazlehurst City School District board members Paul Rhodes, Oscar Tanner, and Corey Murray voted to hire a new interim superintendent on June 5, 2026 Credit: Leonardo Bevilacqua/Mississippi Today
The sheer volume of problems state investigators found with Hazlehurst schools’ special education department was alarming to Danita Munday, who worked in the state Department of Education’s special education monitoring division before departing.
“I think it would have been quicker to write a report about what they’re actually doing well because apparently it’s nothing,” Munday said.
Students with mild and severe disabilities missed out on services that made learning possible. Nearly a dozen student files were missing a learning plan all together. Without a learning plan, the state education officials can’t verify if those students are receiving required help in the classroom. 
State regulators found that school district officials greenlit learning plans for some special education students without involving parents and without regard to data, considering tests, and with no mention of student behavior.
When parents did request services or appealed department decisions, they sometimes waited for a response past federally mandated deadlines.
A student with failing eyesight and a partially deaf student lacked documented support services. Regulators also could not verify whether students with disabilities at the district alternative school got federally mandated support.
‘You’re just a teacher’ 
Hazlehurst School Superintendent Cloyd Garth, Jr. at the Hazlehurst City School District Administration Building on Monday, April 13, 2026, in Hazlehurst. Garth left the district on June 8, and school board members would not confirm whether he resigned or was fired. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
Three former Hazlehurst special educators, who worked in district classrooms, told Mississippi Today the dysfunction within the district’s department wasn’t limited to parent outreach and records management. They said the department’s leaders were more concerned with documenting services for students than offering them.
One former instructor said Vasser withheld full reports that analyze student eligibility for special education services. Without that information, it was more difficult to craft learning plans that fully accommodated the student’s disability. The instructor asked not to be named out of fear of retaliation from district leadership,
The educator said Garth threatened to fire them after they challenged the legality of a separate learning plan and sought guidance from the state Education Department. 
The learning plan was to have an elementary school student with a significant cognitive disability complete a packet of classwork each week at home alone in lieu of in-person instruction. The educator said they reminded Vasser the child’s family did not speak English
The educator also said Garth accused them of breaking the chain of command by calling the state Education Department.
“I’m not mad at (Vasser), but her rights end where mine begin. I nor my students will be mishandled,” the educator wrote in an April 2023 email to Vasser and Garth, which an educator gave Mississippi Today. “My concern is the response to my advocating for my students.”
Gardner Wooten left the Hazlehurst special education department in 2023. He said district leadership forced him to cancel meetings with parents of students with disabilities so he could substitute teach and proctor tests.
“Those students really got the short end of the stick,” he said. “I complained about it, too. They didn’t care. Their attitude there is that you’re just a teacher.”
‘This is not just a paperwork problem’
Two positions for special education teachers in Hazlehurst schools have not been filled since 2023.
Fewer staffers means existing special education teachers and officials have to manage larger caseloads. 
Cyn’tra Catchings, 8, enjoys time with his grandmother Cynthia Catchings, 55, of Hazlehurst, at Chautauqua Park in Crystal Springs on Tuesday, June 2, 2026. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
Catchings, Cyn’tra’s grandmother, said she knows the department is short staffed, but ending  special education services for her grandson will limit his future opportunities. She worries he will continue to fall behind.
Cyn’tra said he found it harder to focus after January, when he lost access to special services. The classroom sounded louder and the noises were distracting without the aid of a special education teacher to provide clear guidance for class assignments. He misses the teacher who would take him to a separate, quieter room to go over the classroom work.
“When I didn’t have her around, it would be way harder to read,” he said. “When we follow along with the story, I can read back to her.”
Teachers would better understand his behavior and be able to manage it without calling Catchings to intervene throughout the day, Catchings told Mississippi Today.
Cynthia Catchings, 55 of Hazlehurst and her 8-year-old grandson Cyn’tra Catchings at Chautauqua Park in Crystal Springs on Tuesday, June 2, 2026. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
Without an individualized education plan, known as an IEP, teachers don’t know Cyn’tra needs questions read aloud and time to sound out words, Catchings said. His next teachers won’t know that he needs built-in breaks between tasks, a visual aid and extra time on tests.
Catchings has taken Cyn’tra to a psychiatrist who can retest Cyn’tra for cognitive and psychiatric needs and recommend special education services for him. A separate psychiatrist had been waiting on Vasser to present the contract for his testing services to the Hazlehurst school board for reimbursement approval, according to Catchings.
It’s been six months.
“This is not just a paperwork problem,” said Munday, the former bureau director for special education policy “This is about a district using flawed processes to push a child out of special education, with no soft place to land.”

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: A proposed moratorium on data centers hits resistance in Mass. Senate
description: The back-and-forth nature of data center policy in Massachusetts raises the question: Do Bay State policymakers want to draw in these facilities, which can provide some jobs and property tax benefits, or not?
text:
TOP SENATE DEMOCRATS are openly wary of the risks posed by artificial intelligence — but they’re not yet willing to block the facilities that power it from calling Massachusetts home. 
Sen. Michael Moore, a Democrat representing areas in and around Worcester, filed an amendment that would impose a one-year moratorium on new data centers in the state to a sprawling economic development package the chamber passed late Thursday night. 
Thirteen senators in total signed on to the measure — a sizable chunk of the 40-member body. And Moore told CommonWealth Beacon that he was “working the room,” believing that he had even broader support. 
Though both the House and Gov. Maura Healey would have had to approve the provision for it to become law, Senate passage of the moratorium would have ushered in intense discussion over the potential for a major potential policy shift on what has quickly become a hot-button issue around the country.  
But the proposal ended in a whimper, crashing out as just one of nearly 600 amendments the chamber considered as part of the larger bill. 
Moore said that Senate leaders, including Ways and Means chair Michael Rodrigues and Sen. Barry Finegold, who co-chairs the joint economic development committee, told him that they did not support a moratorium.  
It would be the second time within a month that Moore’s data center moratorium pitch has been shot down after a proposed amendment to the energy bill the Senate passed last month also failed to advance. 
Moore said that he informed leadership he was planning to request a roll call vote to force members to take a position and see if it would pass — but was told by Rodrigues and Finegold that even if it did succeed, Senate leaders would see that it not make it through a conference committee in which the House and Senate reconcile differences between their two economic development bills.
So in the end, he withdrew his amendment, in addition to a second that would have required data centers be powered with 100 percent renewable energy and ensure that residential ratepayers aren’t burdened with extra costs associated with the increased electricity demand. 
“There’s a disagreement,” Moore said in an interview. “I think there’s a need for it. It’s a missed opportunity.” 
A spokesperson for Rodrigues didn’t immediately return a request for comment, and a spokesperson for Senate President Karen Spilka referred CommonWealth Beacon to Finegold.
Finegold didn’t speak directly to questions about data centers, Moore’s amendments, and Moore’s characterization of events, instead saying in a statement that “there were many good economic development policy proposals, but we could not consider them all in this one bill.” 
To be a leader on AI the US needs data centers to house massive networks of data — but a backlash has taken root over the effect the facilities’ heavy energy and water consumption will have on the communities in which they locate. 
Elected officials nationwide across the political spectrum have been wrestling with the shifting politics around data centers. Some progressive Democrats in Congress have pushed for a national moratorium, and President Trump has called for shielding ratepayers from any costs associated with increased power demand. And a new poll finds that Americans have increasingly soured on their support for the facilities.  
Those tensions have ensnared Beacon Hill, where Massachusetts Democrats are now trying to figure out where to land on the issue.  
Healey, a vocal proponent of AI and the tech sector, signed a data center tax credit into law in 2024. After her administration took 18 months to finalize the tax break, Healey then paused it less than two months after it took effect and released a framework calling on data center developers to “bring your own clean energy.” She also previously said she doesn’t back a moratorium. 
Lowell, home to a data center, enacted the state’s first municipal moratorium earlier this year. Other communities like Westfield and Holyoke have since followed. Lowell residents are now also suing the state for issuing the air permits for the facility there. 
The back-and-forth nature of data center policy in Massachusetts raises the question: Do Bay State policymakers want to draw in these facilities, which can provide some jobs and property tax benefits, or not? 
“Massachusetts is a great case study because while we have not seen those large-scale developments, the policies themselves show that yo-yoing around this issue,” said Dan Dolan, president of the New England Power Generators Association. “The tax credits for data centers were barely live before there were real active discussions, and then ultimately the pause on the tax credits put in place by the Healey administration. That, in and of itself, shows the perception of an economic development engine and opportunity to power a high-tech industry that the Commonwealth prides itself on, countered with the real physics of the electric grid and the public outcry on the impacts of data centers writ large.” 
Moore said that he was told by Senate leaders that there isn’t a strong need for a moratorium because Massachusetts hasn’t yet emerged as a hub for data centers like other states. Plus, the issue was at least partially addressed in the energy bill the chamber passed earlier this month, which included a requirement that data centers meet certain clean energy, water conservation, and labor requirements to qualify for tax credits.  
But for Moore, the Senate leadership’s argument that data centers will not come to Massachusetts while tax credits to lure them here are on the books — albeit in flux after Healey paused them — is “a contradiction.” 
Finegold, who also led the economic development committee when the data center tax credit was passed two years ago, said in an interview earlier this month that he’s comfortable with Healey’s decision to pause the tax breaks, but that the state needs to remain an attractive place for businesses to start and grow.
“We have to look at areas that we can compete on,” he said. “We can no longer, as a state, just sit back and say because we’re Massachusetts, companies are going to come here. No, we have to compete.”
The fragility of the data center issue for Massachusetts Democrats was scrambled further by a historic crackdown taken in a bordering state: New York Gov. Kathy Hochul’s recent move to enact the country’s first statewide moratorium. Her action, taken by executive order, also seeks legislation to repeal state tax breaks for data centers.
That step is contrasted by Maine Gov. Janet Mills’ move to veto a data center moratorium passed by legislators in her state earlier this year. 
In Massachusetts, Chris Anderson, president of the state’s High Technology Council, a coalition of tech executives, sounded the alarm over proposals like Moore’s that he said would run counter to broader efforts to make the state’s economy more competitive and drive down costs in an affordability crisis.  
“While we share the goal of ensuring responsible energy and water use, imposing mandates that make it more difficult or costly to develop data centers here would simply drive investment, jobs, and innovation to competing states,” he said in a statement. “The Senate’s decision to reject this amendment recognizes that our competitiveness depends on attracting — not discouraging — the infrastructure that powers the next generation of artificial intelligence, scientific research, and technology-driven economic growth.” 
Don’t expect the issue to go away, though, as quietly as Moore’s amendments did. 
He vowed to “watch for other vehicles that come up between now and the end of the session” to gain traction on his moratorium push.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: After delays, CT finalizes $53M in federal disaster relief for farmers
description: Eligible CT farmers will soon get to apply for a portion of disaster relief from a federal grant for smaller farming states.
text:
More than a year and a half after Congress created a federal grant for smaller farming states, Connecticut finalized its $53 million allotment — and eligible farmers will soon get to apply for a portion of that disaster relief.
The state and federal agriculture agencies worked through the final steps in early July of approving the program design and executing a contract that unlocks Connecticut’s funding. The Connecticut Department of Agriculture is now working to get the application portal up and running by early fall.
Federal lawmakers, led by U.S. Rep. Rosa DeLauro, enacted the $220 million Farm Recovery and Support Block Grant program included in a government funding deal in December 2024. But its implementation hit a number of snags and delays: a clash over the terms of the program and a record-long government shutdown that interrupted negotiations.
Now, the years-long effort to get recovery funds into the hands of farmers who experienced damages caused by disasters and extreme weather events in 2023 and 2024 is nearing the finish line. Connecticut Commissioner of Agriculture Bryan Hurlburt said his agency is working with contractors to go “full speed ahead” on developing the application portal and providing webinars and demos for farmers to learn how the program will work.

Commissioner of Agriculture Bryan Hurlburt at a press conference at Cecarelli’s Harrison Hill Farm in Northford on July 24, 2026.  Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror

Once the portal is ready, he expects the initial application period to open for four weeks with the state agency processing those on a rolling basis. Hurlburt said it’s a “pretty low threshold to qualify.” Farmers are eligible if they earn $1,000 in farm revenue for given years, experienced a minimum loss of $500 in disaster-related losses in 2023, 2024 or both. Hurlburt expects people to start receiving payments about six to eight weeks after they apply.
The first application period is expected to open in September, with another one for later in the fall.
Farmers and lawmakers attended a press conference at Cecarelli’s Harrison Hill Farm in Northford on Friday about the news of the grant and the next steps. Along with a number of local farmers, the event was attended by DeLauro, Hurlburt, Gov. Ned Lamont, Lt. Gov. Susan Bysiewicz, U.S. Rep. John Larson, U.S. Rep. Joe Courtney and U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal.
It was organized by William Dellacamera, who helped lead the charge to get federal funding to help smaller farmers. A hail storm in August 2024 destroyed his crops in 13 minutes.
A month after the storm, Dellacamera traveled to Washington, D.C., on his tractor to push for help from the federal government. As months went by with little developments and ongoing negotiations, he came back to the nation’s capital to ask about the status of the farm block grant. He met with U.S. Agriculture Sec. Brooke Rollins last spring and made his plea for the quick rollout of the money for small and midsize farmers.
Dellacamera made repeated trips to D.C. to advocate for the implementation of the $220 million block grant to be divided between all states in New England and Hawaii and Alaska. Connecticut was awarded $53 million of that last August, but it has not been able to start the process of doling out that money until the state and federal agriculture agencies worked out an agreement and executed a contract.
“It was certainly not the path that we expected, not the path that we were told to expect in the beginning,” Hurlburt said in an interview, noting that the program they recently submitted for approval “is not significantly different that we submitted for review last July” to the U.S. Department of Agriculture.
Connecticut famers have been awaiting access to such relief after experiencing damages caused by disasters and extreme weather events in 2023 and 2024. In 2023, farmers were badly hit after flooding along the Connecticut River. A year later, Connecticut saw flash floods in the western part of the state and a hail storm in the central part — the same one that took out Dellacamera’s crops.

Kaitlyn Kimball, co-owner of Sunset Farm in Naugatuck and Milford, at a press conference at Cecarelli’s Harrison Hill Farm in Northford on July 24, 2026.  Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror

Another farmer at Friday’s event, Kaitlyn Kimball of Sunset Farm, got hit by the flooding in August 2024. Her 3-acre field in Naugatuck was under a foot of water for almost a week, killing all of the tomatoes. Kimball told The Connecticut Mirror last year that she lost years of compost and materials to improve the soil.
The federal program was geared toward smaller farming states that grow more specialty crops and don’t typically benefit from federal aid in the same ways as larger commodity producers.
“We all need it, that’s for sure,” Dellacamera said in an interview ahead of Friday’s event. “Now, hopefully, within a few months, we all get some real money we need.”
As a constituent of DeLauro’s, Dellacamera worked with the congresswoman on the creation of this fund and throughout the process of getting it up and running. DeLauro, who serves as the ranking member on the House Appropriations Committee, called the block grant program a “success story” and credited Dellacamera’s persistence on the issue when the timeline of the funding looked murky.

Rep. Rosa DeLauro, D-3rd District, at a press conference in Northford on July 24, 2026. DeLauro is a major supporter of the farm block grants for disaster relief.   Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror

“From the outset, I think there was a sense that, finally, we were looking at standing up a program that was specific to specialty crop farmers. And that’s incredible, because … nothing trickles down for them, and so this was really one of the first efforts to be able to do that,” DeLauro said in an interview from the Capitol ahead of the event.
“[Farmers] have been patient with the ups and the downs,” DeLauro said. “I wish it didn’t have to take a year and a half or over, but you’d never give up in that effort.”
The Farm Recovery and Support Block Grant program hit a number of speed bumps since Congress enacted it in late 2024.
Following Dellacamera’s visit to D.C. in the spring of 2025 and DeLauro’s push at the hearings, disagreements emerged over the rollout of the disaster aid block grant.

William Dellacamera at a press conference at Cecarelli’s Harrison Hill Farm in Northford on July 24, 2026.  Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror

USDA gave states two options: they could run their own crop loss program by using the block grant tailored for them, but they wouldn’t get access to larger supplemental disaster aid, or they could go with the latter, run by the federal agency, but face limits on what gets covered by the block grant. Connecticut ultimately decided to go with the former, developing a state-run program using the federal block grant. That meant the state wouldn’t get access to the $21 billion Supplemental Disaster Relief Program.
That led to a clash among DeLauro and other congressional Democrats who argued that wasn’t what they intended when they wrote the language for the block grant. But now, the New Haven congresswoman believes it’s the “best outcome” for Connecticut.
Hurlburt echoed that assessment. Based on the structure of the Supplemental Disaster Relief Program, he said, Connecticut farmers will be able to get more relief from the state’s crop loss program and won’t be on the hook — like they would for the federal program — to purchase one of the crop insurance tools for at least two years to qualify.
Discussions between the Connecticut Department of Agriculture and the U.S. Department of Agriculture also stalled during the government shutdown last year. Once it reopened in mid-November, talks picked up to hammer out the final details.
At the end of 2025, Connecticut officials gave a loose timeline of wrapping up negotiations and finalizing the state’s contract before the 2026 planting season. And at a mid-April hearing before Congress, Rollins told DeLauro that the long-awaited federal block grant was “at the finish line for Connecticut.” 
Payments will be determined by identifying a farmer’s best revenue year between 2020 and 2025. They will take that number and subtract the disaster losses from 2023, 2024 or both years. A farmer can expect to get 95% of that difference up to $1 million as the maximum award. Any past crop insurance payments will be deducted.
“A bunch of us who need this money, we don’t even know how we’re surviving now,” Dellacamera said. “It’s coming in the bank account and going right back out. It’s going to pay bills.”
Dellacamera said there are larger problems and barriers for smaller farmers, such as the structure of crop insurance that can help farmers weather disaster events. Hurlburt agreed that crop insurance needs to be reformed.
If the application portal is not ready by the anticipated timeline, Dellacamera said, “There will be a lot of angry people.”
He recalled a few farmers telling him that advocating for the funding won’t be a solo mission: “This time you’re not going to have to worry about doing it alone.”

title: Delaware Whiskey Festival brings premium pours, cocktail contest to Wilmington
description: Saturday’s tasting event will feature 50 whiskey selections, VIP access and support for scholarships benefiting local students WILMINGTON — Whiskey enthusiasts will have an opportunity to sample bourbons, ryes, single malts and international selections Saturday as the Delaware Whiskey Festival returns to Wilmington. text:
Saturday’s tasting event will feature 50 whiskey selections, VIP access and support for scholarships benefiting local students
WILMINGTON — Whiskey enthusiasts will have an opportunity to sample bourbons, ryes, single malts and international selections Saturday as the Delaware Whiskey Festival returns to Wilmington.
The second annual festival will be held from 6 to 9 p.m. July 25 at The Venue, 2409 Lancaster Ave. A limited VIP session begins at 5 p.m., giving ticket holders early access to the event and its specialty pours.
Organizers say the festival will feature 50 curated whiskey expressions, ranging from bold American bourbons and ryes to refined single malts and internationally produced whiskeys. The event is designed for experienced collectors as well as people who are beginning to explore the differences among whiskey styles.
General admission includes access to the whiskey tastings, a commemorative tasting glass, vendor experiences and a live whiskey cocktail competition.
During the competition, local bartenders will prepare original cocktails using featured whiskeys. Guests will be able to watch as the bartenders combine traditional techniques with new flavors and presentations.
VIP admission includes entry from 5 to 6 p.m., before the general-admission session begins. VIP guests receive first access to limited and specialty pours, a smaller tasting environment and a commemorative glass, along with the benefits included with general admission.
Organizers said the inaugural festival sold out, and VIP tickets are intentionally limited.
The evening also has a charitable purpose. A portion of the festival’s proceeds will benefit Overflow Season Inc., a nonprofit organization that provides scholarships to local high school seniors.
The Delaware Tourism Office lists general admission beginning at $36.42, although prices and ticket availability may change as the event approaches.
The festival is open only to guests 21 and older. Organizers recommend elevated casual attire and encourage guests to arrange safe transportation after the tasting.
To Go Box

What: 2026 Delaware Whiskey Festival
When: General admission, 6 to 9 p.m. Saturday, July 25; VIP admission begins at 5 p.m.
Where: The Venue, 2409 Lancaster Ave., Wilmington
Highlights: Tastings of 50 whiskey selections, live cocktail competition, specialty vendors, commemorative tasting glass and limited VIP pours
Admission: General admission begins at approximately $36.42; VIP and other ticket prices vary
Age requirement: 21 and older
Tickets and information: Available through the Delaware Whiskey Festival’s Eventbrite page

title: New dashboard tracks Kansas Affordable Care Act enrollment by legislative district, county
description: TOPEKA — A new dashboard tracks the number of Kansans enrolled in health insurance through the Affordable Care Act marketplace, offering data for legislators and others to understand the effects of policy changes, a health organization said. The Kansas Health Institute designed the dashboard to create an easy way for people to access data and […]
text:
A new dashboard created by Kansas Health Institute shows enrollment in the Affordable Care Act marketplace health insurance by county and by legislative district. (Photo by Morgan Chilson/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — A new dashboard tracks the number of Kansans enrolled in health insurance through the Affordable Care Act marketplace, offering data for legislators and others to understand the effects of policy changes, a health organization said.
The Kansas Health Institute designed the dashboard to create an easy way for people to access data and see how federal and state changes to marketplace health insurance affects enrollment, said analyst Kaci Cink. 
The organization already had been maintaining maps to track ACA enrollment, but KHI wanted to break the data down not just to the county level but to legislative districts levels, as well, she said
“We’ve been doing maps for the marketplace for a long time, and we wanted to explore creating something that was a little bit more interactive and was also able to get down to legislative districts, the community level, your neighborhood essentially,” Cink said. 
The dashboard shows the percentage of people in a county, state Senate or House legislative district or federal congressional district enrolled in the ACA. By county, Hodgeman County has the highest percentage of enrollees with 21%, or 340 people, and Riley County has the lowest percentage at 3.3%, or 2,373 people.
Kansas’ 4th Congressional District, which is served by Republican Rep. Ron Estes, has the highest enrollment among federal districts at 7.2%, or 53,958 people. The 1st District, represented by Republican Rep. Tracey Mann, is 5.5%, or 40,255 people.
The dashboard also compares the state by peer counties, showing the differences in population density between rural and urban counties through categories defined by the Kansas Department of Health and Environment, Cink said.
Linda Sheppard, KHI senior analyst and strategy team leader, said the organization shared the dashboard information with legislators so they know the number of people in their districts affected by ACA.
The One Big Beautiful Bill Act eliminated premium help that many people were receiving to enroll on the ACA marketplace. Area health experts said 20% of Kansans enrolled in 2025 didn’t re-enroll in 2026.
Sheppard said the state is seeing a further decrease in ACA enrollment as people are not paying their premiums, even though they were enrolled for 2026.
That information isn’t included on the dashboard, because the federal government doesn’t update enrollment data until the next open enrollment, for 2027.
“I think the expectation is that maybe for 2027 we’ll see a more significant drop in that initial open enrollment period because maybe some of those people that figured out that they couldn’t afford it anymore just won’t enroll,” Sheppard said.

title: Burgum, Gordon discuss Western values, agriculture, Colorado River Basin water at Cheyenne Frontier Days
description:
Governor, Interior secretary and Acting U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche join parade. Cheyenne Frontier Days declares the “Day of the American West” for America’s 250th anniversary. 
The post Burgum, Gordon discuss Western values, agriculture, Colorado River Basin water at Cheyenne Frontier Days appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
CHEYENNE—Gov. Mark Gordon welcomed members of President Donald Trump’s Cabinet to Cheyenne Frontier Days on Thursday as they took part in the Western-themed parade through downtown.
Gordon, Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum and Acting U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche all rode on horseback through the parade.

Acting U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche rides in the parade Thursday during the 130th anniversary of Cheyenne Frontier Days. (Christina Spindler/Wyoming Tribune Eagle)

Cheyenne Frontier Days declared Thursday the “Day of the American West” in coordination with a formal order Burgum issued last August to honor and celebrate America’s 250th anniversary. The day is meant to highlight the important tradition and cultural history of the West, specifically rodeo, Native American dance and culture and Western art.
Both Gordon and Burgum spent time recognizing and appreciating Western values. Burgum stressed the “values that exist in the West around hard work, around self-reliance, around living off the land, and the stewardship of that land for multiple generations.”
Gordon and Burgum spoke of other issues, as well, such as mineral rights, water rights and energy development during a media event at the Cheyenne Frontier Days Old West Museum. Gordon’s opening remarks highlighted the importance of an open line of communication between the Department of Interior and Wyoming due to the responsibility the federal government has related to the state’s mineral rights, land and water distribution.
Burgum credited his department and the Trump administration’s focus on meeting people where they are.
“Meet with these working families and get ideas about how we can make life easier for them and how we can work better to protect the land and the wildlife,” Burgam said when asked why it is important to have an understanding of these issues and not make arbitrary decisions that impact people’s lives from an office in Washington.
Burgum’s own experience as governor of North Dakota shaped his current philosophy. 
“You can’t make a decision unless you talk to the people, the communities, the companies, the people that are working on that,” he said.
This outlook has led to him viewing the people who have grazing leases and are building energy infrastructure as “our customers. They’re someone that we serve. And we have got to do everything to help them.”
Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum serves as the grand marshal of the Cheyenne Frontier Days parade Thursday in downtown Cheyenne. (Christina Spindler/Wyoming Tribune Eagle)
Both Burgum and Gordon spoke about how federal and state governments are working in tandem to help Wyoming ranchers and farmers. First, they must ensure they have the support they need and are not hamstrung by high-priced grazing leases, Burgum said. Gordon added that they also need to lower the price of beef to allow them to grow their herds.
Gordon also touched on his Cowboy State Agriculture Initiative, which helps ensure “families are able to transfer (their ranches) from one generation to the next.”
Burgum addressed concerns surrounding the potential restrictions and issues Wyoming and other states face with the Colorado River Basin. As Wyoming is one of seven states involved in the Bureau of Reclamation water agreement, due to the current drought, ranchers and agriculture could suffer. All seven states have convened in an attempt to solve the problem, but no consensus has been reached, causing the federal government to step in.
Burgum was emphatic that all seven states must work with one another and the federal government and not begin suing one another.
If they do, that could lead to “a judge that has not spent a lifetime in hydrology, has not spent the last 18 months in negotiation, and has not listened to user groups across seven states, having to make a decision on how you operate, meaning how much water is released and where it goes.” 
The better alternative is finding consensus among all seven states, he said, acknowledging, “If we come up with a plan that nobody likes, we probably have the right plan.”
This water shortage has only been compounded by the growing population in the region.
“We have one-fourth of the water and four times the people,” Burgum said of the states in the Colorado River Basin.
All of the states impacted have been working on potential solutions because “there’s an idea that everybody wants their appropriated share,” but “the water just isn’t there,” Burgum said. 
If no consensus can be reached, the buck will stop with the “Department of Interior and the Secretary, specifically, to step in as the water master and release a plan.”
But the goal of “moving toward something that’s optimal for all the seven states” remains, he said.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Q&A: Richard Nelson, Louisiana Community and Technical College System president
description: The leader of the Louisiana Community and Technical College System said he plans to entice more young Louisianians to pursue workforce training by opening a charter school that would allow high school students to attain credentials alongside their diploma.  LCTCS President Richard Nelson took office in January after previously working as Louisiana’s revenue[...]
text:
Richard Nelson, president of the Louisiana Community and Technical College System, says plans are in the works to open a charter school that will allow high school students to gain workforce skills while completing their high school diploma. (Photo by Henrietta Wildsmith for the Louisiana Illuminator)The leader of the Louisiana Community and Technical College System said he plans to entice more young Louisianians to pursue workforce training by opening a charter school that would allow high school students to attain credentials alongside their diploma. 
LCTCS President Richard Nelson took office in January after previously working as Louisiana’s revenue secretary and a state representative. A key ally of Gov. Jeff Landry, Nelson highlighted their collaborative work on workforce development in a wide-ranging interview this week. 
The conversation has been edited for length and clarity. 
Piper Hutchinson: After being in the job for about six months and settling in, what are your priorities for the system moving forward? 
Richard Nelson: About 70% of the jobs in Louisiana do not require a four-year degree. My perfect world would be we get the 70% of the state that needs to be here, we get them all a job when they walk out the door. Then we’ll have solved all of Louisiana’s problems, frankly. That’s the perfect world. If we get anywhere near that, then we’re doing a good job.
We need to make sure that people, when they’re coming into our institutions, know where those jobs are and that they’re going to get the return for the time and money they put into it. And then I think on the other side — the connections to the employers — I think we need to focus on apprenticeships and paid internships and those kind of things with students, so that they have that kind of real world experience when they walk out the door
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Hutchinson: A big chunk of your students are non-traditional students who are 26 and older. They also come with more challenges than some of the younger students. They often have kids. They’re working a job. How do you overcome those challenges and get them an education?
Nelson: There’s pretty much three significant barriers, right? So one is financial, just out the door. Like, it costs money. If they’re not 18 with no responsibilities and living with their mom and dad, you know financial concerns are important. We’ve done some stuff with the legislature last year. We expanded the MJ Foster [Promise] Program, we basically doubled the funding for that program to help them get those high-value credentials. We expanded Tops Tech, too, so that should help a little bit in giving a little bit more flexibility to the people that are able to come to our institutions. 
The other two gaps that we have are childcare and transportation.We have some childcare facilities on site at some of our institutions. We’re looking at how we can expand those and partner with operators so that they can come in and run those facilities, which will give us some double benefit, too. 
Transportation is another issue. Depending on where you are, there may not be reliable public transportation. One of the things we’re looking at specifically is expanding a program to help people get their driver’s license. You know, if you don’t have a driver’s license in the state, it’s very difficult to get around. 
Hutchinson: You have recently announced the system intends to open a charter school to get those younger students into the system. What is your plan for that? 
Nelson: We do a lot of dual enrollment with either the local high school or with other charter school kids, but we’d like to make that available to everybody across the state. It’s going to focus mainly on 10th grade, 11th grade, 12th grade, those older kids that maybe want to get an associate’s degree, maybe they want to go get technical training. They’ll be able to graduate with their high school degree as well as you know some either an associate’s degree or some advanced technical skills. 
We’re trying to … make it available to everyone in the state that wants it. We have about 7,500 students right now that have dropped out of school but would be eligible had they remained in school. This is kind of an alternative experience for them to say, maybe you know going 45 hours a week to high school wasn’t the thing for you for whatever reason. 
Hutchinson: Over the past few years, the legislature has expressed an interest in increasing opportunities for incarcerated and formerly incarcerated people to get some sort of community or technical education. What programs are in place for those students?
Nelson: Louisiana has what is pretty much the highest incarcerated population in the country, if not the world. Reducing the recidivism rates in that population would be better for all of us, right? We have partnerships that may offer welding or some other kind of technical training, HVAC. 
We’re actually looking to significantly increase that partnership. If you ask me, the best solution would be that everyone if someone gets incarcerated, they walk out the door and they have at least their high school diploma equivalency, or they have some kind of technical training, whether it’s a [commercial driver’s license] or HVAC or welding or electrical or whatever else they can do.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Ayotte chooses former Manchester police chief as acting child advocate
description: Gov. Kelly Ayotte said Friday she would nominate former Manchester Police Chief Allen Aldenberg to be the state’s acting child advocate, a role he would fill temporarily until the state can find a permanent person. The announcement came on Cassandra Sanchez’s final day in the role. Sanchez, who was appointed by Gov. Chris Sununu in […]
text:
Allen Aldenberg (left) formerly served as chief of police in Manchester. At right is then-Assistant Chief Peter Marr, who is now the chief. (Photo by Andrew Sylvia/Manchester Ink Link)Gov. Kelly Ayotte said Friday she would nominate former Manchester Police Chief Allen Aldenberg to be the state’s acting child advocate, a role he would fill temporarily until the state can find a permanent person.
The announcement came on Cassandra Sanchez’s final day in the role. Sanchez, who was appointed by Gov. Chris Sununu in 2022, is leaving after Ayotte declined in January to nominate her to a new term. 
Aldenberg will need Executive Council approval to take the role; the body’s next meeting is July 29. If confirmed, he would serve for up to 90 days, according to the governor’s office. 
Allen Aldenberg has served in the National Guard for 34 years. (New Hampshire National Guard photo)
Aldenberg, who served as police chief for the Queen City from 2020 to 2025 and is currently a brigadier general in the New Hampshire National Guard, would bring an unusual law enforcement background to the role. 
Established by lawmakers in 2018, the Office of the Child Advocate is an independent watchdog agency originally charged with overseeing the Division for Children, Youth, and Families after a string of deaths of children under that agency’s care. In 2020, lawmakers expanded its mandate to investigate child welfare concerns over all state departments and agencies as well as contractors. 
New Hampshire’s first child advocate, Moira O’Neill, had previously served as the assistant child advocate in Connecticut. Sanchez, the second person in the role, had previously worked in the Massachusetts Department of Children and Families. 
Aldenberg graduated from the FBI National Academy and earned a master’s in strategic studies from the U.S. Army War College and a master’s in justice administration from Norwich University, according to the governor’s office. He has served in the National Guard for 34 years, previously served as chief military and veterans services officer at Easterseals New Hampshire, has worked on a police department crisis intervention team, and served on the board of the Mental Health Center of Greater Manchester.
In her announcement, Ayotte called him “an outstanding public servant.” 
“As chief in Manchester, Al saw firsthand what happens when systems fail to protect children, and he will be a steadfast leader for the Office of the Child Advocate during this period of transition.” 
Ayotte said she would continue to search for a permanent director.
The governor’s choice to appoint Aldenberg contradicts previous assumptions that Sanchez’s deputy, Jason Taylor, would take the interim role. In an interview with the Bulletin this month, Sanchez said she assumed Taylor would be picked, and in his own email to the Bulletin this week, Taylor said: “I don’t think that I have any choice.”
Leadership in the office has been tumultuous in recent months. When Ayotte first announced in January she would not reappoint Sanchez, she did not give a direct reason, calling it a standard administrative change. Sanchez later told the Bulletin she believed she was being replaced due to her opposition to Republican legislation that would target transgender children and athletes; Ayotte has denied that claim.
In March, Ayotte’s first pick to succeed Sanchez, Diana Fenton, withdrew her nomination after a contentious public hearing and opposition from some on the Executive Council. 
In his email to the Bulletin Tuesday, Taylor expressed frustration with the changes and with what he said was a lack of transparency by the governor’s office. 
“We’re very disappointed by the lack of professional courtesy shown to our team, and we plan to take steps to address this,” he wrote. “The public is who we serve, and we will continue to do so, despite the frustrations we have regarding the forced changes in leadership for our office.”
Bulletin reporter William Skipworth contributed to this story.

name: Delaware
title: Crystal Spa arrests expose Delaware’s hidden human trafficking problem
description: Three adult women were identified as trafficking victims following a Foulk Road raid; advocates warn that exploitation also targets Delaware children online WILMINGTON — The arrest of a massage business operator and two alleged customers in Brandywine Hundred is drawing attention to a crime that law enforcement officials and advocates say frequently remains[...]
text:
Three adult women were identified as trafficking victims following a Foulk Road raid; advocates warn that exploitation also targets Delaware children online
WILMINGTON — The arrest of a massage business operator and two alleged customers in Brandywine Hundred is drawing attention to a crime that law enforcement officials and advocates say frequently remains hidden in plain sight.
New Castle County police announced Friday that 71-year-old Nan Son Yim of Flushing, New York, was arrested following a human trafficking investigation at Crystal Spa in the 1700 block of Foulk Road.
Detectives with the New Castle County Division of Police Drug and Human Trafficking Investigations Team began investigating suspected trafficking and illicit activity at the business in May, police said.
Officers executed a search warrant July 15 and encountered three women, ages 47, 54 and 56, whom investigators identified as victims of human trafficking. Police allege the women were forced to work 12-hour shifts, seven days a week, without proper compensation.
Detectives seized $15,975 in cash, bulk quantities of condoms and other items they said were consistent with the operation of an illicit massage business.
Yim was charged with three felony counts of human trafficking for forced labor, two felony counts of human trafficking for sexual servitude, one felony count of second-degree promoting prostitution and one felony count of second-degree conspiracy.
She was arraigned in Justice of the Peace Court 11 and committed to the Delores J. Baylor Women’s Correctional Institution after failing to post $108,000 cash bail.
The charges are allegations. Yim is presumed innocent unless proven guilty.
Two men found inside the business were also arrested.
Police identified them as 78-year-old Thomas Hofer of West Chester, Pennsylvania, and 45-year-old Jesse Wasmer of Kingsville, Maryland. Each was charged with one misdemeanor count of attempting to commit patronizing a prostitute and released on his own recognizance.
Owner sought by police
Investigators identified the owner of Crystal Spa as 54-year-old Meilan Quan.
Police later searched Quan’s residence on Mallard Circle in Claymont and said they found additional evidence connecting her to the operation of the business.
Quan remained wanted Friday and is believed to have connections in Delaware and the Flushing, New York, area.
Police said Quan will face three felony counts of human trafficking for forced labor, two felony counts of human trafficking for sexual servitude, one felony count of second-degree promoting prostitution and one felony count of second-degree conspiracy if she is located.
All three women identified as victims were referred to the New Castle County Police Victim Services Unit for support and assistance.
The Delaware Division of Professional Regulation, Delaware Department of Justice, Delaware Anti-Trafficking Action Council and Homeland Security Investigations assisted with the investigation.
A crime hidden in plain sight
Human trafficking does not necessarily involve kidnapping or transporting someone across state or national borders.
Trafficking occurs when a person is exploited through force, fraud or coercion for labor or commercial sex. Victims may be controlled through threats, withheld wages, debt, isolation, confiscated identification documents, language barriers or fear of law enforcement.
The crime can occur inside homes, hotels, restaurants, agricultural operations, construction businesses and massage establishments without being immediately visible to customers or neighboring businesses.
“Human trafficking is a hidden crime,” New Castle County Police Chief Col. James J. Leonard III said. “The New Castle County Division of Police remains committed to holding accountable those who exploit others while ensuring victims receive the support, resources and care they deserve.”
Delaware Attorney General Kathy Jennings said businesses allegedly supported by trafficking should not be viewed as harmless or victimless.
“The crimes committed by these illicit massage establishments are not victimless,” Jennings said. “They depend on exploiting a steady stream of trafficked individuals to keep their doors open, create a dangerous environment for all involved and act as a nuisance to the surrounding community.”
Advocates warn about risks to children
Although the three victims identified at Crystal Spa were adults, trafficking advocates warn that children and teenagers are also targeted in Delaware.
“Cases like this are deeply disturbing, but they are not rare,” said Marcia Ferranto, president of the Delaware Coalition for Human Trafficking Survivors, a statewide organization that supports trafficking survivors and advocates for systemic change.
“The numbers we see publicly are only a fraction of the young people who are exploited, groomed or at risk,” Ferranto said.
Traffickers no longer need to approach young people in person, she said. Online platforms allow predators to communicate directly with children while concealing their identities and intentions.
“They don’t need to be physically present anymore,” Ferranto said. “They reach kids through apps, games and social media. That’s why early education and community awareness are essential.”
Traffickers may initially offer friendship, attention, money, gifts, housing or emotional support. The relationship can gradually become controlling after the trafficker obtains personal information, photographs or other material that can be used to threaten or manipulate the victim.
Ferranto’s organization, formerly known as Meet Me at the Well Delaware, provides individualized support to trafficking survivors and advocates for improvements in Delaware’s social and judicial systems.
Delaware numbers show only identified cases
The National Human Trafficking Hotline identified 32 trafficking cases involving 61 victims in Delaware during 2024, the most recent full year for which state-level figures are available.
Those cases included 19 involving sex trafficking, seven involving labor trafficking and six involving both sex and labor trafficking.
The identified victims included at least 18 adults and 11 minors. Demographic information was not available for every victim.
Since 2007, the hotline has identified 301 Delaware trafficking cases involving 662 victims.
Those figures do not measure the full prevalence of trafficking in Delaware. They reflect only cases reported to or identified by the hotline.
Advocates and law enforcement officials say fear, financial dependency, language barriers, immigration concerns and isolation can prevent victims from asking for help.
The Crystal Spa investigation illustrates why trafficking can be difficult to detect. The business operated along a heavily traveled commercial corridor surrounded by stores, offices, homes and legitimate service businesses.
To people passing by, there may have been little outward indication of what police now allege was happening inside.
Potential warning signs can include workers who appear fearful, cannot speak privately, live at their workplace, work unusually long hours, lack control of their identification or money, or appear to be closely monitored by another person.
Anyone in immediate danger should call 911.

title: USDA union leaders rally against proposed DC downsizing
text: A group of current and former U.S. Department of Agriculture employees are calling on the Trump administration to halt the mandated relocation of more than 2,500 employees from its Washington, D.C., headquarters to five regional offices across the country. In an online briefing hosted by federal union leaders Thursday, speakers said the reorganization process USDA Secretary Brooke Rollins has led will amount to widespread layoffs, as many workers will choose not to relocate across the country. Rollins' effort, launched one year ago Friday, would move department staff away from the nation’s capital. The department should have no more than 2,000 employees in the region, according to a July 2025 memo Rollins signed. Kevin Shea, former acting secretary of the USDA under President Joe Biden, said the relocation could impact the department’s ability to carry out its core services such as fighting pests and diseases, protecting forest land and ensuring food safety. “All of this requires an adequate and qualified workforce,” he said. “These new proposed actions, added to the damage already done, all but ensures that we'll not have one.”Department layoffsSince President Donald Trump returned to office last year, the USDA has lost more than 20,000 employees,  according to Office of Personnel Management data. Most left through early retirement or buyouts offered by the U.S. Doge Service, union officials said. But speakers Thursday warned that thousands more will choose to leave instead of relocating across the country to a regional USDA office. Those offices, as outlined in Rollins’ July 2025 memo, include Raleigh, North Carolina, Kansas City, Missouri, Indianapolis, Indiana, Fort Collins, Colorado and Salt Lake City, Utah. In that memo, she wrote that the relocation will ensure that the USDA is “closer to the people it serves while achieving savings to the American taxpayer.” But most USDA staff already work outside the nation’s capital. The department had about 4,600 employees in Washington when Rollins announced the reorganization efforts last year. A majority of the staff reductions have come from across the country. ‘A forced choice’Genny Kotyk, a Forest Service employee and president of the National Federation of Federal Employees’ Forest Service Council, said the impacts of federal cuts are already being felt. She said that the employee reductions and reorganizations of the Forest Service, which is the largest U.S. firefighting agency, are affecting the response to the damaging wildfire season currently impacting Canada and some Midwestern and northern states. In 2025, the Forest Service saw more than 6,500 employees leave through a combination of layoffs, buyouts and early retirements, according to OPM. “We're looking to lose, potentially, another 6,500 employees that are going to be forced to either change their job duties, have a longer commute, or move completely across the country, or resign, or retire,” she said. “Forty percent of those employees have some kind of fire qualification, and because they're higher level staff, they typically also have a more seasoned career and have higher level fire qualifications.”Kotyk said that her union polled nearly 3,000 of its bargaining unit employees about the reorganization, and only 7% said they’d be willing to relocate. Chearice Vaughn, who works for a USDA office that oversees grants and loans for rural development projects, said she and 45 members of her team received a notice to relocate from Washington to Dallas, Texas. She said of those who received relocation notices, 86% were people of color. “It's a forced choice: uproot your entire life, or leave federal service,” Vaughn, also president of the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees Local 3870, said. Still, she said, it's not about “45 names on a spreadsheet in Washington.”“It's about whether the next little town waiting on clean water gets it in time,” she said. “It's about whether the next small business owner in a town with no other lender gets a chance at all. We built these things once. We're asking to be allowed to keep building them.”Legal challengeAlthough USDA is continuing with its relocations and department-wide reorganization, some employees are seeking to block the change. Several national labor unions, as part of their efforts over the past year to block the Trump administration’s reshaping of the federal government, filed a request for an injunction in federal court in San Francisco seeking to block USDA from ordering the relocations. The case is ongoing. USDA spokespeople did not return a message seeking comment Friday.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Surgeon General suggests high measles counts could be tied to abortion opposition
description: Florida Surgeon General Joseph Ladapo suggested Friday that opposition to abortion could have helped fuel a measles outbreak in Florida since many cases are tied to a private Roman Catholic college. Federal data show Florida had 141 confirmed measles cases as of July 23, ranking the state fifth in the nation for most infections. During […]
text:
Dr. Joseph Ladapo talks to reporters after the Florida Senate confirmed him as state surgeon general on Feb. 23, 2022. (Photo by Imani Thomas/Florida Phoenix)Florida Surgeon General Joseph Ladapo suggested Friday that opposition to abortion could have helped fuel a measles outbreak in Florida since many cases are tied to a private Roman Catholic college.
Federal data show Florida had 141 confirmed measles cases as of July 23, ranking the state fifth in the nation for most infections.
During a press conference in Orlando Friday, a reporter asked Ladapo about his level of concern about the measles cases and what he’d tell Florida families about the rising number of cases.
The surgeon general, long known for his vaccine skepticism, initially replied, “Oh no. Everyone’s got to take a vaccine.”
But he followed noting that “a lot of those cases” were reported at Ave Maria University, a private Roman Catholic college in Collier County. Ninety-three measles cases were reported in Collier County where the university is located.
“You know, for some people — people may or may not know that the measles vaccines is developed with the cells that are a progeny from … an aborted fetus, and you know whether there’s a connection between the fact that you know some of the students at this university chose not to receive that vaccine, and it happens to be a vaccine that is related to the practice of abortion, I’m not sure.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Measles vaccines are made from two cell strains that came from human fetal lung tissue in the 1960s. These original tissues were collected from elective abortions, and scientists used them to grow the live measles virus safely. These same fetal cells have continued to grow in the laboratory and are used to make vaccines today. No further sources of fetal cells are needed to make these vaccines.
 The Pontifical Academy for Life in 2017 issued updated moral considerations on vaccinations, telling Roman Catholic parents they should vaccinate their children for the good of the children and the community, and they can do so with a “clear conscience,” the Catholic Standard reported.
Ave Maria University did not immediately respond to Florida Phoenix’s requests for comment.
According to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, measles spreads through the air when a sick person coughs or sneezes. The virus can stay in the air for two hours after the infected person leaves. It is so contagious that about nine out of 10 people who come near a person with measles will become infected if not vaccinated.
The best way to avoid measles is with the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine. To stop the spread of the measles virus and for a population to be considered safe from infection, referred to as herd immunity, 95% of the population should be vaccinated.
According to the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, 89% of kindergarten students in the 2024-25 academic year were vaccinated against measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine series.
Meanwhile, Toluwalasè A. Ajayi, M.D., chair of the American Medical Association, urged families Friday to get vaccinated as the number of measles cases surge.
“The MMR vaccine has protected our communities for decades. There is no cure for measles, but vaccination is a safe and effective way to prevent it,” he said in a prepared statement. 
“Choosing to vaccinate protects not only you and your family, but also babies, people with weakened immune systems, and others who can’t be vaccinated. Protecting yourself helps protect your entire community. If you have questions about measles, please talk with your doctor.”
Ladapo and his boss—Gov. Ron DeSantis—tried unsuccessfully to change Florida law to make it easier for parents to turn down vaccines during the 2026 session.
It was killed by the Florida House. DeSantis, who is term limited out of office, promised to keep the issue on the front burner during his last months in the Governor’s mansion.
